title: Warm load_settings() still pays the full ADR-126 admission handshake on every call (TASK-32804.1 fixed only get_cli_setting)
trigger: The finder's deterministic sys.monitoring counts (console-cpu-profile/runs/*/counts.json) show exactly 1 load_settings body and 1 admission per credential-poll tick (idle: 20 ticks = 20 admissions), 1 per keystroke (30 keys + 7 ticks = 37), and 322 load_settings / 402 admissions across the first send. The callers are the 0.25 s set_interval poll, the DraftChanged handler, and the send dispatch, all on the loop.
cost: Measured warm load_settings at 13.5-16.8 ms/call at config depth 12, and ~21 ms at depth 16-20 (loaded host). get_cli_setting and load_cli_config_and_ensure_existence measured 0.0011-0.0018 ms. A load_settings nested inside an outer operation(config) measured 0.046 ms against 13.8 ms top-level, which confirms the cost is the handshake and not the cache. The finder's linear fit of ~4.8 ms/call at a real ~/.config/tldw_cli depth is plausible and matches TASK-32804.1's 4.8 ms figure for the pre-fix get_cli_setting.
fix: Mirror _warm_config_cache_hit: an unguarded load_settings wrapper checks the _SETTINGS_CACHE, _SETTINGS_CACHE_SOURCE and generation/external-edit stamp lock-free and returns on a hit. Only a miss or force_reload enters the @guarded rebuild. That is one change in the shared function, covering every caller. Pin it with the existing structural test plus a per-call admission counter of 0 on a warm hit (Tests/test_config_warm_read_no_handshake_task32804.py pattern).
fix_notes: guarded() enforces a function-name allowlist and a module-attribute identity check (getattr(config, fn.__name__) is wrapped). An unguarded outer load_settings therefore has to delegate misses to a guarded inner whose name is in config_participants.guarded's `allowed` set: either add a new name, or reuse the already-allowlisted _load_settings_uncached under _settings_rebuild_lock. Otherwise import raises ValueError('config_source_not_supported') or calls raise RecoveryRequired. Mirror the existing _cache_hit check exactly (_SETTINGS_CACHE non-None and _SETTINGS_CACHE_SOURCE == effective path; optionally also a _CONFIG_GENERATION stamp). Adding _external_edit_detected would be a behaviour change: today's load_settings hit does not stat the file. As with get_cli_setting, a warm hit will no longer raise storage_locally_paused during maintenance. Callers like _provider_readiness_app_config already fall back on any exception, so serving the cache is the same trade-off TASK-32804.1 accepted. Sibling cost worth folding in: get_user_data_dir is also @guarded with no fast path and measured 30-45 ms/call at the same depth (31 ms even when nested), because verified_user_data_directory re-pins directories every call. It is the root of F6 and F7. In-repo alternative precedent: ChatScreen._run_console_config_sync opens one operation(config) so that nested reads cost about 0.05 ms.
reason: config.py:1862-1924 on pin 840ed2ca58: load_settings is decorated @_config_participants.guarded and its _cache_hit() runs INSIDE that wrapper. config_participants.guarded (Backup_Recovery/config_participants.py:377-422) wraps every call in operation(source), which takes _settings_rebuild_lock and _config_file_lock and enters raw._scope, where the verified-parent and pinned-directory opens happen. So a warm hit pays the full ADR-126 handshake. TASK-32804.1 added _warm_config_cache_hit (config.py:6479) only in front of load_cli_config_and_ensure_existence, which get_cli_setting uses. load_settings has no equivalent. The task file's own notes scope the fix to get_cli_setting, and its AC#2 ('amortised per derivation or per scope') is still unmet for load_settings. That makes this new scope on an open task, not a duplicate. The hot caller is chat_screen.py:7700: _provider_readiness_app_config calls load_settings() whenever app.app_config has the [general]/[logging] marker sections, which is always true in production because app.py:7824 sets app_config = load_settings(). There are 85 load_settings() call sites repo-wide. I re-measured under isolation (HOME, XDG_* and TLDW_CONFIG_PATH in scratch, TLDW_TEST_MODE=1, 50-100 warm calls). The host was heavily loaded, load avg 14-42.

title: Idle Console burns 7.7-9.7% of a core on the 4 Hz credential-readiness poll
trigger: Yes. 4 Hz while the Console is the current screen (the default working screen), including fully idle. Covered or suspended screens pay only the timer wakeup because of the is_current gate.
cost: Per tick is about one warm load_settings admission: measured 13.5-21 ms at scratch depth, ~5 ms extrapolated to ~/.config/tldw_cli depth. That is ~20 ms/s, about 2% of a core, plus the readiness build, which is above the rubric's ~1% idle bar. The finder's 7.7-9.7% main-thread figure reflects the deeper probe path and a loaded host.
fix: F1 removes most of the per-tick cost. Beyond that, the TASK-32804.3 remainder applies: gate the rebuild on an expiry-aware revision (subscription cache versioning expires_at crossings), and stop and re-arm the timer in on_screen_suspend/on_screen_resume.
fix_notes: F1 removes nearly all of the per-tick cost. TASK-32804.3's notes warn that a revision-only gate would miss time-based credential expiry (status() flips on expires_at_ms with no revision bump). Keep the (revision, status) snapshot until anthropic_subscription exposes an expiry-aware version. Stopping on suspend needs a matching re-arm in on_screen_resume, because the timer is currently armed once in on_mount.
evidence:
self._console_credential_poll_timer = self.set_interval(
    0.25, self._poll_console_credential_readiness
)
# each tick: _active_console_settings_readiness_uncached -> _build_console_provider_selection
#   -> _provider_readiness_app_config -> load_settings() -> admission
reason: chat_screen.py:16947 arms set_interval(0.25, _poll_console_credential_readiness) in on_mount for the screen's whole life. It is stopped only at teardown (:17135), not on suspend. The tick at :11994-12022 returns early unless attached, reconciled and is_current. Otherwise it already runs inside _console_derivation_scope() (the TASK-32804.3 partial fix), so each tick costs exactly one load_settings admission. The finder's deterministic counts agree: idle_console window, 20 poll ticks = 20 admissions = 20 load_settings bodies. TASK-32804.3 is open (In Progress) and its notes already record exactly this residual: '~49 ms -> ~8 ms/tick', a remaining expiry-aware revision gate, and a remaining on_screen_suspend/on_screen_resume re-arm. The finding's only new lever is that the residual per-tick cost is the load_settings handshake, which is F1's content. No new scope is left for this finding, so it is known.

title: First send spends 6.5-11.8 s before the provider call; the Console UI sync passes run with no derivation scope and saturate the loop with ~400 admissions
trigger: Every send. The first send runs 11 sync passes (counts.json send_0). In the finder's fake-gateway runs, later sends show only 1 pass because the run finishes in under 0.2 s. With real multi-second streaming, the 0.2 s transcript poll runs a full pass at 5 Hz for the whole run, so the cost is also a per-tick streaming tax, not just a pre-dispatch one.
cost: Admission count is deterministic (402 per first send, 136-152 on later sends). Per-admission cost measured 13.5-21 ms at probe depth, ~5 ms at production depth, so roughly 1.5-2 s of loop CPU per first send and ~0.7 s per later send at production depth. That is consistent with the finder's scaled estimate. The 6.5-11.8 s wall figures are inflated by a host at load avg 14-42, and they also include F5 and F6 costs.
fix: Wrap _sync_native_console_chat_ui, _sync_console_rail_and_controls, _sync_console_mode_bar and the Enter dispatch/turn-context build in _console_derivation_scope() so each pass pays at most one config read, with F1 making that read free. While a run is active, have _poll_transcript skip the provider/readiness legs; readiness cannot change mid-stream except via the credential poll.
fix_notes: Do NOT wrap the whole async _sync_native_console_chat_ui in _console_derivation_scope(). The memo is a screen instance attribute, not task-local, and it is re-entrant, so any handler interleaving during the pass's awaits (keystrokes, the credential poll) would silently reuse the tick's memo. That would defeat the poll's expiry detection and break the PR #660 rule that rail visibility is computed fresh after the awaits, since session tabs can create or activate a session. Scope only the synchronous segments. Alternatively make the memo task-scoped like _workspace.tick_workspace_build_scope (TASK-22201), or extend the existing _run_console_config_sync operation(config) wrapper to the other synchronous legs (mode bar, live-work rows, final rail state), never across an await since it holds the rebuild and file locks. Having _poll_transcript skip readiness legs mid-run is risky: build_console_settings_readiness takes active_run=, and the mode bar and run chip must track VALIDATING->STREAMING->terminal each tick. With F1 landed, most of the residual cost disappears anyway.
evidence:
async def _sync_native_console_chat_ui(self) -> None:   # no _console_derivation_scope()
    ...await self._character_context.refresh_if_scope_changed()
    ...self._sync_console_rail_and_controls() / _sync_console_mode_bar() / _current_console_rail_state()
self._console_transcript_sync_timer = self.set_interval(0.2, _poll_transcript)
# only 3 `with self._console_derivation_scope()` exist in chat_screen.py (9622, 12012, 21965)
reason: chat_screen.py:18645 `async def _sync_native_console_chat_ui` has no _console_derivation_scope(). Repo-wide grep finds exactly 3 `with self._console_derivation_scope()` sites (chat_screen.py:9622, 12012, 21965) and none in Console_Modules. Inside the pass, _sync_console_rail_and_controls already runs under one operation(config) via _run_console_config_sync (:21750-21796), so its nested reads are cheap (measured 0.046 ms against 13.8 ms). The finder missed that. But the other legs run outside both the memo and the operation: _sync_console_mode_bar (:18587, full _build_console_control_state, then provider selection with its own scope, so 1 admission per call), _sync_console_live_work_readiness_rows, _sync_console_settings_recovery_surfaces, _character_context.refresh_if_scope_changed (F5), and the final _current_console_rail_state() at :18769, which rebuilds the full inspector state. The 0.2 s _poll_transcript at :18947 awaits the whole pass on every tick while any run is active or in flight. prompt_queue.py:878 dispatch is an async coroutine on the loop that calls the blocked-reason accessors and the capture_configuration lambda (session._build_console_turn_execution_context) synchronously. The finder's deterministic counts for send_0 are 402 admissions, 322 load_settings, 11 sync passes and 188 uncached provider selections. No open task covers the sync-pass scope gap; TASK-32804 is only the umbrella.

title: Each typing pause fires a 250-415 ms loop stall: debounced spend refresh rebuilds settings summary and inspector state outside any derivation scope
trigger: Yes. It fires once per idle typing pause of 0.2 s or more, which is extremely common, and after sends that edit the draft. It is cancelled while a run is active. Deterministic evidence: the finder's run2 typing phase with one SpendRefresh.refresh shows 60 admissions, against a 37 baseline for the same 30 keys + 7 ticks in run3. That is ~23 admissions for a single refresh.
cost: About 23 admissions per fire, at ~5 ms each at production depth, is ~115 ms plus derivation compute per typing pause (250-415 ms measured at probe depth on a loaded host). That is borderline P0 on this Mac, and larger on slower hosts. It collapses to low-P2 once F1 lands.
fix: Wrap ConsoleDraftSpendRefresh.refresh (or _sync_console_settings_summary plus _sync_console_cost_chip) in screen._console_derivation_scope(). Skip the inspector/agent-section rebuild when the inspector rail is hidden (see TASK-2902). F1 removes the remaining per-pass read cost.
fix_notes: Wrapping refresh() (synchronous, no awaits) in screen._console_derivation_scope(), or routing it through _run_console_config_sync, is safe and small. Skipping the inspector or agent-section rebuild while the rail is hidden conflicts with TASK-251's documented deviation in _sync_console_control_bar_under_config: tests assert the collapsed inspector's content stays fresh, and a hidden-rail skip broke them before. The agent-section payload needs rail_state.agent_open, so a cheaper visibility-only derivation would be needed rather than a straight skip.
evidence:
def _sync_console_settings_summary(self) -> None:
    self._apply_console_settings_summary_state(
        self._build_console_settings_summary_state()   # no derivation scope
    )
screen._console_draft_spend_refresh = ConsoleDraftSpendRefresh(
    schedule_timer=lambda delay, callback: screen.set_timer(delay, callback),
    sync_settings_summary=lambda: screen._sync_console_settings_summary(), ...)  # delay_seconds=0.2
reason: The chain was traced on the pin. chat_screen.py:20249: the composer's hidden Input.Changed handler calls _console_draft_spend_refresh.route_edit(run_active=...) on every draft mutation. console_spend_projection.py:370-406: when no run is active, ConsoleDraftSpendRefresh.schedule() replaces a 0.2 s set_timer (wired at wiring.py:2328), and refresh() at :404 calls screen._sync_console_settings_summary() and screen._sync_console_cost_chip() directly. They are not routed through _run_console_config_sync and not inside any derivation scope. _sync_console_settings_summary (:9378) builds readiness unscoped (_active_console_settings_readiness_uncached: session settings, provider selection with its own scope = 1 admission, and _provider_readiness_app_config = 1 admission). _apply_console_settings_summary_state then calls _sync_console_agent_section, whose Console_Modules/agent.py:1651 payload unconditionally calls _current_console_rail_state(), which rebuilds the full _build_console_inspector_state. _sync_console_cost_chip adds another unscoped provider display. No open task covers it.

title: Character-context publishes rebuild the whole inspector rail state (readiness included) on every begin/publish
trigger: Yes. On every _sync_native_console_chat_ui pass where the ChaChaNotes conversation or message revision moved, which is every send, run completion and conversation switch. It publishes at least twice per refresh.
cost: The finder sampled 3.0 s under refresh (split 1.38 s _begin and 1.62 s _publish) on the first send at probe depth under heavy host load. Each publish is a full inspector-state derivation with several uncached load_settings admissions, ~5 ms each at production depth, so tens to low hundreds of ms per send. That is P1 as a component of F3's total.
fix: Only recompute rail visibility when the character state field that drives it changed (compare old and new state). Build the rail state from a memoized derivation, via _console_derivation_scope() around the presentation sync. Skip it entirely for the PHASE-only _begin publish.
fix_notes: The category is a repeated derivation and config read, not rendering, so it is reclassified from render to caching. Skipping the rail recompute for the _begin (PHASE/loading-only) publish looks safe: the code comment says rail visibility depends on the settled recent-chat result. Verify that _build_console_rail_state does not read the character state's loading or phase fields first. Wrapping the presentation sync (synchronous) in _console_derivation_scope() is safe. It must not be widened across refresh()'s awaits, for the same instance-memo reason given in F3.
evidence:
def _sync_character_context_presentation(screen, state):
    widget.sync_state(state) ... rail.sync_character_context(state)
    current_rail_state = screen._current_console_rail_state()   # full inspector state
    screen._sync_console_rail_visibility_if_changed(current_rail_state)
# character_context._begin() and ._publish() both call self._state_changed(state)
reason: wiring.py:204 _sync_character_context_presentation (wired as state_changed at wiring.py:1241) ends with screen._current_console_rail_state() plus _sync_console_rail_visibility_if_changed on every publish. character_context.py:285 _publish calls it, and _begin (:289) publishes a phase-only state before every refresh, so each refresh() makes 2+ full rail and inspector derivations outside any scope or operation. _current_console_rail_state (chat_screen.py:13957) always builds _build_console_inspector_state when none is passed. New evidence that strengthens frequency: the scope fingerprint includes get_character_conversation_search_revision(), and the DB triggers (DB/recovery_operations.py:774-781) bump that revision on every conversations and messages INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. The refresh therefore re-fires on the sync pass after essentially every send (message persist), not only on the first send or a conversation switch. Callers: chat_screen.py:18730 (the every-tick native sync), :23835, character_context.py:984 and 1316, and Widgets/Console/console_character_context.py:130.

title: First send cold-builds the RAG ConfigProfileManager on the event loop via an eager rag_defaults.top_k, even with RAG unused
trigger: Yes. The first Console send of each process with the agent or native path. RAG does not need to be used, because the top_k is computed eagerly regardless.
cost: In isolation on a heavily loaded host (load avg 33-42), the first library_rag_profile_top_k() took 1.75-2.24 s (plus 260-560 ms import) and the second took 0.01 ms. The finder saw 794 ms sampled and 1003 ms cProfile. At production depth on an idle host this is plausibly 150-300 ms, once per process: a first-send stall.
fix: Resolve top_k lazily, only when auto-retrieve or the RAG chip actually runs: pass the accessor into the turn context, or compute it in the retrieval leg. Alternatively warm get_profile_manager() in a thread during deferred startup.
fix_notes: The turn execution context is a captured snapshot. Resolving top_k lazily in the retrieval leg is fine only if that leg runs off-loop, and it slightly changes the capture-at-send semantics. The simplest safe options are warming get_profile_manager() via asyncio.to_thread or deferred startup (it is lock-guarded), or fixing the root: stop 12x guarded get_user_data_dir in RAGConfig.__post_init__ by memoising default_chroma_persist_directory per construction, or via a get_user_data_dir fast path. Either also speeds the Library RAG and Settings surfaces.
reason: session.py:3611-3614: _build_console_turn_execution_context evaluates rag_defaults={'top_k': self._rag_top_k_accessor()} eagerly on every turn context. That accessor is chat_screen.py:7490, lambda: _console_library_rag_profile_top_k(), which leads through library_rag_state.py:663 library_rag_profile_top_k, then resolve_active_rag_top_k and _resolved_active_profile, to get_profile_manager() at config_profiles.py:1345. That is a process singleton, constructed on first use. It is reached synchronously from the loop via prompt_queue dispatch's capture_configuration lambda (wiring.py:2207). No boot or deferred-startup warmer exists: get_profile_manager() callers are only RAG services, the settings adapter, pipeline_loader and active_config. So a user who goes straight to Console and sends pays the construction on the loop. Root cause, measured with cProfile under isolation: ConfigProfileManager._load_builtin_profiles builds 12 RAGConfig objects whose __post_init__ calls default_chroma_persist_directory, which reaches the guarded get_user_data_dir. That is 13 get_user_data_dir, 67 acquire_storage, 104 operation() and ~21k posix.open for one construction.

title: Agent run bind resolves the full sensitive-path set twice per run, fanning out to ~17 guarded config accessors each time (3.6 s of the send critical path)
trigger: Yes. Every agent turn (the Console's default agent runtime path), on the agent worker thread, is on the send critical path before the provider request. That means added time-to-first-token and GIL contention, not a direct loop freeze.
cost: Measured resolve_sensitive_context at ~2.9 s per call and get_user_data_dir at 154 ms per call on a host at load avg 42, so these are heavily inflated. At lower load get_user_data_dir measured 42-46 ms at probe depth. At production depth, with ~20 get_user_data_dir x 2 resolves per bind, this is plausibly several hundred ms of worker latency per send. Call counts are deterministic.
fix: Resolve the SensitivePathContext once in bind() and pass it to every is_within call. is_within already accepts context=. Memoize the DB-path accessors per resolve (they all derive from one get_user_data_dir call). With an F1-style warm-hit bypass on the guarded path accessors, each resolve drops to about one admission.
fix_notes: Resolving the context once in _bind_under_scope and passing context= to both is_within calls is safe and halves the cost. Memoising the DB-path accessors per resolve needs a refactor, because each accessor also honours its own [database] *_db_path override through _get_custom_database_path; that part is already cheap via the get_cli_setting fast path. Only the get_user_data_dir leg is shareable. A get_user_data_dir warm fast path would fix this and F6 globally, but get_user_data_dir performs security-relevant directory verification (ownership and mode, pinned identity) and must not be bypassed casually.

            if not is_within(base, root):      # context=None -> resolve_sensitive_context()
            if not is_within(run_dir, root):   # again
# _sensitive_db_paths: for accessor_name in _DB_PATH_ACCESSOR_NAMES: accessor()
#   -> each get_*_db_path is @guarded -> get_user_data_dir (guarded) -> admission

A third call at :705 runs only when a legacy dir is migrated. is_within (Tools/file_operation_tools.py) passes context=None to is_sensitive_path, which calls resolve_sensitive_context() (sensitive_paths.py:610) each time. That calls get_user_data_dir, then _sensitive_db_paths (:355) looping ~13-15 config DB-path accessors that each call get_user_data_dir, and then the direct-child container dirs. No open task covers it.

title: Every keystroke still pays ~1.2 config admissions through the pristine-session stale-default check; the census test is blind to it
trigger: Yes. Every printable keystroke while the active session is pristine (first prompt of a blank chat). The finder's counts show 30 keys + 7 poll ticks = 37 admissions, so exactly 1 per key.
cost: One warm load_settings admission per key: measured 13.5-21 ms at probe depth, ~5 ms at production depth, plus the remaining derivation. That is roughly 6-9 ms per key at production depth, below the rubric's ≳10-20 ms P1 bar and limited to pristine sessions, so downgraded to P2. It is effectively F1's keystroke manifestation.
fix: F1 alone reduces this to about 0.1 ms per key. Add a per-key admission counter (config_participants.operation calls) to test_console_keystroke_work_census.py so the regression is pinned. Separately, fix that test's empty==loaded equality: it fails on context_estimate_max_rows 0 vs 1, below its own ≤1 bound.
fix_notes: F1 alone removes the admission. Adding a per-key admission counter to the census (count config_participants.operation entries via sys.monitoring; do not monkeypatch load_settings, because guarded() checks module-attribute identity) is a cheap regression pin. The 'empty==loaded equality' remark about context_estimate_max_rows is a test-correctness issue outside this perf audit and was not verified.
evidence:
# sampled chain per key (run G): _handle_console_composer_draft_edit
#  -> _sync_console_workbench_actions_from_draft (scope opened, memo empty)
#  -> _build_console_control_state -> _active_console_provider_model_display_uncached
#  -> session._ensure_active_console_session_settings -> _maybe_refresh_stale_default_console_settings
#  -> wiring.py:1488 provider_readiness_app_config -> load_settings() -> admission
reason: chat_screen.py:22872-22908: the @on(ConsoleComposerBar.DraftChanged) handler calls _sync_console_workbench_actions_from_draft (:21950), which opens one derivation scope with an empty memo per key. Its control-state build reaches session.py:3825 _maybe_refresh_stale_default_console_settings. In a pristine session (no user work, baseline == settings, and has_messages false) that calls self._provider_readiness_app_config() (wiring.py:1488 lambda to the screen method) BEFORE its _pristine_defaults_checked identity gate. The first read in the scope therefore pays one load_settings admission per key, and the rest are memo hits: 7.17 calls/key, 1 admission/key. Once the session has messages, the method returns earlier and this leg costs nothing, so the trigger is limited to composing the first prompt. The census test Tests/Performance/test_console_keystroke_work_census.py counts readiness builds, template builds and row traversals, but has no admission or load_settings counter; its only load_settings use is a setup force_reload. So the claim that it is blind to this cost holds. TASK-24454 (open) covers readiness on the keystroke path, but its '~30 ms per 43-key burst' cost statement is stale, because the per-key cost is now admission-dominated. That is new evidence.

title: Warm Console visit (reused screen) still restyles all 533 nodes on resume: 63% of a ~185 ms visit
corrected: tldw_chatbook/app.py:13595 (switch_screen on the reused instance); .venv textual/app.py:3022 (ScreenResume() defaults to refresh_styles=True); .venv textual/screen.py:1479-1480 (update_node_styles on resume); tldw_chatbook/UI/Navigation/screen_registry.py:84; tldw_chatbook/UI/Screens/chat_screen.py:23668 (on_screen_resume); tldw_chatbook/Chat/console_runtime.py:1508 via :3881 (unseen-marks read)
known_task: TASK-24452 (In Progress, but its re-mint premise is stale; remaining AC#7 moved to TASK-31520, which is Done). No open task covers the resume restyle. TASK-2902 (open) would shrink the tree. TASK-25811 (Won't Do) predates reuse.
trigger: Every navigation back to the Console: NavigateToScreen -> app.py:13595 switch_screen on the installed ChatScreen -> ScreenResume(refresh_styles=True) -> textual screen.py:1480 update_node_styles over the whole tree. Reproduced in a headless isolated app.
cost: measured: 537 nodes and 597 Stylesheet.apply calls per resume. The restyle alone took median 153.6 ms main-thread CPU (min wall 295 ms under DEBUG logging and a loaded box); the finder measured 123 ms. Whole warm visit: 196-240 ms main CPU. Unseen-marks read: about 10-16 ms on the loop.
fix: Skip the resume restyle when neither the stylesheet nor the theme generation changed since suspend. BaseAppScreen can record the generation in _on_screen_suspend and short-circuit update_node_styles in an overridden _on_screen_resume; that is medium risk, so verify with the theme editor. Otherwise shrink the tree: defer the hidden inspector rail and task surface (TASK-2902). Move the unseen-marks read off the loop.
fix_notes:
The mechanism is feasible with a small change. Textual's MRO dispatch (documented in base_app_screen.py:549-560) runs a subclass `_on_screen_resume` before Screen's, and ScreenResume.refresh_styles is a mutable dataclass field. A BaseAppScreen `_on_screen_resume(self, event)` that sets event.refresh_styles=False and does NOT call super would work. The skip key must cover more than the theme, though:
(1) app._css_update_count. It is bumped only by theme and ansi-dark changes, and refresh_css only re-stamps screens that are on the stack.
(2) A stylesheet rules/source generation. _load_screen_css adds CSS for newly built screens, and TieAwareStylesheet and theme-editor reparses change rules without bumping the count.
(3) App classes and pseudo-classes. WideViewportTierMixin.on_resize (app.py:7474) toggles `-wide-viewport` on the App, and App.update_styles(App) walks only screen_stack, so a suspended Console misses that change unless the resume restyle catches it.
(4) After a real restyle, stamp self._css_update_count yourself.
Tests needed: theme switch while away, a resize across WIDE_VIEWPORT_COLUMNS while away, theme-editor custom CSS, and first visit to a new screen before returning. Overriding a private Textual hook is pinned to <9 and needs a guard test. Shrinking the tree (TASK-2902) is lower risk but saves proportionally less. Moving the unseen-marks read off the loop must keep recompute_console_attention's revision/attention-lock fencing.

        self.update_node_styles(animate=False)   # 593 Stylesheet.apply over 533 widgets

title: ChaChaNotes execute_query wrapper adds ~15-20 us per statement (26x raw) and the list path logs INFO per call
corrected: tldw_chatbook/DB/ChaChaNotes_DB.py:3998 (execute_query), tldw_chatbook/DB/ChaChaNotes_DB.py:3449-3451 (_core_access in _get_thread_connection), tldw_chatbook/Backup_Recovery/participants.py:392 (_core_access body: imports + storage._lock per call), tldw_chatbook/DB/ChaChaNotes_DB.py:11216 (INFO line)
trigger: Every ChaChaNotes statement routed through execute_query, and every get_connection()/transaction() acquisition. Many of these run synchronously on the event loop during Console and Library use, at tens to hundreds of statements per visit or send. The INFO log fires only in list_all_active_conversations, whose 6 callers are all cold paths.
cost:
Measured: ~11 us of wrapper overhead per statement over the quiescent execute (12.8 vs 1.67 us). Breakdown:
- get_connection: 8.2 us, of which _core_access is ~4.2 us and the quiescence registry is the rest
- metrics (disabled): ~1.0 us
- lazy debug: ~0.4 us

That is ~1.1 ms per 100 statements. The INFO line adds ~7 us per call on cold paths only.
fix:
- Short-circuit `log_histogram`/`log_counter` before building label dicts when metrics are disabled.
- Skip `_core_access` on the hot `get_connection` path when the thread already holds a registered connection and the admission generation is unchanged (shares the F2 mechanism).
- Demote the per-call INFO lines in list methods to DEBUG.
fix_notes:
Metrics short-circuit: this saves only ~0.5-0.7 us per statement. Avoiding the label-dict literals entirely would need call-site guards, which is not worth it on its own.

The INFO -> DEBUG demotion is pure hygiene.

The real lever is _core_access. The generation-skip in the proposed fix is correctness-sensitive, so fix_risk is MEDIUM, not low. _core_access enforces backup/recovery admission: storage pause, retiring threads, operation provenance, and closed participants. A cached "thread already admitted" fast path is only safe if every pause, retire, close, or operation transition bumps a generation that the fast path reads, and it must still raise RecoveryRequired mid-recovery. Getting this wrong risks a borrower touching the DB during a restore, which is a data-integrity hazard.

Lower-risk first step: hoist the three function-local imports (participants import in get_connection; storage_admission and RecoveryRequired inside _core_access) to cached module refs, and memoise _repository_types(). Then pair the lock-free relaxed-flag approach with the TASK-31502 fix, and extend TASK-31502's scope or AC3 to name _core_access explicitly.
evidence:
per-call: raw SELECT 1 0.61 us | quiescent conn.execute 2.45 us | get_connection 9.5 us | execute_query 16.1 us
log_histogram(...labels={...}); log_counter(...)   # dict copies even with metrics disabled
logger.info(f"Found {len(conversations)} active conversations ...")  # list_all_active_conversations
reason:
The code exists as quoted. execute_query (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:3998) calls get_connection, runs `logger.opt(lazy=True).debug`, then log_histogram + log_counter with label dict literals. list_all_active_conversations (:11160) logs at INFO per call (:11216-11218).

I measured each layer (isolated env; scratch HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH; file DB in scratch; loguru null sink at INFO; metrics disabled):
- raw sqlite3 SELECT 1: 0.38 us
- quiescent conn.execute: 1.67 us
- _core_access(db) alone: 4.16 us
- get_connection(): 8.20 us
- execute_query("SELECT 1"): 12.80 us

execute_query is therefore ~34x raw and ~11 us over the quiescent execute. The metrics pair costs 0.96 us total with metrics disabled (is_metrics_logging_enabled returns early, after a _get_labels dict copy). The lazy debug costs 0.42 us. So logging and metrics are only ~1.4 us of the ~11 us, and the finder's `logging` category is wrong: the dominant cost is connection acquisition, which is `db-query` per-statement overhead.

get_connection's cost has two parts. One is the quiescence registry begin/finish_acquisition plus is_registered, which open TASK-31502 covers. The other is `_core_access` (Backup_Recovery/participants.py:392). Per statement it does:
- 3 function-local imports
- a _repository_types() call and participant validation
- an acquisition of the process-wide `storage._lock`

git log -S shows _core_access landed in get_connection on 2026-09-16 (b5251e9a6e, TASK-32628). That is AFTER TASK-31502 was filed and measured on 09-04 at 1.94 us per statement, so TASK-31502's description does not name it. It is new scope: ~4.2 us per statement, more than the whole quiescence tax TASK-31502 measured, plus a new process-wide lock contention point.

The INFO line is cold. list_all_active_conversations has 6 callers (ChatbookCreationWindow, Tools_Settings_Window, a chat_screen export/pager, ChatbookCreationWizard, MCP resources, RAG ingestion), none of them per-keystroke or per-send. It costs ~7 us to a null sink.

title: Each new private-SQLite connection on macOS/Linux forks a Python helper process, and run_owned_db_call retires the connection after every call
known_task: TASK-24457 (partial: Library per-visit connection churn only)
trigger: Yes. The fork happens on every first connection per thread for private-SQLite owners, and on every run_owned_db_call that opens a handle. 12 of these are synchronous on MainThread before _ui_ready (finder's run10 counts, consistent with the code).
cost: My probe: an open+close cycle through the helper adds about 63 ms wall (69 ms vs 5.8 ms on a persistent connection) and 38.5 ms of child CPU per fork at load ~30. That is consistent with the finder's ~45 ms child CPU per fork. 12 MainThread forks ≈ 0.5-0.8 s of boot critical path.
fix: Keep one persistent helper per process and send prepare requests over its pipe, instead of fork/exec per connection. Alternatively, cache the helper's prepare verdict per (path, st_dev, st_ino, mtime) for the process lifetime and re-verify with fstat. Give run_owned_db_call a small dedicated executor whose threads retain their connections. Coordinate with the backup/recovery owners: this is a security boundary.
fix_notes: High risk: the per-request, isolated (-I -S) helper is a deliberate security boundary (it validates the artifacts without opening their inodes in-process). A persistent helper changes its isolation model, and an inode/mtime verdict cache weakens the TOCTOU re-verification it exists for. Both need the Backup_Recovery/private-sqlite owners' sign-off. The lowest-risk lever is to reduce the number of connection opens: give run_owned_db_call a dedicated executor that retains handles, registered with the quiescence registry so backup pause can still retire them. That leaves the per-open security check intact.

title: Backup-maintenance monitor polls a 36-open filesystem admission probe at 10 Hz forever via asyncio.to_thread
trigger: Yes. The loop polls 10 times per second for the whole app lifetime, off-loop via to_thread, but with about 4 loop handle runs per poll (task, to_thread future, shield, sleep).
cost: My isolated probe: 34 open + 2 flock per probe, 1.03 ms thread CPU at load ~18, so about 1% of a core in the executor. The finder's run10 bench shows 1.29 ms thread CPU per call. Add about 40 loop handle runs/s and 10 self-pipe wakeups/s. This is borderline against the >~1% P0 idle threshold (under 1% on a quiet machine), so it stays P1.
fix: Keep the gate fds open and probe only with flock(LOCK_SH|LOCK_NB), which is 1-2 syscalls with no registry parse or root realpath. Recompute _groups/_tokens only when registry.lock's inode/mtime changes. Drop the cadence to 0.5-1 s, or block a daemon thread on a kqueue/inotify watch of the admission dir and post to the loop only on change. Keep the 'responsive poll' tests from TASK-32562 green.
fix_notes: Lowering the cadence to 0.5-1 s delays a backup's pause acknowledgment by at most that much, well inside the settle (30 s) and admission (60 s) deadlines, but re-run the TASK-32562 'responsive poll' tests. Keeping gate fds open must still detect gate-file replacement or remap and keep raising admission_scope_changed and remap_recovery_required, so compare fstat identity (and _observe_gate) on each probe. A kqueue/inotify watcher is a larger, platform-specific change; Windows has a separate path.

    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    requested = await _poll_local_pause_requested()   # create_task(asyncio.to_thread(storage._local_pause_requested)) + shield

title: Scheduler tick resolves default_emergency_stop_path() -> get_user_data_dir() on the event loop every 30 s

The chain continues tick -> _dispatch_due:631 -> _emergency_stopped -> default_emergency_stop_path() before the first await.
cost: Measured in isolation at load 16-35: default_emergency_stop_path 53-55 ms CPU per call (1,620 open, 51 listdir, 52 flock), and the same inside execution_scope. There are also 2 synchronous execution_scope entries of ~7.9 ms each in the same handle. Total loop stall is about 40-70 ms per tick. The heartbeat path adds ~55 ms of CPU in a thread per tick, contending for the GIL.
fix: Pass emergency_stop_path= and heartbeat_path= into SchedulerLoop at app.py:10587, resolved once off-loop. Alternatively, move the path resolution inside the _offload callable.
fix_notes: Do NOT resolve the paths at SchedulerLoop construction in app.py:10587. That runs in App.__init__, before first paint, adding ~2x50 ms to boot, and it freezes a path that cannot follow a data_dir or profile change. TASK-32562 also showed that default_emergency_stop_path can raise RecoveryRequired under native maintenance intent, so resolution must stay inside the fail-safe try. The safe minimal change is to move resolution into the offloaded callable, e.g. `await self._offload(lambda: is_emergency_stopped(self._emergency_stop_path or default_emergency_stop_path()))`. Exceptions still propagate into the try and read as stopped. Then memoise the resolved path off-loop, invalidated on config generation or profile change. Offloading alone still burns ~50 ms CPU per tick in a thread. Apply the same memo to default_heartbeat_path. Separately, the doubled execution_scope per tick (run() plus the tick decorator) is redundant admission on the loop.
reason: Code matches the quote. loop.py:599-602 calls default_emergency_stop_path() synchronously before `await self._offload(...)`, and the result is never cached. app.py:10587 builds SchedulerLoop(...) with neither emergency_stop_path= nor heartbeat_path=, and no caller anywhere in tldw_chatbook passes either one (grep count is 0). Call chain: app.py:16261 `run_worker(self.scheduler_loop.run(), exclusive=True, group='scheduling')` is a coroutine worker, not a thread. The comment there says it is deliberately kept on the loop. Each iteration runs `await self.tick()` (every poll_interval, default 30 s, and earlier on reload_event), then @_admitted_dispatch, then _dispatch_due:631, then _emergency_stopped, then default_emergency_stop_path, then config.get_user_data_dir. get_user_data_dir takes the fast verified_user_data_directory path only when a config_participants operation is active; execution_scope does not set one. Measured in an isolated env with an audit hook guard (real profile confirmed unchanged afterwards): get_user_data_dir took 46.8 ms CPU median, default_emergency_stop_path 53.5 ms, with 1,620 open, 51 listdir and 52 flock per call. Called INSIDE execution_scope it was still 55 ms. is_emergency_stopped(path) itself costs 0.01 ms. A sibling issue the finder missed makes the single handle longer: execution_scope (acquire_storage) runs synchronously on the loop twice per tick, once in run() at :461-464 and again in @_admitted_dispatch at :44-47, measuring ~7.9 ms each. Everything up to the first await runs in one handle, so each tick stalls the loop for roughly 40-70 ms, always on for the app's lifetime. default_heartbeat_path, run in the thread at :568, costs another ~55 ms CPU per tick. No open task covers this. TASK-32562 (In Progress) only moved the resolution inside the fail-safe try, for a correctness reason. Upgraded to P1 because the rubric lists per-tick/timer ≳10-20 ms as P1, and this is a 40-70 ms single-handle stall every 30 s that shows up as a periodic hitch while typing or streaming.

title: @recovery_review.unqualified runs acquire_storage synchronously at the entry of every wrapped provider call (55 entry points)
corrected: tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls/recovery_review.py:77-84 (_ordinary_operation), :109-117 (async wrapper), :331-338 (_Operation.__init__ acquire_storage+_history), :476-478 (_using re-runs check/_history), :462-469 (_identity keyed on current_task); tldw_chatbook/Chat/console_provider_gateway.py:3736,4612,4914,5093,7186; tldw_chatbook/Chat/local_server_discovery.py:483,556
trigger: There are 2 wrapped calls per llama.cpp-family Console send: resolve_for_send -> resolve_llamacpp, then stream_chat -> stream_llamacpp_chat, both awaited on the app loop. The first-run/unconfigured setup card runs discovery as a coroutine worker (chat_screen.py:15437-15471) with 11 admissions. The settings modal probe (console_settings_modal.py:943) runs per click, and the catalog refresh runs at startup.
cost: Measured in isolation at load 16: 7.8 ms CPU per wrapped async call; 79 ms of loop CPU for 10 gathered probes. The finder measured 4.2 ms at load 10 for _ordinary_operation alone (excluding the duplicate check).
fix: Skip the admission when no recovery history exists (the common case), using a negative result cached per config generation. Alternatively, acquire the operation in asyncio.to_thread before entering the wrapped coroutine. F1's amortized admission reduces it too.
fix_notes: 'Skip admission when no recovery history' is NOT safe. The acquire_storage lease is the backup/restore maintenance fence, not just a history read, so skipping it lets provider I/O run during a restore. Acquiring in asyncio.to_thread is risky too: storage_admission keeps thread-local state (_operation_local, admission._local.admitted), and a lease acquired on a worker thread would then be used and closed on the loop thread. Lower-risk wins: drop the redundant check()/_history immediately after construction in _using; let gathered child tasks inherit the parent operation, so discover_local_servers pays 1 admission instead of N+1; amortise admission across a send (resolve plus stream). Keep fix_risk at medium-high.
reason: Code confirmed. In the async wrapper (recovery_review.py:109-117), `_ordinary_operation()` runs synchronously before the first await. It builds _Operation, which calls acquire_storage(path) and then _history(path, lease) (lines 331-338). _using() at :476-478 then calls operation.check(), which runs _history AGAIN straight after construction. _identity() at :462-469 includes asyncio.current_task(), so child tasks created by asyncio.gather never reuse the parent's operation. There are 55 `_provider_recovery.unqualified` sites, but only 10 are async and so reach the loop. The other 45 (chat_with_*, summarize_with_*) are sync functions that run in worker threads, so the '55 entry points' framing overstates loop exposure. On-loop async sites: console_provider_gateway resolve_llamacpp (3736), stream_llamacpp_chat (4612), complete_llamacpp_chat (4914), _post_without_high_level_http_log (5093), _is_reachable (7186); local_server_discovery probe_models_endpoint (483) and discover_local_servers (556); realtime connect ×2; refresh_stale_configured_providers (app.py:15161, the model catalog refresh). Triggers traced: resolve_for_send -> _resolve_for_send_unclassified:4226 -> resolve_llamacpp, plus stream_chat:6013 -> stream_llamacpp_chat. That is 2 full admissions per llama.cpp-family Console send, and stream_chat is awaited in the controller coroutine on the app loop. chat_screen._maybe_start_console_local_discovery runs discover_local_servers as a coroutine worker whenever the setup modal blocks (first run or unconfigured), which costs 1 + N admissions because the gathered probes each run in their own task. Measured in isolation: the full wrapper on an async no-op took 7.8 ms CPU (acquire_storage+close 4.6 ms, _history 1.3 ms), and 10 gathered wrapped no-ops took 79 ms of loop CPU. The finder's boot probe shows probe_models_endpoint first-step handles of 34-94 ms. No open task covers this. Kept at P2: about 15 ms per send is split across 2 handles and applies only to llama.cpp-family providers, and the discovery burst happens only on unconfigured or first-run launches.

However, start_async_lifecycles' docstring says the independence from preview creation is deliberate, so check for pinning tests first. Keep the 0.25 s prompt-revoke latency while a preview or gateway is live. Driving the watcher from a config publish or generation signal is better, but it must still catch external edits to the config file.

self._start_canvas_policy_watcher()   # in __init__ and start_async_lifecycles (app.on_mount)
while not self._canvas_maintenance_closed:
    reader = asyncio.create_task(asyncio.to_thread(self._canvas_enabled))
    enabled = await asyncio.shield(reader)

title: Always-on 2 Hz widget polls plus a 10 Hz watchdog thread keep the idle process waking
trigger: The nav bar is mounted on every screen and the Console rails for the Console screen's lifetime. Textual intervals keep firing on background screens; the nav bar returns early there. The watchdog thread starts with the heartbeat at app.py:11942.
cost: Estimated from the code; the finder measured 0.004-0.018 ms of work per tick. The cost is wakeups (about 6 per second on the loop and 10 per second on the thread), not CPU.
fix: Drive the progress counts from the progress-changed message or reactive, and overflow hints from on_resize/scroll events (the signature gate already exists). Have the watchdog block on an Event armed by the heartbeat instead of sleep-polling.
fix_notes: The watchdog must not depend on the heartbeat to wake it, because the heartbeat is exactly what stops during a stall. Keep a timeout. Replace the fixed 0.1 s sleep with Event.wait(timeout=(last_heartbeat + limit) - now) so the thread sleeps until the stall deadline, which is about 1 wakeup per heartbeat instead of 10 per second. Moving the progress counts to message or reactive updates would also remove the timer that TASK-32639 and TASK-32517 are about. For overflow hints, on_resize already exists; scroll changes would also need a hook.

self.set_interval(0.5, self._sync_progress_counts)
self._progress_timer = self.set_interval(0.5, self._sync_progress_count)
_watch_loop: while not closed: time.sleep(min(0.1, stall_threshold_ms/2000)) ...

It is enabled by default (diagnostics.ui_responsiveness_enabled defaults to True) and armed at app.py:11942. The open tasks TASK-32639 and TASK-32517 touch the left-rail progress timer only for correctness (a crash or query before mount), not for perf. P3 is correct.

title: croniter import on the app import path forks `file -b <python>` via platform.architecture()
corrected: tldw_chatbook/Scheduling/db/scheduled_tasks_db.py:19; tldw_chatbook/Scheduling/services/scheduling_service.py:20 (second boot-path import the finder missed); tldw_chatbook/app.py:487,493

fix_notes: The croniter import must be made function-level in BOTH scheduled_tasks_db.py and scheduling_service.py, the same ADR-097 pattern schedule_compute already uses. Deferring in one file alone is a no-op for boot. The UI forms that import croniter are screen-lazy. Deferring also takes croniter (and possibly dateutil) out of the ui_ready module census, which helps the ratchet headroom tracked in TASK-32644/TASK-31816. Do not pre-seed platform.architecture; that is a hack against library internals. If needed, the first scheduler tick after _ui_ready will load croniter off first paint.
evidence:
from croniter import croniter
# croniter/croniter.py:54 `if is_32bit():` -> platform.architecture() -> subprocess.check_output(['file','-b', sys.executable])

title: load_settings() cache hit still pays the full ADR-126 admission handshake (381 fd opens, 9-40 ms) and is on the keystroke, idle-poll and Console-visit paths
known_task: TASK-32804.3 (poll; In Progress, residual ~8 ms/tick acknowledged) + TASK-32804.1 (In Progress; fast path applied to get_cli_setting only) + TASK-24454 (keystroke readiness recompute). TASK-32562's notes also record 'load_settings itself guarded, even cache hits acquire' without a fix. New scope: load_settings warm-hit root cause plus the keystroke and visit paths.
trigger: yes: 0.25 s set_interval credential poll -> _active_console_settings_readiness -> session._ensure_active_console_session_settings / _build_console_provider_selection -> _provider_readiness_app_config -> load_settings, running for as long as Console is the current screen. Composer and derivation paths outside the 3 derivation scopes also reach it.
cost: yes (isolated microbench): 11.6-15.2 ms and 609 opens per warm load_settings hit, vs 0.001 ms for the fast-pathed get_cli_setting. The finder's 381 opens was counted at a narrower edge; the cost holds either way.
fix:
- Give load_settings the same lock-free warm-hit fast path that TASK-32804.1 gave load_cli_config_and_ensure_existence: rename the guarded body to _load_settings_guarded, and make a thin unguarded load_settings that checks _SETTINGS_CACHE / _SETTINGS_CACHE_SOURCE / _CONFIG_GENERATION / _external_edit_detected exactly like _warm_config_cache_hit (config.py:6481) before falling through.
- In session.py:3874, test the pristine-defaults memo / has_user_work before fetching config.
- Memoize _provider_readiness_app_config per config generation instead of per derivation pass.
- Add a warm load_settings benchmark pin, and count config admissions in the keystroke census.
fix_notes: (1) guarded() has a hard allowlist of function names (config_participants.py ~377-393) and requires getattr(config, name) to be the wrapped object. A renamed _load_settings_guarded must be added to that allowlist and installed at module level under its own name, or it raises ValueError('config_source_not_supported') at import. title: Automatic gen-2 GC pauses of 272-871 ms fire about every second screen visit; no gc.freeze or threshold policy anywhere
trigger: plausible and consistent: allocation-heavy screen visits (Console re-mints ~559 widgets, TASK-24452) and boot push survivors past the 3.12 25%-of-long-lived gen-2 heuristic. Frequency is taken from the finder's gc.callbacks measurement.
cost: partially: the per-object full-collection cost was measured in isolation (~205 ns/object at load 16, 347k objects = 71 ms), extrapolated to the finder's heap sizes. The in-app pause list (272-871 ms) was not re-run.
fix:
- After _ui_ready (app.py:16160), and again when the pre-import pass finishes (app.py:17105), call gc.collect() then gc.freeze(). That moves the ~0.6-1.4M boot-resident objects (module dicts, classes, functions, CSS RuleSets) out of every later collection.
- Consider raising the gen0 threshold (gc.set_threshold) so screen mounts are not collected mid-compose.
- TASK-31966 AC#2 requires an ADR for a global GC policy. Re-measure with the same 3-round tour and gc.callbacks probe.
fix_notes: gc.collect()+gc.freeze() after _ui_ready (app.py:16160) freezes only the ~0.56M boot-resident objects. The ~0.8-1.0M objects added by a screen tour stay collectable, so post-tour pauses shrink by roughly a third, not to zero. Find out why the heap grows 564k -> 1.5M (retained screens or caches) before, or alongside, any GC policy. After freeze, long_lived_total drops, so under the 3.12 heuristic gen-2 runs more often but each run is cheaper; re-measure the frequency too. Anything cyclic that is frozen is never reclaimed, hence collect first. freeze after the pre-import pass can be called from its thread (the effect is process-wide), but the pass runs paced and parks during navigation, so hook its completion rather than a timer. Raising gen0 thresholds trades memory for fewer pauses. TASK-31966 AC#2 requires an approved ADR before any global GC policy.

title: Storage admission re-verifies directory chains per operation: 207k open() + 205k close() syscalls and 572 acquire_storage calls to reach _ui_ready
trigger: yes: every guarded config read/write, DB open and raw participant scope, from boot onward, both on the loop and in pools.
cost: partially: the per-admission open counts (609 / 1,620 per call) were reproduced in isolation. The whole-boot cProfile totals (207k opens, 572 acquire_storage calls) were not re-run but are consistent.
fix:
- Amortize admission per generation: cache verified directory pins as (dirfd, st_dev, st_ino) per admission generation and re-open relative to a held root dirfd instead of re-walking from the filesystem root.
- Memoize qualified_for / startup_permission / _registry results per generation.
- Keep the per-operation check to a single fstat of the pinned fd.
- Owners: the ADR-126 / TASK-32562 backup stream. Add a boot-phase syscall/admission budget guard.
fix_notes: High risk. The per-op re-walk from / is how ADR-126/127 catch an ancestor renamed or swapped by a symlink (TOCTOU). A cached dirfd plus a single fstat keeps pointing at the old inode after an ancestor rename, so it does not preserve that check; re-validating (st_dev, st_ino) against a lexical lstat of each ancestor would. Two lower-risk levers come first. (a) Scope amortization: hold one admission across a batch, such as the TldwCli.__init__ wiring block or one Console derivation pass; nested ops are measured at ~free. (b) Memoize _registry/startup_permission/qualified_for per bootstrap-record generation, since these are file reads keyed by records that change only via backup/restore. Any change needs the ADR-126 owner (TASK-32562 stream), whose notes explicitly disallow speculative caches, plus native Windows re-qualification.
evidence:
cProfile, 1 warm boot to _ui_ready (all threads):
  posix.open 207,141 calls (3.2 s self); posix.close 205,537
  storage_admission.acquire_storage 572 calls, 10.3 s cumulative
  private_paths._open_directory_component 109,864 calls, 7.0 s
  bootstrap.pinned_directory 12,366 calls, 4.0 s; _registry 2,999 calls, 3.9 s
  qualification.qualified_for 1,144 calls, 4.5 s; bootstrap.startup_permission 1,222 calls, 3.6 s
reason: Code at the cited lines matches. private_paths.py:434 _open_verified_parent opens the filesystem anchor and walks every component with openat via _open_directory_component (line 206). bootstrap.py:33-41 pinned_directory re-runs that walk for each pin. storage_admission.py:835 acquire_storage builds a fresh _Acquisition per call. Nothing amortizes across operations: each outermost config_participants.operation() re-verifies from /. My isolated probe matches the per-op multiplier: 609 open events per warm load_settings (one admission) and 1,620 per get_user_data_dir (4 admissions). Ten load_settings calls nested inside one already-held operation cost the same as one, so only the outermost admission pays and scope-level amortization is effective. This is the shared root cause behind F1 and F2 and every other guarded op. TASK-32562 (In Progress, the backup stream) independently measured '100 cached config reads 1.351s: 500 redundant path admissions 1.143s, 83,000 native opens' and on Windows '264 acquisitions 27.97s', but records 'no cache/guard change approved or in progress'. No perf task owns it. Kept at P1 rather than P0 because its user-visible stalls are already filed as F1/F2; this is the structural lever behind them.

title: MCP visit: every MCP store read pays a full storage admission on the event loop (~240 per visit)
known_task: TASK-32804 (umbrella only; no specific open task; TASK-32804.7 Done covered config reads, not store admission)
trigger: Every MCP destination visit. MCPScreen is non-reusable, so each visit mounts a new MCPWorkbench whose _start_initial_load runs reload() as a coroutine worker on the event loop, and every permission, local and context store read inside it goes through mcp_sources.guarded.
cost: Isolated-profile probe (HOME, XDG and TLDW_CONFIG_PATH in scratch, admit_startup held, audit-tree import asserted). One MCPPermissionStore.get_kill_switch() makes about 6,801 open() calls; read_profile_inventory_snapshot about 6,456; load() about 5,763; selected_path() alone 346. Wall time was 300–700 ms per call, but load average was 25 on 18 cores, so treat the ms as inflated; the open counts do not depend on load. My probe used a fresh, absent store file, so per-call counts in the app may differ, but the order of magnitude supports the finder's measured 438–876 ms single stalls. P0 holds: stalls well over 100 ms on a primary-destination visit.
fix: (1) Root: memoize `selected_path` / binding witnesses per store per admission generation, or per backup-intent epoch invalidated by the recovery coordinator. A steady-state read should not re-walk the pinned directory chain. (2) Give the workbench one read scope per reload/_sync_children pass: take one permission-store snapshot, one kill-switch value and one context load, and pass them down; this is the same pattern as Console's `_console_derivation_scope`. (3) Collect snapshots with `asyncio.to_thread` and apply them on the loop. TASK-32804.7 (Done) removed only the config-read part of this path; the store-admission part is new.
fix_notes: Fix (1), memoizing selected_path per admission generation, weakens the ADR-126 recovery-selection guarantee. A stale memo across a restore or activation could send reads or writes to the wrong generation, so it needs the backup/recovery owner's sign-off (TASK-32562 area). There is a safer root fix inside the same file. Within one active raw operation the lease is already held, so `binding()` calls from members(), preflight(), the history check and nested guarded re-entry can reuse `state.selected` instead of calling selected_path → acquire_storage again. That removes most of the ~17 selected_path-equivalents per call without changing cross-operation semantics. Fix (2), one snapshot per reload/_sync_children pass passed down (the _console_derivation_scope pattern), is UI-only and low risk. Fix (3), offloading _collect_snapshots and _capture_permission_render_state with asyncio.to_thread, is compatible with the stores' threading locks (writes are already offloaded via to_thread in 32804.7). Results must be applied on the loop, and the mutation_fence plus before/after inventory consistency check must run entirely inside the thread.
evidence:
mcp_source_participants.py:53 _selected -> `return selected_path(canonical)` (MCP stores mcp.local/permissions/context)
recovery_activation.py:132 def selected_path(canonical): with observed(canonical) as witnesses:  # observed -> acquire_storage(path)
mcp_workbench.py:2148 capture(): before = self._tool_policy_inventory(); effective = self._resolve_effective_states(tools); after = self._tool_policy_inventory() ...
mcp_workbench.py:2725 kill_switch = bool(get_kill_switch())
reason: The cited code matches the pin. mcp_source_participants.py:53 `_selected` calls recovery_activation.selected_path (line 132), which runs `observed()` and then acquire_storage, whenever `_recovery_original_path == canonical`. Every MCPPermissionStore, local store and context store constructor sets that attribute via `select(self)` (permission_store.py:747, local_store.py:709, unified_context_store.py:39), so every bound store takes this path. Every read method on MCPPermissionStore is `@mcp_sources.guarded` (load, read_snapshot_strict, read_profile_inventory_snapshot, get_kill_switch...). `guarded` enters raw_participants._scope, which does four things per call: calls selection() → binding() → selected_path (one admission); calls members() and preflight(), which call binding() again; runs the `mcp.history` binding check; and does one acquire_storage per admission path (selected, .tmp, .bak). A nested guarded call (get_kill_switch → load → _load_locked) re-enters through the previous-operation branch and calls selection() → selected_path again. On the loop side, MCP is not a reusable route (screen_registry.py:143). The workbench starts `run_worker(self._reload_guarded(), ...)` with no thread=True, so it is a coroutine worker on the loop. reload() → service.load_context() (async def but a sync context_store.load()) → _collect_snapshots (sync local_external_catalog and store bundle) → _sync_children → sync `_capture_permission_render_state` (calls _tool_policy_inventory 2–3× under mutation_fence) and a sync get_kill_switch at mcp_workbench.py:2725. None of these reads is offloaded; TASK-32804.7 offloaded only the writes and the config reads. No open task covers the store-admission cost: TASK-1320's ACs are all checked and only moved mount I/O into a coroutine worker.

title: Every Settings visit leaks its whole SettingsScreen via an un-unsubscribed theme_changed_signal subscription
trigger: Every Settings visit builds a new SettingsScreen (non-reusable route), and on_mount subscribes it to app.theme_changed_signal. Nothing releases it until a theme publish.
cost: The mechanism is verified from source and is deterministic. I did not re-run the finder's leakrate numbers (+~71k objects / +10.7 MB per visit, gen2 151 → 329 ms after 10 visits). They are consistent with a full screen tree being retained per visit. The retention is unbounded until a theme change, so P0 under the leak rule.
fix: In SettingsScreen.on_unmount add `self.app.theme_changed_signal.unsubscribe(self)`, and add the same to ThemePicker (an on_unmount with unsubscribe). The repo already has the pattern at console_selection_menu.py:593 and console_session_switcher_modal.py:563. Add one leak test: visit Settings twice, gc.collect(), and assert the first instance's weakref is dead.
fix_notes: Add `self.app.theme_changed_signal.unsubscribe(self)` to SettingsScreen.on_unmount, and an on_unmount with the same call to ThemePicker. Unsubscribe is idempotent (pop with default), so this is safe. Caveat for the proposed weakref leak test: SettingsScreen has 37 `thread=True` worker sites, so the F4 ContextVar pin can still keep an instance alive after this fix. The test should force a follow-up thread worker, or allow for F4, or it will flake.
evidence:
settings_screen.py:4187 self.app.theme_changed_signal.unsubscribe(self)
4188 self.app.theme_changed_signal.subscribe(self, self._refresh_appearance_theme_summary)
4213 def on_unmount(self): ... (no theme_changed_signal.unsubscribe)
settings_theme_picker.py:363 self.app.theme_changed_signal.subscribe(self, lambda _theme: self.refresh_catalog(rescan=False))
# textual/signal.py: _subscriptions = WeakKeyDictionary(); value closure captures `node` -> key never dies; pruned only on publish()
reason: settings_screen.py:4187-4190 on_mount unsubscribes, then subscribes `self._refresh_appearance_theme_summary`. on_unmount (line 4213) stops the timer and fences results but never unsubscribes. In textual/signal.py (Textual 8.2.8), `_subscriptions` is a WeakKeyDictionary whose value list holds a `signal_callback` closure that captures both `node` (non-immediate branch: `node.call_next`) and the bound-method callback. The value therefore strongly references the key, so the entry never dies. Pruning happens only inside publish(), which needs a theme change. Textual has no auto-unsubscribe on removal: the only unsubscribe in the package is screen.py:1308 for its own layout signal. The same leak exists at settings_theme_picker.py:363 (a lambda closing over the picker, with no on_unmount in that file). Settings is non-reusable (screen_registry.py:149), so every visit leaves a new instance on the app-owned signal. Repo-wide grep: these are the only two theme_changed_signal subscribers, and neither unsubscribes on unmount.

title: Departed PersonasScreens pinned by Textual thread-worker ContextVar (active_worker never reset on pool threads)
trigger: Every visit to a non-reusable screen that runs a Textual thread worker (Personas, and also Settings, MCP and others) pins that screen instance to one executor thread until another Textual thread worker runs on that thread.
cost: Mechanism verified by a standalone repro. The finder's per-visit numbers (6 of 10 Personas instances alive, about +14 MB per retained instance) are plausible and not re-measured. The ceiling is min(32, cpu+4) threads, which is 22 on this machine.
fix: Upstream a one-line Textual fix: `token = active_worker.set(self); try: return work() finally: active_worker.reset(token)`, or run the callable in `contextvars.copy_context().run`. Until that lands, either add a small shim that wraps `Worker._run_threaded`'s callable runner, or move these two sync loaders to `asyncio.to_thread`, which copies the context per call. Also making Personas reusable (F6) would cap retention at one instance.
fix_notes: The upstream Textual fix (a reset token in run_callable/run_awaitable) is the right root fix. A local shim over the private `Worker._run_threaded` is version-fragile. Textual is pinned >=8,<9, so add a version guard and a test that fails if upstream changes the runner. Moving the two loaders to asyncio.to_thread fixes only these two sites (235 thread=True sites remain) and drops Worker semantics (exclusive/group cancellation, state events). The two cited loaders use generation and attempt tokens rather than get_current_worker(), so they would tolerate the switch. Making Personas reusable (F6) caps retention for Personas only.
evidence:
textual/worker.py:306 def run_callable(work):
    active_worker.set(self)   # set in the executor thread's persistent context, never reset
    return work()
leak probe referrers of a departed PersonasScreen: Worker(name=load_character_1 group=ccp-load-character state=SUCCESS) <- hamt_bitmap_node (contextvars)
Worker(group=personas-conversations state=SUCCESS) <- hamt_bitmap_node
reason: textual/worker.py `_run_threaded` defines `run_callable`, which does `active_worker.set(self); return work()`, and dispatches with `loop.run_in_executor(None, runner, self._work)`. run_in_executor does not copy or run in a fresh Context, so the set lands in the executor thread's persistent context and is never reset. The Worker keeps `_node` and `_work` (a partial over a bound method), and Textual never clears them after completion. I verified the mechanism with a standalone script: an object passed through run_in_executor + ContextVar.set stays alive after gc and is visible to the next work item on that thread, while asyncio.to_thread (copy_context().run) does not retain it. The cited sites are real: ccp_character_handler.py:470-476 (`run_worker(partial(self._load_character_sync...), thread=True)`) and personas_conversations_controller.py:309-317. Personas is non-reusable. Retention is bounded by the number of default-executor threads, and any later Textual thread worker on the same thread overwrites it; there are 235 `thread=True` sites repo-wide. So this is capped rather than unbounded, and P1 (not P0) is right.

title: Every MainNavigationBar mount runs a synchronous ChaChaNotes attention query on the loop
trigger: Every MainNavigationBar mount: each visit to a non-reusable destination and each Home whole-screen recompose.

A mount-time fresh read may exist to catch durable marks written without a runtime recompute, and removing it outright could leave a stale badge. Also consider pushing the limit into SQL (LIMIT, plus an index on mark_type or a non-LIKE prefix range). Today the query fetches all rows before truncating.

    self.apply_console_attention()
    ...
    recompute = getattr(runtime, "recompute_console_attention", None)
    if callable(recompute): recompute(force_projection=True)
console_runtime.py:1519 marks = tuple(list_marks())  # under self._attention_operation_lock (threading lock)

The recompute is written to be thread-safe: it publishes through app.call_later and explicitly avoids call_from_thread deadlocks. No open task covers it.

title: No GC policy: 660k-object boot heap makes each automatic gen2 collection a 130–370 ms UI stall; gc.freeze() after boot measured ~0 ms
trigger: Automatic generation-2 collections fire during allocation-heavy screen switches. CPython 3.12 runs a full collection once long_lived_pending exceeds long_lived_total/4, which a ~660k-object boot heap plus per-visit screen rebuilds and the F3/F4/F5 retention will keep reaching.
cost: I verified the lever with a synthetic heap on the same interpreter (Python 3.12): 448k tracked objects took 17.6–143.6 ms per full collection (load average 25 inflates the upper value) and 0.0 ms after gc.freeze(). I did not re-measure the app's 660k-object heap or the in-tour pause frequency.
fix: Write the ADR that TASK-31966 AC#2 requires, then call `gc.freeze()` once after `_ui_ready` and the deferred-startup settle (app.py ~16160 / 16333), optionally preceded by `gc.collect()`. This is new evidence for TASK-31966, whose scope is Console activation at 79 ms: the cost appears on any switch, is 2–4× larger, and has a measured fix. Fix F3, F4 and F5 first, because they keep feeding gen2 with post-boot objects.
fix_notes: TASK-31966 AC#2 requires an approved ADR first. Run gc.collect() before gc.freeze(). Frozen objects are never scanned again, so boot-time objects that later become cyclic garbage (the splash, first-run and wizard trees, and any boot-mounted non-reusable screen) become permanent. Freeze only after those are torn down. Fix F3, F4 and F5 first so post-boot retention does not keep re-inflating gen2. Re-check under Python 3.13+, where incremental GC changes the cost model.
evidence:
gcfreeze.py (in-app, after boot settle): tracked objects 662,052; full gen2 136.2 / 141.8 / 133.2 ms
after gc.freeze() (657,429 frozen): 0.0 / 0.1 / 0.0 ms
# grep: no gc.freeze / gc.set_threshold anywhere in tldw_chatbook
reason: Grep over tldw_chatbook finds no gc.freeze, gc.set_threshold or gc.disable. The only gc use is import gc in Embeddings_Lib and PDF_Processing_Lib for explicit collects. app.py:16160 (`self._ui_ready = True`) and 16326 (`_schedule_deferred_startup_work`) are real candidate hook points. TASK-31966 (To Do) owns GC pauses but is scoped to Console character-switch activation (a 79 ms gen2). Its AC#1 already names a 'frozen baseline' comparison and its AC#2 requires an ADR for any global GC policy. The finding adds new evidence: automatic gen2 pauses fire on ordinary destination switches (Settings, Personas, Home, Notes) at 130–370 ms, larger than the task's 79 ms, and the freeze lever is measured. That makes this confirmed with known_task set, not 'known'.

title: Scheduler tick resolves the emergency-stop path (get_user_data_dir admission) on the loop every 30 s; residue of Done TASK-31507

The syscall count grows linearly with HOME depth: +104 opens per path component (1,695 / 2,007 / 2,319 opens at 15 / 18 / 21 components), and wall time rose with it (60-67 ms at 21 components). The finder's 43-87 ms figure was therefore inflated by the deep scratch HOME. First, a memo goes stale if `[paths] data_dir` or `general.users_name` changes at runtime, so key it on the config cache identity or accept a restart. Second, the comment at loop.py:596-598 says config can refuse the lookup during native backup settlement. A cached path skips that refusal, so confirm with the backup/recovery owners that reading the sentinel through a previously verified path is acceptable; the fail-safe of treating a read error as stopped still holds. The 2 per-tick `execution_scope` admissions are by design (they hold admission across dispatch) and are not part of this fix.

600     default_emergency_stop_path()   # on the loop
601 )
602 return await self._offload(is_emergency_stopped, path)
emergency_stop.py:95 def default_emergency_stop_path(): return get_user_data_dir() / "emergency_stop.json"
reason: The code matches at loop.py:599-602. `path = getattr(self, "_emergency_stop_path", None) or (default_emergency_stop_path())` runs synchronously on the loop, and only `is_emergency_stopped` goes through `_offload`. title: Per-connect storage admission makes Library/Notes/Home/Console connection churn expensive on worker threads (GIL pressure during visits)
corrected: tldw_chatbook/DB/private_sqlite.py:1517 (admission); tldw_chatbook/DB/private_sqlite.py:1878 (prepare_in_helper per connect); tldw_chatbook/DB/private_sqlite_process.py:366 (helper subprocess Popen, cap 4 at :159); churn sources: tldw_chatbook/Chat/chat_conversation_scope_service.py:193, :404; tldw_chatbook/Notes/notes_scope_service.py:1965, :2101
trigger: Visits to Library (reused), the Notes alias, Home and Console run scope-service list and count reads through `asyncio.to_thread` or thread workers. Each read opens a fresh connection and closes it. The finder's recorder shows 8-13 connects on warm visits, all on worker threads and none on the loop except for 2 on the first cold Home visit.
cost: Measured standalone in an isolated profile. Each `connect_private_sqlite` took 45-68 ms wall, with 8-14 ms of parent CPU (the GIL-holding admission and path walk: 278 opens at 15 HOME components, +17 per component) and 44 ms of child-process CPU (helper interpreter startup). A bare sqlite3 connect plus WAL is 0.5 ms. Twelve concurrent connects on 12 threads took 299 ms wall because of the 4-helper cap. A warm Library or Notes visit therefore spends about 0.3 s of wall time before all its reads can start, about 0.5 s of child CPU, and about 0.1-0.17 s of parent CPU competing with the loop for the GIL. That is per-visit on common screens, which makes it P1 rather than P2. The loop is not blocked directly; the impact is data-population latency, CPU/battery, and GIL contention.
fix: Hold connections (the held-connection idiom from TASK-15466) so each visit stops re-connecting, and amortize the admission per store per generation instead of per connect. New evidence for TASK-24457: every connect carries a 600–1600-open admission, so the churn costs far more than the plain connect cost.
fix_notes: First remove the per-read `close_connection()` in the scope services so pool-thread connections are held. That is rung 2: the held-connection idiom already exists, and the pool threads are long-lived. Before doing that, find out why the closes were added. They probably exist so backup/recovery quiescence can drain (`_core_closing`, `retiring_threads`, and `participant.drain` refuse live borrowers), and a connection held on a pool thread must still be retirable when capture pauses storage. Consider one dedicated long-lived DB thread per store instead of the shared pool. Any cache of the helper's prepare verdict per (path, inode, admission generation) must be signed off by the private-path/ADR-029 owners. TASK-24457 AC#3 requires the policy check on every logical open, so update that AC rather than silently skipping it. Medium risk.
evidence:
admission recorder (thread side, warm round):
library r2: private_sqlite.py:1517 admitted <- :1928 connect_private_sqlite  n=12  1349 ms
notes r2:   same site n=11  1928 ms
home r2:    same site n=8    696 ms
chat r2:    same site n=5    137 ms
reason: private_sqlite.py:1517 is `lease = acquire_storage(Path(database))` inside `_with_storage_admission`. private_sqlite.py:1928 is `connect_private_sqlite` → `_connect_registered_sqlite`. The finder missed the dominant cost. On POSIX, every file-backed connect also calls `prepare_in_helper` (private_sqlite.py:1878), which starts a subprocess (private_sqlite_process.py:366, `[sys.executable, "-I", "-S", private_sqlite_helper_entry.py]`). That is a fresh Python interpreter per connection. Transient helpers are capped at 4 process-wide (private_sqlite_process.py:147/159), so bursts are serialized. TLDW_TEST_MODE does not affect this path. The churn does not come from screen construction as TASK-24457 assumed: Library is now reusable (screen_registry.py:114, TASK-31521), and the finder's own admit2.json still shows 13 connects on the reused warm Library visit (and 11 on Notes, 8 on Home, 4 on Chat). It comes from scope services that connect and close around every read on executor threads: `list_and_close` → `db.close_connection()` at chat_conversation_scope_service.py:193 and :404, and notes_scope_service.py:1965 and :2101. Thread-local held connections (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:3487, Client_Media_DB_v2.py:1127, Prompts_DB.py:458, base_db.py:823) are therefore discarded on every call. Textual's thread workers and `asyncio.to_thread` share the default pool, so without those closes the pool threads' connections would be reused. TASK-24457 is open and covers Library connection churn, but it prices each connect as PRAGMAs plus a file open. This finding adds real scope (Notes, Home, Console, Personas), the actual root cause (close-after-read in the scope services), and a much higher per-connect cost.

title: Semantic chunker calls sklearn cosine_similarity once per adjacent sentence pair
trigger: PDF ingestion with default settings (chunk_method 'semantic') plus any explicit semantic chunking: once per sentence pair, in the ingest worker.

Compute it once before the loop and index `sims[i]`. The per-pair try/except fallback to 1.0 becomes moot; keep a whole-array fallback if the multiply raises. Low risk; the chunk boundaries are unchanged.

A correct memo needs its own probed-set keyed by module_name, for example a private `_PROBED: dict[str, bool]` or @functools.cache on an inner `_probe(module_name)`. It must still write DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE[feature_name] on every call, must be cleared in reset_dependency_checks (optional_deps.py:~1427), and must keep the kokoro_onnx Windows special case. Also check the 17 test files that reference check_dependency or DEPENDENCIES_AVAILABLE[...], because tests that simulate absence by patching imports would then need a reset. Cheapest safe alternative: only log on the first probe of a module. Given the cold callers, 'leave as is' is also defensible.

title: The UI-stall watchdog and diagnostics drain threads wake at 10 Hz each, forever, when idle

The queue is bounded at 64, so close() must use put with a timeout or drop an item to make room, or the sentinel can be lost when the queue is full. Keep the existing `_diagnostic_closed` check as a fallback.
