title: Turn configuration snapshot deep-copies config, world books and dictionaries at capture, then re-freezes the already-frozen snapshot per execution context (2-3x per send)
trigger: Every send: capture at the wiring.py:271 submit path, then re-freeze at the controller's _finalize_turn_execution_context (console_chat_controller.py:22820). Both run on the loop. There is an extra re-freeze on promotion (:8313) and on a new attempt (console_turn_preparation.py:211/403), not on every send.
cost: Measured in an isolated env under load: 10.3 ms to freeze and 10.8 ms to re-freeze for 3x300 world-book entries plus 200 dictionary entries; 2.5 us for an empty payload. That is 2x per send, so about 20 ms on the loop for heavy lorebooks and negligible otherwise.
fix: In _freeze, return immutable scalars (str, int, float, bool, None, bytes, enums) as-is and return MappingProxyType or tuple values that _freeze itself produced unchanged (keep a module-level WeakSet or marker, or re-freeze only mutable containers). Have _detached_configuration and _execution_context_with_attempt copy an already-detached snapshot (dataclasses.replace with a skip-refreeze flag, or object.__new__ plus slot copy) instead of re-running __post_init__.
fix_notes: The proposed WeakSet marker does not work: MappingProxyType is not weakref-able (verified: 'cannot create weak reference to mappingproxy object'). An id()-based set is unsafe after GC. The safer and shorter fix: in `_detached_configuration`, when `type(configuration) is ConsoleTurnConfigurationSnapshot`, return the instance itself. It is frozen, and every field is already detached by its own `__post_init__`. Failing that, copy slots through object.__new__ and skip `__post_init__`. The scalar short-circuit in `_freeze` is safe only for exact immutable types (str, int, float, bool, None, bytes, Enum). Keep deepcopy for any other leaf. Separately, the capture calls _collect_active_world_books and the world-book manager, which opens one ChaChaNotes transaction per book on the loop. Each of those pays the F9 admission, which is a bigger per-send cost for lorebook users than the freeze.
reason: console_turn_context.py:155 `_freeze` rebuilds every Mapping as a new MappingProxyType and calls deepcopy on every key and leaf, including str and int. The `__post_init__` at :286 applies `_freeze` to prompt_transform_inputs, skill_context_maximum, capabilities, rag_defaults, tool_configuration, provider_payload_settings and persona_policy_rules, and deepcopies the other fields. `_detached_configuration` (:454) builds a new snapshot from an already-frozen one, so `__post_init__` walks everything again. `ConsoleTurnExecutionContext.__post_init__` (:554) calls it on every construction: console_chat_controller.py:22820 `_finalize_turn_execution_context` on every ready send, :8313 on promotion, and console_turn_preparation.py:842 `_execution_context_with_attempt`, but only on a new attempt (retry or pause), not every send. The capture runs on the loop. The send submit is wiring.py:271, inside a sync UI path after record_send_stage('ui_submit'), and it calls `session._build_console_turn_execution_context` (session.py:3499/3573). The finalize happens in the async controller method `_capture_and_resolve_turn_execution_context`, also on the loop. prompt_transform_inputs carries full world-book dicts with an entries list of 15-key dicts per entry, plus the chat-dictionary entries (console_chat_controller.py:1250). I measured the same shape (3 books x 300 entries with 400-char content, plus 200 dictionary entries): 10.3 ms CPU to freeze and 10.8 ms to re-freeze. With no lorebook it is 2.5 us. That makes about 20 ms per send on the loop only for heavy-lorebook users, so P2 (the cost only scales with large data) is right. No backlog task covers it.

title: mark_response_started runs a synchronous BEGIN IMMEDIATE on the event loop when the first streamed chunk arrives
trigger: Once per provider call, on the first streamed or semantic item, inside the stream_chat async generator on the event loop (console_provider_gateway.py:5857/6062/6092 → :5533 → :2110).
cost: Measured about 5.5-7.9 ms per send by the finder's probe (s13/probe2.out). That is consistent with my own F9 transaction measurement (7.2 ms CPU under load) plus two PRAGMA statements. The worst case is a busy_timeout wait of up to 15 s when a writer holds the lock.
fix: It is already best-effort (failures are swallowed), so fire it off-loop on the F3 trace-writer executor (for example loop.run_in_executor(trace_writer, marker)) and keep the ordering guarantee by serialising on that single writer thread before settlement.
fix_notes: The code has no 'F3 trace-writer executor'; that belongs to the finder's own proposal. There is an ordering hazard. `ConsoleTraceCallBoundary.mark_response_started` sets `self._response_started_at` only after the marker succeeds, and settle_response and the settlement handoff read it. The durable state must also be RESPONSE_STARTED before settlement advances it. If the marker is offloaded, settlement has to await that future, or both have to run on the same single-thread executor. The executor thread gets its own thread-local ChaChaNotes connection, which is fine. Fixing F9 removes most of the steady-state cost, but not the lock-wait tail.
reason: console_provider_gateway.py:5417 `async def stream_chat` defines the closure `observe_response` (:5520). On the first semantic item it calls `_mark_trace_response_started(trace_call_boundary)` (:2110). That runs `ConsoleTraceCallBoundary.mark_response_started` (console_trace_service.py:401) → `ConsoleTraceService.mark_response_started` (:1540) → `ConsoleTraceSettlementCoordinator.mark_response_started` (console_trace_settlement.py:192). The last of these runs `trace_critical_write_checkpoint_policy` (two PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint round trips) and `database.transaction(immediate=True)` with get_call and advance_call_state, all synchronously. observe_response is invoked from the stream_chat async generator body at :5857, :6062 and :6092, which is on the Textual loop. Nothing offloads it. By contrast, the voice-boundary settlement uses asyncio.to_thread and mark_dispatch_started runs on the worker thread. No backlog task mentions mark_response_started or the first-chunk trace write. The finder's probe measured 5.5-7.9 ms on the loop, which matches my F9 measurement of about 7 ms CPU per outermost transaction. ChaChaNotes connections use timeout=15 (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:3492), so BEGIN IMMEDIATE can block the loop for up to 15 s if another thread holds the write lock. P2 is right: 5-8 ms once per call, below the P1 threshold of 10-20 ms, but at time-to-first-token and with a lock-wait tail.

All the writes happen on the event loop (inside async methods or submit/_failed), so a plain asyncio.Event with no call_soon_threadsafe is enough. title: ebook_chapters forks the whole process per chapter-detection call by default
trigger: Every ebook_chapters chunk or chunk_with_metadata call (the EPUB, FB2 and ebook ingest default, plus re-chunk of ebooks) forks once. The 2 s stall happens whenever the markers pickle to more than 64 KiB, which is about 2,500 matches.
cost: Measured in an isolated environment. With a small parent process, the fork path took 5.7-11 ms against 0.5-2.6 ms for the thread path, and the finder reports +10-20 ms at 490 MB RSS. Stall threshold: 2,300 markers (59.7 KB pickled) took 8 ms, and 2,600 markers (68 KB) took 2011 ms (TIMEOUT). An end-to-end chunk() call with 3,000 markers took 2016 ms, against 4.8 ms on the thread path. The result stays correct only because the thread fallback re-runs the regex.
fix: Default to the existing thread-timeout path (set _disable_mp=True by default), or use re2 when available. The patterns already pass _validate_regex_pattern and the DANGEROUS_PATTERNS screens. Keep the process path as an opt-in config setting.
fix_notes: Setting _disable_mp=True globally drops the hard-kill guarantee for user-supplied custom_chapter_pattern. A timed-out thread keeps burning CPU after the timeout because it cannot be killed. A safer minimal fix: (1) run the trusted built-in CHAPTER_PATTERNS with a plain re.finditer or the thread path, since they are linear and hard-coded; (2) keep process isolation only for custom patterns; (3) in `_run_finditer_process`, read the result with `q.get(timeout=timeout_s)` BEFORE `p.join()`, which removes the 2 s pipe-buffer stall; (4) prefer the forkserver or spawn context over fork when the parent may be multithreaded, noting that spawn pickles the text across the process boundary.

ctx = mp.get_context("fork") if hasattr(mp, "get_context") else mp
q = ctx.Queue(); p = ctx.Process(target=self._finditer_worker, ...); p.start(); p.join(timeout_s)
reason: The code matches. ebook_chapters.py:89 defaults `_disable_mp = False`. No shipped config sets regex_disable_multiprocessing; only the tests set it. Line 255 uses `mp.get_context("fork")`. chunk() (lines 433/435) and chunk_with_metadata (line 606, default pattern) both go through the fork path, because the built-in CHAPTER_PATTERNS contain parentheses and fail `_is_simple_safe_pattern`. NEW evidence beyond the finding: `_run_finditer_process` calls `p.join(timeout_s)` (line 260) BEFORE draining the Queue (line 267). A child cannot exit until its queued payload is flushed into the pipe. When the pickled result exceeds the 64 KiB pipe buffer, join therefore always waits the full REGEX_TIMEOUT (2 s). Then the parent kills the child, logs 'timed out - possible ReDoS attack', and re-runs the regex on the thread path. The default pattern has no ^ anchor, so every inline 'Section N', 'Part N' or 'Chapter N' reference counts as a marker. Where it runs: for ingest, inside the spawn-context parse pool worker (app.py:3884), which is off the UI. For re-chunk, inside worker threads of the multithreaded TUI process (library_rechunk_run.py:41-43 with thread=True, and asyncio.run in a thread at local_media_chunk_tool_service.py:1153). That second case is fork-from-a-threaded-process, which is unsafe on macOS and deprecated in Python 3.12. No backlog task covers this.

title: AgentRuns orphan reconcile still parses every step of every terminal run on each process launch, holding the write lock and spiking memory
trigger: First AgentRunsDB construction with reconcile_on_init=True per process, from Console runtime's to_thread receipt service init or other worker constructions, plus the Settings panel's on_mount thread worker. All off-loop, once per app launch.
cost: Measured: 1.8 s wall, +106 MB tracemalloc peak at 100k step rows, BEGIN IMMEDIATE held for the whole sweep. Grows linearly with history.

1. Persist a sweep watermark (max created_at or rowid already checked) and scan only newer terminal runs.
2. Do the lifecycle check in SQL instead of hydrating everything in Python: `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM agent_run_steps s WHERE s.run_id = r.id AND json_extract(s.payload, '$.kind') = ?)`, which avoids loading every payload.
3. Run the scan in a DEFERRED read and take BEGIN IMMEDIATE only when a repair row must be inserted.

The file's own comments warn that a DEFERRED read-then-write hits SQLite's non-retryable snapshot/upgrade deadlock. Instead, run the scan in a separate read transaction, then open a fresh IMMEDIATE transaction that re-verifies each candidate before inserting the repair diagnostic. A json_extract(payload,'$.kind') EXISTS in SQL avoids hydrating payloads. A persisted watermark needs an agent_runs schema bump.

    "AND agent_kind IN ('primary', 'subagent')").fetchall()      # no watermark / LIMIT
_hydrated_terminal = self._batch_hydrate_steps(conn, [row["id"] for row in terminal_rows])  # json.loads every payload
(inside `with self.transaction() as conn:` -> BEGIN IMMEDIATE)

Inside `with self.transaction()` (BEGIN IMMEDIATE), reconcile_orphaned_runs (AgentRuns_DB.py:2526-2533) selects every non-running primary/subagent run with no bound, then _batch_hydrate_steps (:1702-1742) fetches and json.loads every step payload for all of them. The sweep runs once per path per process (the _swept_paths guard). Callers are ensure_activity_receipt_service (documented as called via asyncio.to_thread), the Settings panel's thread worker, change_retention and worktree recovery workers. Every caller is off the loop. Measured on 2000 runs x 50 steps: reconcile 1,806 ms, and 2,745 ms under tracemalloc with a 106 MB peak, holding the agent_runs.db write lock throughout. The task is In Progress with every AC ticked, so the linear full scan and memory spike are left untracked. This is new evidence rather than a duplicate. Severity: off-loop, once per launch, and it only bites with large lifetime history, so P2 rather than P1.

title: The 'image-free' projections (TASK-15474) still read every avatar and image BLOB, because hot columns are stored after the BLOB in the row

list/count WHERE deleted = 0 AND json_extract(... extensions ...) IS NULL   # both after the BLOB

get_message_tree_rows_for_conversation: (m.image_data IS NOT NULL) AS has_image, m.image_mime_type, ... m.metadata_json

The list projection (:8854) excludes `image` but still selects columns stored after it. count_character_cards (~:9609) applies _USER_VISIBLE_CHARACTER (:9508), a json_extract over extensions, which also sits after the BLOB. get_message_tree_rows_for_conversation selects m.timestamp and later columns (actual SELECT at :12228; :12213 is its docstring). title: The messages_fts backfill 'no-work' probe scans every message on every boot under BEGIN IMMEDIATE, with no completion marker
trigger: Every app boot: staggered boot worker (thread=True) -> backfill_chachanotes_messages_fts -> first chunk probe finds nothing -> returns after one full scan under BEGIN IMMEDIATE.
cost: Not independently re-timed. The finder's 390 ms first / 11-12 ms warm on 45k messages is consistent with a full leaf scan plus a fresh helper open (~50-96 ms measured in F3) plus admission (~5-15 ms measured in F1). The overflow-chain part of the evidence is wrong, but the conclusion stands.
fix: Persist a 'messages_fts_backfill_complete' marker (a metadata row, set when a full pass reports 0) and skip the probe while it is set. The FTS triggers keep the index current afterwards. Run the probe in a DEFERRED read transaction and switch to IMMEDIATE only when rows are found.

Probe in a read transaction, then start a fresh IMMEDIATE transaction and re-select only when rows are found. A completion marker must be invalidated by anything that resets messages_fts: the v45->v46-style reset, 'rebuild'/'delete-all' maintenance, and restore/replace. Keeping it in the same DB means restores carry their own marker. Alternative with no marker: probe `SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM messages WHERE deleted=0) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM messages_fts_docsize)` cheaply, noting that COUNT on messages still scans unless a covering index exists.

with self.transaction(immediate=True) as conn:
    rows = conn.execute("SELECT rowid, content FROM messages WHERE deleted = 0 AND rowid > ?
        AND rowid NOT IN (SELECT rowid FROM messages_fts_docsize) ORDER BY rowid LIMIT ?", (after_rowid, chunk_size))
# driver: 'The no-work path (first chunk finds nothing -- every boot after completion) ...'
# `deleted` (col 10) sits after content(4)+image_data(5): the scan walks overflow chains
reason: The code is as quoted. backfill_messages_fts (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:21300) opens transaction(immediate=True) and runs `SELECT rowid, content FROM messages WHERE deleted=0 AND rowid > ? AND rowid NOT IN (SELECT rowid FROM messages_fts_docsize) ORDER BY rowid LIMIT ?`. When the index is complete, that walks the whole messages b-tree. The driver (chachanotes_fts_backfill.py:107) runs it on every boot from app.py:16446 (run_worker thread=True, STAGGERED boot tier, boot_worker_policy.py:184), and there is no completion marker. The worker wraps it in operation_owned_connection, so it also pays a fresh connection (helper spawn) plus admission. The cost is the full leaf-page scan plus NOT IN docsize under the write lock. It is off-loop and once per boot, but it holds BEGIN IMMEDIATE for the whole scan in the early-boot window, and that grows with total message bytes. P2 fits (scales only with large data).

cost: Measured in an isolated scratch env on this box. HelperLease.start median 54.3 ms plus close 10.8 ms, about 65 ms per open, vs raw sqlite3.connect+close at 0.11 ms. A bare 'python -I -S -c pass' spawn+exit is 25 ms. GIL probe with a 600 MB touched heap and a thread looping Popen: the main-thread 1 ms sleep loop's max gap went from 16 to 37 ms and p99 from 5.7 to 16 ms (50 MB: no measurable change). Measured stall at 600 MB drops from max 22 ms to 7 ms. (3) Needs an owner decision, because the 2026-09-07 spec's 'Rejected alternatives' covers it: a stat-only already-private fast path. Use os.stat(follow_symlinks=False) on main/-wal/-shm/-journal: regular file, uid == euid, mode 0600, nlink 1. That opens no fd, so POSIX locks are safe. Fall back to the helper only when the file must be created or hardened, or a check fails. The pathname race is the same one verify_expected_named_identity already accepts. Keep the helper for TTS proof leases.
fix_notes: Option 3 (stat-only fast path) and any persistent helper pool are both explicitly rejected in ADR-125 'Alternatives' and in the 2026-09-07 design spec 'Rejected alternatives' ('A metadata-only fast path does not handle wrong-mode hardening or live proof closes'). Either needs an owner decision and an ADR amendment, not a perf PR. Option 2 (posix_spawn): CPython 3.12 on macOS takes the posix_spawn path only when close_fds=False, because there is no closefrom file action. That puts the burden on proving no inheritable fd leaks; PEP 446 and SQLite's O_CLOEXEC make that likely but not guaranteed across native extensions. A child inheriting an fd does not cancel the parent's POSIX locks. Lowest-risk levers: batch or share boot opens (one helper prepare per database, not per constructor-internal reopen), move the boot constructors at app.py:8118-8121 into the existing parallel phase, and cut per-call reopens (F2). title: Owned DB calls close their thread handle after every call, and ChaChaNotes close runs a blocking wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE), so hot async paths can pay F1 on each call
known_task: TASK-31501 (partial: the 1 Hz loop exists, but that task predates the owned-call reopen/TRUNCATE-per-tick cost)
trigger: There are 47 non-import run_owned_db_call/operation_owned_connection lines (console_fleet_wake 15, character_context 8, app.py 7, trace service/runtime 9, and others). Two hot paths verified: the 1 Hz maintenance loop (console_runtime.py:3290) and the 5 Hz run-time poll -> refresh_if_scope_changed -> _capture_scope (2 owned calls per tick). A reopen happens only when the executor thread chosen has no registered handle.
cost: Per reopen: helper start+close measured at about 65 ms on the worker, plus a GIL stall on the loop at large heap (measured max gap 37 ms at 600 MB), plus PRAGMA journal_mode and a wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) that fsyncs the DB and invokes the 15 s busy handler while a writer or older-snapshot reader is active. The frequency (fraction of owned calls that reopen) is estimated, not measured.
fix: The ideal fix is for owned calls to keep healthy handles: retire them lazily and let the quiescence registry close them for maintenance, rather than closing per call. Alternatively run owned calls on one small dedicated executor whose threads keep a registered handle. Give the 1 Hz maintenance loop a single long-lived connection (TASK-31501 removes the poll; this removes the per-tick reopen). Drop wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE) from close_connection: use PASSIVE or rely on wal_autocheckpoint, and keep TRUNCATE for explicit shutdown and backup.
fix_notes: TASK-32628 added the per-call close deliberately so executor threads do not hold handles that block backup/recovery quiescence. Any keep-alive scheme must still let the quiescence registry retire idle handles on demand. A small dedicated executor with long-lived registered handles is the cleaner option. Do not remove TRUNCATE from close_connection globally, because explicit shutdown and backup rely on it to bound WAL size. Instead skip the checkpoint, or use PASSIVE, only on the owned-call retirement path. Add a connect counter test (idle 60 s plus one streamed turn) to pin the reopen rate.

title: Console Character search runs a full DB pipeline on every keystroke, with no debounce and no cancellation, including a BEGIN IMMEDIATE write
trigger: Every keystroke in the Console Character section search input. The cost is off-loop on default-executor threads, but it contends for the ChaChaNotes write lock and can trigger F2 reopens that stall the loop.
cost: Per keystroke: 5 executor hops, 1 BEGIN IMMEDIATE plus UPDATE (a WAL frame each time), about 10+ small read transactions, 2 FTS MATCH queries (COUNT plus candidates), 8 full-transcript projections (F6, about 1.25 ms each at 500 messages). Estimated, not measured end to end.

Build the repository or service once per scope fingerprint instead of per call. Compare the fingerprint with one owned call, not two before and two after.

Cancelling an awaiting coroutine does not stop an in-flight to_thread callback, so also check the generation before issuing _search_sync. Move ensure_keyword_index to activation or first focus, or at least skip the state UPDATE when activated=1 and the policy/authority are unchanged. It must still run whenever the revision advances, otherwise results stay stale until maintenance runs.

title: Keyword-index maintenance does O(corpus) work inside one BEGIN IMMEDIATE and rewrites every document's source_revision each pass
trigger: The first character search after any message or conversation write triggers a dirty pass: O(dirty projections) plus an O(all documents) UPDATE. The first search after importing or creating a character card with no chats triggers a full reconcile over every local character conversation, holding the write lock throughout. Both run off-loop in owned calls.
cost: Estimated. A full reconcile is about 1.25 ms per 500-message conversation (the finder's measurement, plausible given the json.dumps plus sha256 per projection), so 300 conversations is about 0.4-2 s holding the ChaChaNotes write lock. Streaming persistence and other writers block for that time, up to the 15 s busy timeout.
fix: Chunk maintenance the way the build path does: one short transaction per at most 128 conversations, with the fts_backfill_pacing INTER_CHUNK_PAUSE between chunks, fenced by _require_ready_ownership each chunk. Store the maintained source_revision on the generation row only, and have the search SQL compare against the generation instead of `d.source_revision = ?`, so a pass stops rewriting every document. Run maintenance in a background worker, not inline in the search (see F3).
fix_notes: Chunking into multiple transactions breaks the current atomic invariant that every document in the ready generation shares the generation's source_revision. The search SQL requires d.source_revision = generation.source_revision, so mid-maintenance chunks would fail closed and hide results unless the fence design changes as well. Moving the maintained revision onto the generation row only is the bigger win (O(changed) instead of O(documents)), but it must keep the dirty-ledger NOT EXISTS exclusion semantics. The medium risk rating is right.

title: keyword_search revalidates each FTS hit by loading, JSON-encoding and SHA-256-ing the conversation's entire message history
trigger: Every Console character search keystroke (8 projections, undebounced, F3). Every Ctrl+K switcher Character-mode query (50 projections, debounced at console_session_switcher_modal.py:1336). Personas searches.

fix: The candidate SQL already excludes stale documents via NOT EXISTS against the trigger-maintained dirty ledger plus the generation fence, so per-hit reprojection is redundant while the index is activated. Drop it. Alternatively, compare a cheap stamp stored on the document, such as conversations.version plus the max message rowid, instead of re-deriving the digest.
fix_notes: 'Drop it' conflicts with ADR-120 ('candidates are revalidated against authoritative SQLite state before display and activation'), so it needs an ADR amendment and cannot ship as a perf PR alone. A cheaper stamp is ADR-compatible only if it changes on every eligibility-relevant edit: message insert, update or delete, variant selection, active_leaf change, card delete or rename. conversations.version plus max(message rowid) misses in-place content edits and variant flips. The trigger-maintained per-conversation dirty ledger is the natural stamp: compare dirty.source_revision with d.source_revision, which the SQL already does. Arguing that this satisfies 'authoritative revalidation' is the ADR question.

title: Run-log append takes storage admission twice and reopens the segment file for every record (~12 ms per record)
known_task: TASK-32804.1 (related: the same per-call admission handshake, fixed only for config reads; the run-log site is not covered)
trigger: Every agent run with a Console scratch space (default path): at least one model record per step, plus a tool_call and tool_result record per tool call, through RunLogWriter.append -> _append_under_scope. Runs on the agent worker thread; sub-agents serialize on writer._lock for the inner acquire and write.
cost: Re-measured in an isolated scratch HOME with startup admission held. acquire_storage alone: median 8.6 ms (p90 31.7 ms). RunLogWriter.append of a 2 KB record: median 25.2 ms (p90 66.9 ms). A raw open+write+flush of the same bytes: 0.09 ms. This is worse than the finder's 12.1 ms (my machine was noisy), but it is the same order of magnitude and far above the P1 threshold for each step.
fix: Acquire one StorageLease in bind() (or per segment) and hold it until close() or segment roll. Keep the segment file handle open and do write+flush per record. Drop the nested acquire_storage in _write_bytes when the caller already holds the writer's lease. If maintenance needs to drain holders, have the lease expose a cheap revoked/generation flag and re-acquire only when it flips. Also worth filing for Backup_Recovery separately: acquire_storage re-reads control records and re-walks ~145 path components on every call and has 88 call sites.
fix_notes: Holding one StorageLease from bind() until close() is risky. Leases are deliberately per-operation so that maintenance (_LocalPause.drain / backup capture) can drain holders. A lease held for the whole run would make any backup or restore started during a long agent run time out on drain. The safe first step, with no semantic change, is to drop the nested acquire_storage in _write_bytes when it is called from _append_under_scope, _close_under_scope or _write_manifest_under_scope: the outer lease on log_dir already covers the segment file under it. That halves the cost. Keeping the segment fd open across records is fine only if it is closed or reopened whenever admission is lost. The larger lever belongs in storage_admission itself: amortise the admission handshake per generation, as TASK-32804.1 did for config reads. That benefits all 86 call sites, so file it against Backup_Recovery rather than only run_log.

    with self._lock:
        ...
        self._write_bytes(self._segment_path(), payload)

with acquire_storage(path):               # inner, per record again

Each call runs bootstrap.startup_permission twice, _scope twice (bootstrap._records control-record reads plus _registry, which opens admission/registry.json under flock), qualified_for and _execution_selection_for, all under the module-global _lock RLock. It runs on the agent worker thread, not the event loop, but it adds wall time before every step's next model request, so per-send and per-step. title: Nested AGENTS.md resolution re-walks and re-reads the whole target directory chain on every tool batch, under the shared ledger lock. Over SSH that means 4×depth remote ops per batch plus 4 per send
trigger: Every tool batch that touches a path-aware local fs tool (read/grep/ls/edit) in a Console run with a project-instruction binding, via AgentRuntime prepare_tool_calls -> ledger.prepare. P1 applies to SSH remote bindings (shipped in PR #2838): 1 stat per path component plus 3 fs_read per absent directory, every batch, plus ping + 3 reads per send. On local bindings the same re-walk costs only a few ms on a worker thread, which would be P3.
cost: Op counts were verified by reading the code: a depth-3 remote target costs 3 stat_path + 9 fs_read = 12 executor ops per batch, the same on every batch, and startup costs ping + about 3 reads per send. The SSH latency per op (50-150 ms) is ESTIMATED, not re-measured. Even at an optimistic ~30 ms per mux op it adds at least 0.36 s per remote tool batch, against 1 op for the tool itself. The local figure (2.65 ms / 521 lstat for depth 5) is plausible given that _capture_ancestor_identities walks to / for each directory; I did not re-measure it. Serialization of fleet chains under the ledger RLock was confirmed in the code.

Resolution is already pinned to dispatch_started_wall_ns, since a later-created file would only yield a content-free 'stale' outcome. Only resolve directories not seen before. (2) For remote bindings, reuse the status cache's identity chain (cfg.cache.identity_for) instead of RemoteInstructionIO.ping() per send, or cache the IO per binding. Add one batched worker op that stats a chain and reads both candidates in one round trip. (3) Resolve outside the ledger lock and merge results under the lock with an activation-revision check.

With a memo it would silently stay absent. That is probably acceptable, but this is a trust boundary (ADR-068/069), so it needs a security review and a pinning test. Key memo entries by canonical path, and invalidate them on any resolution_failed. Caching RemoteInstructionIO per binding across sends must still honour the status cache's identity re-capture: a stale or retargeted root must re-ping. A batched worker op (stat the chain and read both candidates in one round trip) is the highest-value lever, but it needs a worker bundle and protocol change. Resolving outside the ledger lock requires a revision check on merge. The lowest-risk first step is to memoise absent scopes plus walked directories for the ledger lifetime.

Also, a byte cut can split an ANSI escape: the ESC byte is dropped by the control filter, but the '[31m' residue remains as text, so strip ANSI before cutting, or cut and then drop a trailing partial escape. str.translate with a precomputed deletion table for C0 (minus \n and \t), DEL and C1 is behaviour-identical. The bare stop from dictation start (dictation.py:2172) and hands-free barge-in (hands_free.py:1521/2095) reaches the sync stop at :2843 whenever _last_played is set.
cost: From the code on macOS: an unconditional 100 ms sleep per play, plus Popen and the prior-clip stop, so at least ~110 ms of frozen loop per ack or Play click. I did not re-measure Popen, but the finder's 11-27 ms is plausible for a large process. On Linux there is no sleep, so cost is Popen plus terminate+wait, bounded at 2.5 s in pathological cases. Stop-only paths are typically 1-10 ms. The _await_legacy_playback poller costs one to_thread hop every 50 ms per clip, which is minor.
fix:
Keep the change inside tts_events:
1. Replace `play_audio_file(audio_file)` with `await asyncio.to_thread(play_audio_file, audio_file)`. Better still, route lifecycle-less plays through the existing _play_legacy_clip_and_await_completion worker (one thread observes completion) and delete the 20 Hz _await_legacy_playback poller.
2. Make the three stop_audio_playback_if_current call sites `await asyncio.to_thread(...)`. The same file already uses this idiom at :2834 and :2991-2993.
3. Offload the Watchlists caller the same way.
TASK-1880 (sink streaming for legacy providers) would remove the openai/kokoro spoken-feedback case but not the stop paths.
fix_notes: Fix the root cause once in audio_player.play(). The Darwin time.sleep(0.1) is redundant because stop() has already kill()+wait()ed the prior afplay process, so deleting it helps all five on-loop callers at once. Low risk, but verify there is no audible overlap or glitch on back-to-back clips. Then offload the calls. Moving play_audio_file to asyncio.to_thread in handle_tts_playback opens the pre-Popen window the file's own docstrings warn about: a bare stop landing during the thread hop sees a stale _last_played and misses the new clip. So route lifecycle-less plays through the existing _play_legacy_clip_and_await_completion with a stop_requested Event, rather than a bare to_thread. That also removes the 20 Hz _await_legacy_playback poller. The sync stop at :3735 runs while holding _playback_handoff_lock and _audio_files_lock, so awaiting to_thread there holds both locks across the hop. That is acceptable but must stay ordered. Library, Watchlists and Artifacts should use `await asyncio.to_thread(play_audio_file, path)`.

trigger: Once per Speech Playground Generate click, plus the prior generation's file cleanup. This is a user-initiated, infrequent path.
cost: I did not re-measure. The finder's numbers (~5 ms per 5 MB write, 0.3-3.6 ms per secure delete, more with ext4 fsync) are consistent with the code. Typical playground WAVs are <1-3 MB (48 KB/s at 24 kHz mono 16-bit), so the usual cost is a few ms. Peak memory is 2x the body.

Streaming chunks into the file can be done where no full-body validation is needed. The clone path calls validate_pcm16_wav(complete_audio) on the whole body, so it must still see the complete bytes.

title: Automatic Console speech resolves the destination 2–3 times per reply, each forcing an audio_cpp catalog refresh
trigger: Once per auto-spoken or guarded Console reply that carries a destination fingerprint (auto Speak replies, Buddy speak_guarded_utterance). The forced refresh applies only when the effective provider is audio_cpp.
cost: Estimated only. There are 1-2 redundant resolver runs per reply, each forcing up to 2 loopback catalog refreshes for audio_cpp. That is plausibly several to tens of ms of added time-to-speech. It is latency, not a loop freeze.
fix: Keep the admission_authorizer check at synthesis time, since it is the real TOCTOU guard. Drop the pre-generation re-resolution in _generate_tts, or pass the already-verified destination through. Within one resolution, memoize read_catalog per provider so catalog_reader and read_native_capability share one refresh.
fix_notes: The admission_authorizer check is the real TOCTOU guard, so keep it. The :1886 pre-check fails fast before the progress event and artifact creation, and the :925 check runs before any rate-limit wait in _admit_tts_generation. Dropping either changes which error surfaces and when ('destination_changed' outcome code and toast); tests likely pin these. Memoizing read_catalog within one _destination_for_resolution call is the low-risk half of the fix.
evidence:
925  destination = await self._destination_for_resolution(resolution)   # admission pre-check
1886 destination = await self._destination_for_resolution(resolution)  # again in _generate_tts
1438 if provider_id == "audio_cpp":
         return await service.get_catalog(provider_id, refresh=True)  # also via read_native_capability
reason: _handle_trusted_message_speech_request resolves the destination at tts_events.py:925 when expected_destination_fingerprint is set. _generate_tts resolves it again at :1886, and synthesis enforces the same fingerprint a third time through admission_authorizer (:1865-1885). In _destination_for_resolution (:1393), read_catalog calls service.get_catalog('audio_cpp', refresh=True) (:1438-1442), and read_native_capability calls read_catalog again (:1446-1452). TTSEffectiveSettingsResolver calls catalog_reader (effective_settings.py:1032) and native_capability_reader (:1141), so one resolution can force up to two audio_cpp refreshes. With refresh=True, AudioCppAdapter.get_catalog bypasses the managed-mode cached catalog (adapters/audio_cpp.py:579-584) and goes through _refresh_catalog -> _ensure_managed_running and an HTTP refresh. Everything is async, so nothing blocks the loop.

title: Worker handler registry is an allowlist, so every unhandled app-owned worker transition logs a WARNING (plus an eager debug f-string)
trigger: There are 26 run_worker sites in app.py and 61 app/app_instance.run_worker sites elsewhere, each producing about 3 transitions per run. Frequency depends on user actions; the boot burst was already fixed by TASK-31806.
cost: Estimated at roughly 0.1-0.3 ms per WARNING record through the loguru sinks, plus microseconds for the eager debug f-string. Negligible per action.
fix: Downgrade the unhandled case to debug. Use logger.debug('{}', ...) lazy formatting, or remove the per-transition debug. Alternatively invert the registry so only groups with real handling are routed and everything else is silently acknowledged.
fix_notes: Downgrading the unhandled case to debug with lazy loguru formatting (`logger.debug('... {} {}', name, group)`) is the minimal, safe change. Check the tests that pin the 'No handler found' warning (TASK-2726/31806 pins) before changing the level.

title: ChatImageHandler exposes async-but-fully-sync image processing, so callers spin up a new event loop in a thread for every attachment
known_task: qa/core-code-review-2026-09-17/report.md:2724 (P3 D3 UI-chat); no backlog task filed
trigger: Yes, but the trigger is user-initiated and infrequent: Console file-picker attach, drag-drop path-paste, and Alt+V clipboard image, through chat_screen._process_console_attachment and the clipboard-grab handler. Both paths are already offloaded with asyncio.to_thread, so the event loop never runs the PIL work.
cost: Measured, not the event loop: about 0.5 ms extra per image or text attachment (nested loop setup and teardown), and about 1.2 ms per PDF, doc or ebook attachment (nested loop plus throwaway executor thread). Everything runs on a worker thread. Zero UI stall.
fix: Make process_image_file and prepare_image_payload plain `def`, and make the file-handler chain sync, so callers use `await asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...)` directly with no nested event loop.
fix_notes: The proposed fix, converting the whole handler chain to sync, is more churn than 'low'. FileHandler.process is an abstract async method with about 9 implementations in Utils/file_handlers.py. _extract_local_ingest_text awaits to_thread internally. `_process_image_data`'s async signature is explicitly pinned by tests. Five test modules call these via asyncio.run: Tests/Chat/test_attachment_core.py, test_image_payload.py, test_chat_image_pixel_bomb.py, and Tests/Event_Handlers/Chat_Events/test_chat_image_events.py and test_chat_image_properties.py. Do NOT 'fix' this by awaiting process_attachment_path directly on the loop: that would move the PIL decode, resize and optimize work and the text-handler file reads onto the UI thread, which is the real hazard. Given the roughly 1 ms off-loop cost, the best disposition is to leave it or fold it into a hygiene task. If it is changed, sync variants plus to_thread is correct.
evidence:
chat_image_events.py:42 async def process_image_file(file_path) -> ...: path.read_bytes(); PILImage.open(...)
199 async def prepare_image_payload(...): pil_image.load(); thumbnail(LANCZOS); save(optimize=True)
chat_screen.py:20511 attachment = await asyncio.to_thread(
    lambda: asyncio.run(process_attachment_path(file_path)))
reason: The code is present on pin 840ed2ca58. chat_image_events.py:42 `async def process_image_file` and :208 `async def prepare_image_payload` contain no awaits of real async I/O; they do PIL open/load/thumbnail/save synchronously. chat_screen.py:20476-20480 (clipboard bytes) and :20511-20513 (file path) wrap the chain in `asyncio.to_thread(lambda: asyncio.run(...))`. A repo-wide grep of process_attachment_path, process_attachment_bytes, prepare_image_payload, process_image_file, load_processed_file and file_handler_registry finds exactly those two production entry points. Both are already off the loop, so nothing blocks the loop and the 'latent risk' is hypothetical, not a present cost. I measured the overhead with a stdlib-only micro-benchmark on the same interpreter, off the loop. `to_thread(asyncio.run(noop))` has a median of 0.69 ms against 0.20 ms for a bare to_thread, about 0.5 ms extra. For PDF, doc and ebook attachments, whose handler (`file_handlers._extract_local_ingest_text:65`) does its own `asyncio.to_thread` inside the nested loop, the nested run spins up and joins a throwaway default executor, measured at 1.27 ms against 0.10 ms. That is about 1 ms per user-initiated attachment, and it runs on a worker thread. title: Provider recovery guard re-runs a ~76-syscall storage and witness check on every streamed chunk
corrected: tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls/recovery_review.py:513 (per-chunk `with _using(self.operation)`); tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls/recovery_review.py:511 (lazy second _Operation for openai_call streams); tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls/recovery_review.py:556-564 (openai_call); tldw_chatbook/Backup_Recovery/generation_witnesses.py:9-74 (the uncached work)
trigger: Every streamed reply through chat_api_call from a sync @unqualified or openai_call handler: groq, deepseek, mistral, openrouter, moonshot, zai, the engine presets via owned_json_post, anthropic, huggingface, qwencloud, the local handlers in LLM_API_Calls_Local, and openai. There is one check() per yielded item, on the gateway to_thread worker. My isolated re-run of the finder's owned_json_post probe over a fake 302-record SSE body counted 303 _history calls during iteration.
cost: Re-measured in an isolated scratch profile (HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH in scratch, admit_startup creating admission plus unbound-owner) on a heavily loaded host (load average about 50). op.check() took 5.5 ms per call. An @unqualified generator cost 5.0 ms per item over 1000 items. owned_json_post streaming cost 3.28 ms per record over 302 records. The finder's 1.29 ms per record under lower load is consistent: same shape, host-inflated. That is roughly 1.3 s or more of mostly-syscall CPU per 1000-chunk reply, and it caps the chunk rate for fast providers. It is worker-thread CPU, not loop time.
fix: Check once per stream, not per chunk. The stream's _Operation holds its admission lease until close(), so witness history should not change underneath it. In _OpenAIStream.__next__, run _using/check only on the first next() (or at a coarse interval, such as every 5 s or 256 records). After that, only set the contextvar. Also skip the second check() that _ordinary_operation (:82) followed by _using (:477) does on borrowed nested calls. Optionally memoise _history() on the bootstrap and registry file identity (st_ino, st_mtime_ns). Add a probe pinning at most one _history call per stream.
fix_notes: The per-iteration check looks deliberate. TASK-32003's notes say 'Guard actual effect/iteration, including iterator created before restored generation', so relaxing it needs an owner review of the recovery design, not just a perf patch. Before switching to check-once-per-stream, confirm that a restore or activation cannot publish a new generation while this stream's StorageLease native hold is live. If it can, keep a check that is cheaper but still sound. One option: memoise _history on the stat identities (st_dev, st_ino, st_mtime_ns, st_ctime_ns) of the bootstrap dir, the registry.json and the witness generation dirs. Another: check on a time or record interval. Separately, dropping the redundant second check() on borrowed nested calls (_ordinary_operation:82 plus _using:477) is safe and cheap. Pin the cost with a probe that counts _history calls per stream.
evidence:
def __next__(self):                      # recovery_review.py:505
    with self.lock:
        ...
            with _using(self.operation):     # :513, once per chunk
                value = next(self.iterator)
def _using(operation):                   # :476
    operation.check()                    # :419 -> _history() -> _witnesses() -> startup_permission/_control_records/_registry
reason: Code matches on the 840ed2ca58 pin. In _OpenAIStream.__next__ (recovery_review.py:505), line 513 runs `with _using(self.operation)` on every next(). _using (:476) calls operation.check() (:419), which calls _history, then _witnesses (generation_witnesses.py:9). That re-runs lease.execution_context, whose two Path.resolve() calls stat every path component, then bootstrap.startup_permission (_records, then _registry, which takes a registry.lock flock and reads a file), then _control_records and _registry again. Nothing in bootstrap.py or generation_witnesses.py is cached; I grepped both for lru_cache and cache. The trigger is real. owned_json_post (hosted_chat.py:628) and every sync @unqualified handler that returns an Iterator is wrapped in _OpenAIStream (:127-131). The Console gateway worker (console_provider_gateway.py:6435, `text = next(normalized_response)`, inside asyncio.to_thread(worker) at :6587) pulls one item per chunk. This runs on a worker thread, so it does not block the loop. openai_call (:556) also builds a second _Operation lazily on the first next() (:511). The prior core review (qa/core-code-review-2026-09-17/slices/LLM.md:216) measured only the per-call 5.8 ms admission. title: Async provider-guard wrappers run the synchronous admission handshake on the Textual event loop (~21–27 ms per llama.cpp send, 75 ms per discovery)
corrected: tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls/recovery_review.py:93 (asyncgen wrapper call), tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls/recovery_review.py:110 (coroutine wrapper call), tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls/recovery_review.py:77-85 (_ordinary_operation borrowed double check), tldw_chatbook/LLM_Calls/recovery_review.py:640-665 (catalog_call)
trigger: Every Console send on llama.cpp: resolve_llamacpp with the nested _is_reachable, then stream_llamacpp_chat entry. Also complete_llamacpp_chat on the fallback and voice paths. discover_local_servers runs once per Console visit while the setup card is blocking, and in the first-run wizard. All of these are coroutines on the Textual loop.
cost: Re-ran the finder's asyncio probe in an isolated scratch profile on a host at load average about 48. The resolve_llamacpp shape (outer plus nested) blocked the loop 28.9 ms. The async-gen stream entry blocked 19.5 ms. Discovery with 8 gathered probes blocked 188.6 ms. The finder measured 12.6, 8.5 and 75 ms under lower load; the ratios are consistent. The guard work is synchronous, so all of it is loop time. That comes to about 20 ms or more per llama.cpp send on the loop, which is P1 per the per-send rubric.

In the async and asyncgen wrappers, build the operation with `operation, owned = await asyncio.to_thread(_ordinary_operation)` and run the first check() the same way. Make borrowed nested calls skip re-checking. Make catalog_call and discovery_call borrow an active operation instead of always building a new one. The F1 memo alone would also shrink these costs to microseconds. Umbrella: TASK-32804 (sync work on the loop).
fix_notes: Watch the contextvar and task-identity semantics. _identity() includes the current task, and _current is a ContextVar. Building the operation in asyncio.to_thread is fine, because _Operation.__init__ does not use _current. But _using() must still set the contextvar in the calling task, and any to_thread check must not rely on the thread identity. Making gather children borrow the parent's operation would change the identity rule, which appears deliberate for leases held per task, so get an owner review first. The lowest-risk wins are dropping the redundant second check() on borrowed nested calls, and a sound _history memo (see F1).

    with _using(operation):                   # sync check() again

# nested/borrowed: _ordinary_operation():82 check() + _using():477 check()

A new _Operation means acquire_storage plus _history, and a borrowed one means check(). _using() then runs another synchronous check(). All of it happens on whichever loop runs the coroutine. I traced the callers. resolve_llamacpp (console_provider_gateway.py:3736) is awaited from _resolve_for_send_unclassified (:4226). The controller reaches that through _resolve_for_send_bounded using asyncio.wait_for on the same loop (console_chat_controller.py:4616-4631), and the submission itself is a run_worker coroutine per the controller's own docstring (:9876-9886), so it runs on the Textual loop. The nested _is_reachable (:3763, decorated :7186) runs in the same task, so it borrows: two more check() calls. stream_llamacpp_chat (:4612) is consumed with `async for` at :6013 on the loop. discover_local_servers (local_server_discovery.py:556) runs from chat_screen.py:15443 via run_worker(coroutine) with no thread. title: Every hosted request builds a new requests.Session, so each send and each agent step pays a fresh TCP+TLS handshake
corrected: tldw_chatbook/Utils/egress.py:1012-1040 (create_default_session, the shared factory; the natural single fix site)
trigger: Every hosted send via chat_api_call, and each agent-loop step, since AgentService re-calls chat_api_call once per step. Also each summarizer chunk and each retry attempt. Local http://localhost providers are unaffected.
cost: Not measured (network calls are forbidden). A fresh HTTPS connection costs at least TCP plus TLS 1.3 (2 RTT) plus a DNS lookup, so tens to low hundreds of ms of time-to-first-token per request. The benefit is certain for back-to-back requests: agent steps, summarizer chunks, retries. It is conditional for human-paced sends, where the server's idle keep-alive timeout may already have closed a pooled socket. It stays P1 because agent steps are per-send-equivalent and the cost is well above the 10–20 ms rubric line. It needs a live A/B measurement before a fix lands.
fix: Keep a long-lived pooled requests.Session per (scheme, host), or one shared per provider module, with the retry adapter mounted once. The stream then owns only the response: closing an unfinished response discards its socket, so Stop and cancel semantics are kept. Keep a dedicated, trust_env=False session only for reviewed and recovered openai_post operations. This needs a one-line amendment to ADR-062's 'stream owns response/session' rule and a check against TASK-30015 (tearing down a wedged read).
fix_notes: Risks the finder did not name: (1) requests.Session is not guaranteed thread-safe, and parallel sub-agents and concurrent workers call handlers from several threads at once. Use a per-thread session, or share the thread-safe urllib3 PoolManager/HTTPAdapter across per-call Sessions: mount one module-level adapter per scheme on each new Session. Mounting a shared adapter keeps each call's own Session and close semantics while pooling sockets, which is the smallest diff. Session.close() closes its adapters, though, so a shared adapter must not be closed by per-call close() (subclass it or override close). (2) recovery_review.openai_post calls operation.own(session), and the operation closes it at the end. OwnedSSEStream also closes its session (the ADR-062 ownership rule). Both must close only the response, never a shared pool. (3) TASK-30015 (tearing down a wedged read) depends on closing the response or socket, and closing a response mid-stream discards its socket, which is fine. (4) Keep the TLS trust policy: the pooled adapter must use tls_trust.requests_verify() per request, which it does via session.verify. The adapter's max_retries differs per call site (Retry objects), which argues for one adapter per retry policy.
evidence:
session = create_default_session()        # hosted_chat.py:710, new pool per call
...
adapter = HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry_policy)
session.mount("https://", adapter)
...
stream = OwnedSSEStream(response=response, session=session)  # session closed at stream end
reason: create_default_session (Utils/egress.py:1012) builds a new DefaultTimeoutSession on every call; there is no shared session or pool. The cited sites each build a session per call: hosted_chat.py:710 (owned_json_post, with HTTPAdapter mounted per call), LLM_API_Calls.py:855, :1750, :2718 and :3559, qwencloud.py:1176, LLM_API_Calls_Local.py:282 and Summarization_General_Lib.py:1039. LLM_API_Calls.py:4299 uses the module-level requests.post, which also makes a Session per call. The session is closed at stream end (OwnedSSEStream owns it) or in a finally block, so no connection ever survives to the next request. The core review listed per-call Session construction as untimed and unverified (qa/core-code-review-2026-09-17/report.md:3031), and no open backlog task covers pooling; I grepped for create_default_session, keep-alive and connection pool.

title: OwnedSSEStream reads with iter_content(chunk_size=8192), which batches tokens into ~8 KB bursts on non-chunked SSE responses
trigger: Every streamed hosted-engine/zai/hosted-summarization response flows through OwnedSSEStream, but the burst only happens when the server sends close-delimited SSE (no Transfer-Encoding: chunked, no Content-Length), which mainstream HTTP/1.1 servers do not do.
cost: When triggered, delivery is held until 8192 decoded bytes, about 30-50 OpenAI-shape delta events (150-300 B each), or until the connection closes. The legacy iter_lines default chunk is 512 B, 16x smaller. The cost is zero on chunked responses. It was not measured, and the finder's estimate is sound.
fix: Iterate with read1-style semantics, for example a loop on response.raw.read1(8192) guarded by decode_content, so each read returns whatever bytes are available. Alternatively use chunk_size=512 to match the legacy behaviour.
fix_notes: urllib3 HTTPResponse.read1(amt, decode_content=True) exists in the installed 2.6.3, but only from urllib3 2.3 onward. pyproject pins neither requests nor urllib3, and requests allows urllib3>=1.21.1, so a read1 loop needs a hasattr fallback. Do NOT switch to iter_content(chunk_size=None): for a response that is not chunked, raw.stream(None) calls read(None), which reads to EOF and is strictly worse. The minimal safe fix is chunk_size=512 at both sites (legacy parity), or a read1 loop with a fallback. Apply the same change to qwencloud_streaming.py:920.
evidence:
self._chunks: Iterable[bytes] = response.iter_content(chunk_size=8192)
# urllib3 2.6.3 HTTPResponse.stream(): "A call will block until amt bytes have been
# read from the connection or until the connection is closed" (non-chunked branch)
reason: The code is real on pin 840ed2ca58. hosted_chat_streaming.py:181 is `response.iter_content(chunk_size=8192)`. It is built at hosted_chat.py:752 inside owned_json_post, which uses requests with stream=True. owned_json_post is the shared transport for hosted_provider_engine.py:1982, zai.py:424, hosted_chat.py:603 and the Summarization_General_Lib hosted streaming paths. I checked the installed libraries (requests 2.32.5, urllib3 2.6.3). requests.iter_content calls raw.stream(8192, decode_content=True). For a response that is not chunked, urllib3 stream() calls read(amt), and read(amt) loops `while len(self._decoded_buffer) < amt and data` (response.py:1146-1156). It therefore blocks until 8 KiB of decoded data arrives or the connection closes, so the finder's reading of the semantics is correct. Chunked responses go through read_chunked and are delivered per chunk, so they are unaffected. The finder missed a sibling site: qwencloud_streaming.py:920 has the same `iter_content(chunk_size=8192)`. The trigger is real but rare. requests always sends HTTP/1.1, and the usual SSE servers answer an HTTP/1.1 client with chunked encoding: uvicorn/starlette, Go net/http, cpp-httplib (llama.cpp), and nginx, which re-chunks a close-delimited upstream by default. Only an unusual close-delimited proxy or server hits the batching. This is a token-delivery latency issue on a worker-side iterator, not loop-blocking. P3 stands.

title: Import canvas rebuilds the full ingest state twice and deep-copies the queue 3x on every registry mutation; a folder submit is O(N^2) on the UI thread
trigger: Library ▸ Import, folder path, Start/Enter. The synchronous per-file submit loop fires the screen listener once per file with the Import canvas selected. Later mark_parsing, mark_writing and mark_done ticks (marshalled via call_from_thread) each fire it again, one loop turn per tick.
cost: Measured with the real LibraryIngestJobRegistry and build_library_ingest_state, using a listener that mirrors the chain (counts + count_duplicate_done + 2 builds + 1 extra jobs()). The machine was loaded, so absolute numbers run high. Submit loop: 1.1 s at 100 files, 14.4 s at 300, 73 s at 1000; with no listener, 3 ms at 100. Clean per-call numbers at 1000 jobs: jobs() 9.3 ms and build_state 10.7 ms, so about 50 ms per tick. These agree with the finder's 333 ms / 2.8 s / 33 s. The queue-panel recompose is not included. It coalesces during the sync loop, but each later tick (its own turn) recomposes every ungrouped row: DONE/QUEUED rows never collapse (_GROUPABLE_ROW_STATES).
fix: (1) Coalesce: the listener only sets `_ingest_regions_dirty` and schedules one `call_later(self._flush_ingest_regions)` per loop turn, so a 1000-file submit pays 1 build instead of 1000. (2) Build once per flush and pass that state to `_resync_library_ingest_footer`/`_library_ingest_shortcuts_for_current_state`, and have check_action read a cached `show_retry_last` instead of rebuilding. (3) Window the queue: build rows for the newest K jobs, plus a counted 'N more in this batch' summary, and extend run-collapsing to DONE/QUEUED batch runs so render and state are O(K) per tick. (4) Combine with F2 so reads are copy-free. Add a benchmark pinning a 1000-file submit with the real screen listener. TASK-32804.5's AC#1 benchmark omitted this listener.
fix_notes: Coalesce only the repaint half, not the whole listener. The batch-settle toast baseline (0->N / N->0 active-count crossings) and the consent-disarm check depend on seeing every mutation synchronously, so keep them per tick; counts() and count_duplicate_done() are copy-free O(N) and cheap. Set a dirty flag and schedule one call_later or call_after_refresh flush for _update_library_ingest_dynamic_regions plus the footer resync. Pass the state already built into _library_ingest_shortcuts_for_current_state instead of rebuilding it, and read show_retry_last from that state instead of calling jobs() again. Tests that assert canvas state right after a synchronous submit will need to await a pilot pause. Windowing the queue (newest K rows plus 'N more') changes the UX, so it needs owner sign-off under the Library design gates; treat it as a separate step. Add a benchmark that drives the real screen listener, which the TASK-32804.5 test omits.

The wrapper calls the screen's repaint, which does a full _build_library_ingest_state: jobs() deep-copies the whole queue at 20615, and build_library_ingest_state walks every job at state:2929 plus the group and count passes. title: LibraryIngestJobRegistry.jobs() deep-copies every job on every read (copy-on-read); six callers sit on per-mutation or per-interaction paths
trigger: Writer claim runs once per written job on the UI thread. The Parakeet listener fires on every registry mutation once the Parakeet source service exists (conditional). check_action runs only on an 'r' keypress; there is no Footer polling in Library. Row actions are per click.
cost: Measured, min of 15 runs: jobs() takes 0.98 ms at 100 jobs, 2.76 ms at 300 and 9.32 ms at 1000, against 0.049 ms for iter_jobs_for_listeners at 1000 (about 190x). A 1000-file import therefore spends about 1000 claims × up to ~9 ms of UI-thread time copying jobs, each spread across its own loop turn.
fix: Make reads free at the root instead of patching callers. Deep-freeze the mutable fields once at write time: MappingProxyType or tuples via a small _freeze() helper in submit/replace paths. The registry already swaps whole jobs with dataclasses.replace, so shared immutable snapshots are safe. Then jobs() returns a cached tuple that is invalidated by a mutation counter, and _copy_job becomes identity. Add a job_id→index dict for _find_index/get_job, and switch library_screen._library_ingest_job_by_id and app.py:4644/6770 to get_job or iter_jobs_for_listeners. Keep jobs()'s immutability contract, which is now enforced by type instead of by copying.

Downstream code mutates options it gets from jobs: _build_local_stt_dispatch does options.update(...), and _enqueue_library_ingest_snapshot does setdefault on the snapshot. A folder batch also shares one dict across jobs, so freezing at submit needs a per-batch copy first. The lazy root fix with no contract change: point the read-only UI-thread callers (claim at app.py:6770, the Parakeet listener, check_action, _library_ingest_job_by_id, and F1's three calls) at the existing iter_jobs_for_listeners or get_job, and add a job_id->index dict for _find_index and get_job. Only freeze at write time and cache jobs() if that turns out not to be enough.
reason: _copy_job (library_ingest_jobs.py:470) does 5 deepcopies per job, and jobs() (1592) copies every visible job on each call. iter_jobs_for_listeners (1609) already exists but has one adopter. Callers, verified one by one: (1) _claim_next_ingest_job_or_release (app.py:6770) runs on the UI thread via call_from_thread once per written job and copies the whole queue, including DONE rows, before finding the first ready payload. That is O(N) per claim, O(N^2) over an import, and not fixed by F1's coalescing. (2) _sync_parakeet_source_scopes (app.py:4644) is a registry listener, but only after _ensure_parakeet_source_service() has run. That happens through dictation, the Parakeet model surfaces, or a parakeet-onnx local STT job, so it is conditional. When present, it repeats the O(N^2)-per-folder-submit shape. (3) check_action('library_ingest_retry_last') (library_screen.py:25485): Library mounts no Textual Footer or KeyPanel (grep), so screen.active_bindings is not polled and this runs only on an actual 'r' keypress. The finder also claims a folder batch shares one ingest_options dict by reference; that is correct (submit stores `ingest_options or {}` uncopied). Rated P2 rather than P1: the triple copy on the listener path is F1's scope, and what is left (claim, conditional Parakeet listener) costs about 10 ms per event only at large queue sizes.

title: Collections-capture wiring runs ~40 ms of sync SQLite + filesystem work on the event loop 0.1 s after mount, every boot
trigger: Every app boot, 100 ms after deferred startup begins, which is inside the first-interaction window. Also every runtime server switch.
cost: Measured on a scratch LibraryCollectionsDB with the DB object pre-built, as in the app (the machine was loaded). The four function-local imports cost 18.4 ms on first call. The wiring per rep: repo ctor 14-27 ms, offline store ctor 18-48 ms, legacy probe 7-8 ms, 52-80 ms total. The finder's 40 ms figure is conservative.
fix: Compose in a worker: `@work(thread=True)` or `asyncio.to_thread`, using `operation_owned_connection(db)` as `_reconcile_collections_capture_startup` already does. Then install the repository, store, service and authority on the loop via call_from_thread. Keep `_DeferredCollectionsCaptureScope` as the placeholder until then. Alternatively, drop the eager timer and let the first Collections use call ensure_collections_capture_services, which already runs from async paths.
fix_notes: Moving the build to a worker needs two guards. (a) An in-flight marker, so a first Collections use arriving through _DeferredCollectionsCaptureScope or ensure_collections_capture_services while the worker runs does not compose a second, concurrent set: either await the worker's future or fall back to sync. (b) LibraryCollectionsDB connections are per-thread, so wrap the worker in operation_owned_connection(db) as _reconcile_collections_capture_startup does, to avoid leaking a pool-thread connection. Install the scope and call _activate_collections_capture_authority back on the loop via call_from_thread, because it touches runtime_policy and the server provider. The simpler alternative, dropping the eager timer and composing on first use, just moves the same ~50 ms onto the first Collections click.

title: Export preview sums LENGTH(CAST(content AS BLOB)) over every media row, forcing a read of the entire media corpus per scope change

Distro Pythons that link the system SQLite (for example Debian 12 with 3.40) lack it, so guard on sqlite3.sqlite_version_info or catch OperationalError ('no such function') and fall back to the current expression. For a UTF-8 database, octet_length(TEXT) equals LENGTH(CAST(... AS BLOB)); I verified the totals were equal, so the byte-count semantics are unchanged.

title: Video URL ingest runs three full yt-dlp extractions (metadata, size probe, download)
trigger: Every Library video URL ingest, in the parse worker.

Lazier than process_ie_result: set yt-dlp's native `ydl_opts['max_filesize'] = self.max_file_size`, drop the probe, and build `metadata` from the dict returned by the single `extract_info(download=True)`.

It then calls `download_video`, which runs another `extract_info(download=False)` probe at :315 and then `extract_info(download=True)` at :339, which returns the full info dict again. title: Non-UTF-8 text/HTML decode runs chardet over the entire file (up to the 50 MB cap)
trigger: Library ingest of a non-UTF-8 plaintext or HTML file with encoding 'auto' (the default), in the parse worker process, not on the UI loop.
cost: Measured, chardet 5.2.0: 0.83 s for 0.71 MB of latin-1 text versus 0.075 s for the first 64 KB, with the same verdict. About 1.2 s/MB, so roughly 58 s at the 50 MB cap.
fix: Detect on a bounded sample, e.g. chardet.detect(raw[:65536]), or feed a UniversalDetector in 64 KB blocks until `.done`. The decode still uses errors='replace', so a wrong guess on a late byte degrades visibly rather than failing. charset_normalizer is already installed and is also faster.
fix_notes: A naive `detect(raw[:65536])` fails when the prefix is pure ASCII. chardet returns 'ascii', and decoding the whole file as ascii with errors='replace' silently turns every later non-ASCII byte into U+FFFD. Instead, feed `chardet.UniversalDetector` in 64 KB blocks until `.done`: it stays undone on pure-ASCII input and keeps reading. Alternatively, map an 'ascii' verdict to cp1252 or utf-8-replace. charset_normalizer (installed as a requests dependency) samples by default and is a viable swap.

A naive two-pointer that advances past a segment once its end is before trans.start can skip a later overlapping segment. Use bisect_right on starts to bound the candidates (start < trans.end), and a conservative lower bound such as a running prefix max of ends. Keep iterating candidates in list order so the tie-break is unchanged: overlaps.sort(reverse=True) is stable and currently picks the earliest segment among equal overlaps.

trigger: Yes. It triggers on Library audio/video file ingest on Mac installs where parakeet-mlx is the (auto-selected) default provider, in the parse worker process. Also on any direct TranscriptionService.transcribe(provider='parakeet-mlx') call.
