title: Message-row class sync removes and re-adds managed classes on every sync, doubly restyling the whole Markdown reply subtree each streaming tick
known_task: none specific (TASK-26834 AC#2 is a related umbrella for Console subtree restyles on click interactions; it does not name streaming or this site)
trigger: Yes. The 5 Hz Console transcript poll runs for the whole duration of every streamed reply and agent turn. Each content delta or activity-status change alters the assistant-turn signature, which reaches _sync_message_classes on the Markdown answer row. Affects the default ROLE_ACCENTS style and IMMERSIVE_RP.
cost: I re-ran the finder's benchmarks in my own isolated scratch env (production bundle plus textual_css_fastpath). _sync_message_classes alone: 9.1 ms (10 paras, 18 nodes), 35.8 ms (40 paras, 54 nodes), 217.7 ms (120 paras, 150 nodes); the guarded version takes ~0.001 ms. Full refresh_messages per streaming tick in a transcript with 30 tools: 34.7 ms → 1.3 ms (40 paras) and 206.9 ms → 2.1 ms (120 paras). Activity-status tick: 38.8 → 7.2 ms and 215 → 6.7 ms. My machine ran ~1.4-1.7x slower than the finder's; the ratios hold. At 5 Hz a long reply occupies most of the loop.
fix: Make the class sync a diff. Compute want = set(_message_row_classes(...)). Then `widget.set_classes((set(widget.classes) - _MANAGED_MESSAGE_CLASSES) | want)`. Textual's classes setter only restyles when the set actually changes, so this is one guarded operation. Equivalently: remove only (current & managed) - want, and add only want - current. It is a one-function change covering both row types. Add a regression test that counts update_node_styles calls on an unchanged sync.
fix_notes: Correct and low risk. Use widget.update_classes({...}) or set_classes((set(widget.classes) - _MANAGED_MESSAGE_CLASSES) | want). The classes descriptor (dom.py:122-131) restyles only on inequality. No dependency on the forced restyle: newly appended Markdown blocks are styled by _register at mount, and Textual's own mount-time update_styles handles order/odd-even pseudo classes (widget.py:1489). No test references _sync_message_classes. Add a regression test that counts update_node_styles on an unchanged sync, and one that runs under NEUTRAL style.
reason: Code matches the pin (840ed2ca58). _sync_message_classes (console_transcript.py:1451) calls remove_class on every managed class and then add_class on every wanted class. In Textual 8.2.8, remove_class/add_class each call update_node_styles whenever the set actually changes (dom.py:1817-1851). App.update_styles (app.py:2504) then restyles the node plus walk_children, i.e. the whole Markdown subtree. The default transcript style is ROLE_ACCENTS (console_roleplay_identity.py:32), so an assistant row always carries the managed class 'console-transcript-message-role-assistant'. It is removed (restyle) and re-added (restyle) on every sync. Trigger traced: set_interval(0.2, _poll_transcript) (chat_screen.py:18947) → _sync_native_console_chat_ui → refresh_key (fingerprint includes content) → refresh_messages (chat_screen.py:18460). _reconcile_rows (console_transcript.py:7107) syncs only rows whose signature changed; the streaming assistant turn changes every tick. From there: _sync_assistant_turn_widget → ConsoleMarkdownMessage.sync_message (:1843) → churn. assistant_markdown defaults to true (config.py:4835). No guard, cache or offload anywhere. Users on NEUTRAL style are unaffected.

title: Selecting or deselecting an assistant Markdown row restyles its entire Markdown subtree on every j/k or click
corrected: tldw_chatbook/css/features/_console.tcss:1617 (source rule; tldw_cli_modular.tcss:7616 is the generated bundle copy)
known_task: TASK-26834 (related umbrella AC#2: Console subtree restyles >100 ms; does not name selection or this site)
trigger: Yes: per j/k keypress while navigating the transcript, and per click selection onto or off an assistant Markdown row.
cost: Reproduced with bench_sel_fp (my machine is slower). Toggling selection a0<->u0 costs 172.9 ms (40 paras) and 286 ms (120 paras) today. With the F1 diff guard it costs 39.3 ms and 126 ms. The slope is roughly linear in Markdown blocks, so the post-F1 residual is almost entirely the one legitimate full-subtree restyle.
fix: Keep the root class but add it with update=False. Then restyle only the nodes that have selection-dependent rules: the row itself, its header, and the .console-markdown-body direct child. Call self.app.stylesheet.update_nodes([...]), not the whole Markdown block tree. Restyle the roleplay-block descendants only when presentation.transcript_style is IMMERSIVE_RP or the row has a roleplay class. Alternative: move the selection accent to a sibling or inline style (styles.border_left) for non-RP rows.
fix_notes: The proposed fix is UNSAFE as written. '.console-transcript-message-selected' sets inherited properties on the row root (color: $ds-focus-fg; text-style: bold underline), and every Markdown descendant inherits them. Textual's Widget.visual_style caches on the node's OWN styles._cache_key (widget.py:4168-4176). _visual_style_cache and _rich_style_cache are cleared only by notify_style_update (widget.py:4683), which Stylesheet.replace_rules calls during a restyle. Restyling only the row, header and .console-markdown-body would therefore leave descendant paragraphs rendering stale selected or unselected styling. A safe variant: after update=False plus a root/header/body restyle, walk the descendants and call notify_style_update() + refresh() without selector matching (restyle the roleplay rp-* nodes fully). Alternatively, move the selection accent off inherited properties. Needs a snapshot test of selected-row rendering. Risk: medium-high.
reason: Verified the selected class is added to the row root (console_transcript.py:1436). select_message (:5319) → call_later(refresh_messages) → row signature (includes selected) → sync_message → class change → App.update_styles restyles the whole Markdown subtree. j/k/up/down in on_key (~:6569) → action_select_next/previous → select_message; clicks go through toggle_message_selection. The class change itself is legitimate, but Textual always restyles every descendant. The residual cost scales with the Markdown block count, so the subtree restyle dominates, not the action-row mount. Source CSS is css/features/_console.tcss:1617-1640 plus _console_panels.tcss:1208; the bundle line cited is its generated copy.

trigger: Yes. It fires on modal open (on_mount, then the first Resize) and on each terminal resize with the modal open. That is a less frequent path than keystroke or stream.
cost: Reproduced on my slower machine. Open plus first paint takes a median 749 ms with 350 class-triggered restyles, against 457 ms and 100 restyles with both syncs stubbed. trigger: Partly. Compose and constructor sites run on every Console visit (TASK-24452 re-mint), and resize and sync handlers run on their events. I did not trace per-visit execution counts end to end.

title.set_styles(height=None)

title: Whole-transcript O(n) walks run every 0.2 s tick regardless of the mounted window
trigger: Yes, 5 Hz during runs (the poll timer stops when idle). Only long sessions make it noticeable.
cost: Reproduced: 0.36 ms at 400 messages and 2.92 ms at 2,000 messages per set_messages; _transcript_rows adds 0.29-0.62 ms. That is about 1.5% of a core at 2k messages during runs, a minor cost.

Keep index_by_id and a message-id→message dict across ticks for thinking_detail_text and _message_by_id. Maintain the pruned-id set incrementally.

The path is library_screen.py:25169, then library_skills_controller.py:1915, then library_skills_canvas.py:1191 set_tool_filter. It runs synchronously on the event loop, with no debounce and no unchanged-guard.
cost: Estimated, not measured. Each keystroke costs O(catalog) Selection construction, one clear_options/add_options and one OptionList re-render. The catalog is builtin plus optional local tools only, with no MCP, so about 10 to 50 rows. That is well under about 1 to 2 ms per keystroke, on a rarely used field.
fix: Debounce the filter by about 150 ms using a set_timer token, or make the input Submitted-driven like the other Library filters. Optionally skip the rebuild when the filtered name list is unchanged.
fix_notes: The cheapest safe fix is to skip the rebuild when the filtered name tuple equals the last one. Store the last tuple on the canvas. This avoids a timer. A debounce is overkill at this row count. If one is added anyway, it must keep the rebuilding_tool_picker guard wrapped around the deferred rebuild, because the SelectedChanged handler (controller.py:1935) relies on it to ignore programmatic changes. It must also drop stale timers when the canvas recomposes or the editor closes. Checked state is re-derived from allowed_tools_csv on every rebuild, so skipping identical rebuilds does not lose selections. Making the filter Submitted-only would change UX, since live filtering is the intended behaviour, and is not recommended.
evidence:
def set_tool_filter(self, value: str) -> None:
        picker = self.query_one("#library-skill-tool-picker", SelectionList)
        self.rebuilding_tool_picker = True
        picker.clear_options().add_options(self._tool_picker_selections(value))
reason: The code matches the quote at tldw_chatbook/Widgets/Library/library_skills_canvas.py:1191-1197. set_tool_filter runs query_one, then clear_options().add_options(self._tool_picker_selections(value)). The caller chain is real and there is no debounce: library_screen.py:25169 @on(Input.Changed, '#library-skill-tool-filter') delegates to library_skills_controller.py:1915 handle_library_skill_tool_filter, which calls set_tool_filter synchronously on every keystroke. The input lives in the Skill editor's advanced_fields block (canvas.py:1671). I checked for a timer, a debounce or an unchanged-guard and found none. The cost is lower than the finder claimed. The catalog comes from _build_library_skill_tool_catalog (controller.py:930), which merges BuiltinToolProvider().list_catalog() with LocalToolProvider (38 LocalToolSpec entries, and only when console.local_tools_enabled is on). MCP tools are NOT included, so the '100+ tools (built-in plus MCP)' upper bound does not hold. Realistically there are about 10 to 50 rows. Each keystroke rebuilds at most about 50 Selection/OptionList rows, which is sub-millisecond to about 1 ms, on a rarely used Advanced-mode field. This is a real per-keystroke pattern but its cost is negligible, so it stays P3 hygiene. It is not on the verified-fine list. The Library 'no per-keystroke DB search' rule does not apply, because no DB is touched. I found no open backlog task covering it (grep of backlog/tasks for tool-filter/tool picker hits only task-19025 and task-13154.6, and neither is about performance).

title: Inspector conversation search: per-keystroke list rebuild plus a BEGIN IMMEDIATE keyword-index transaction, no debounce
trigger: Personas > Characters > select a local character > type in #personas-conversations-search. Each keystroke reaches the handler undebounced, and it only gates on mode, local runtime and character selection.
cost: Bare Textual 8.2.8 bench (scratch/verify65/bench_lv.py; pilot.pause baseline 21 ms). Placeholder swap from 21 rows to 1: 6.6 ms of mutation, about 27 ms including the frame. Rebuild of 21 rows (ListItem>Static): 14 ms of mutation, about 60 ms including the frame. That is about 27 ms on the loop per keystroke, plus about 60 ms whenever a worker result lands between keystrokes. The real app's stylesheet makes this larger. Each keystroke also adds one thread holding a BEGIN IMMEDIATE on ChaChaNotes; they serialize and are all but the last fenced out.
fix: (1) Debounce ConversationSearchChanged the way the library search is debounced: a set_timer(PERSONAS_SEARCH_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS) in the screen handler, or a widget-level timer like the pickers. (2) Call ensure_keyword_index once per character selection or first non-empty query, and use the read-only keyword_index_status() on later queries. (3) Skip the loading-placeholder rebuild when rows are already visible (just swap the tail text). (4) Longer term, render rows through OptionList or recycled ListItems (shared with F2).
fix_notes: (1) Debounce alone captures most of the win: reuse the PERSONAS_SEARCH_DEBOUNCE_SECONDS set_timer shape from :4068 and cancel it in _cancel_search_debounce or on character change. (2) Be careful about calling ensure_keyword_index only once. It also folds the dirty ledger and repairs a stale or failed generation for the current source revision. Using keyword_index_status afterwards would miss conversations created while the box is open (keyword_search revalidates existing candidates but cannot add new ones). A cheaper safe variant: skip ensure only when keyword_index_status() reports READY for the current revision. (3) Skipping the placeholder rebuild when rows are visible is safe via the existing _replace_conversation_tail path. (4) An OptionList conversion must preserve the ListView.Selected tail-action semantics and focus_conversation.

title: BuddyConversationModal 5 Hz projection tick copies the whole session transcript and re-claims decision views every tick
trigger: The Buddy conversation modal is opened through UI/Navigation/buddy_conversation.py:594 and ticks at 5 Hz for as long as it is open and not covered. The Buddy feature is opt-in, so this is a less frequent path.
cost: Bench (scratch/verify65/bench_replace.py): replace() over 1000 ConsoleChatMessage (43 fields) takes 5.1 ms per call, which is about 25 ms/s (about 2.5% of a core) at 5 Hz on a 1000-message session, higher than the finder's 3.44 ms. Typical sessions of 50-200 messages cost well under 1 ms per tick. Add 3 layout-forcing updates per tick on the modal screen. This is moderate and only while the modal is open, so P2 is correct.
fix: Use the existing lazy API: list(islice(store.iter_messages_newest_first(id), 60))[::-1] (console_chat_store.py:11877), or better, gate the whole tick on a store/controller revision counter. Claim the decision view once on mount/resume and release it on suspend/unmount instead of twice per tick. Compare against the last value before each Static.update. Replace repr(payloads) with a tuple of decision ids. Same anti-pattern as TASK-31506 (session switcher 5 Hz) and TASK-22204 (Done, Console tick); this modal is a new site.
fix_notes: Do NOT switch to store.iter_messages_newest_first as proposed. It calls the non-deferred _materialize_stream_buffer, which can persist the pending row to SQLite inline on the loop, regressing task-33081 (messages_for_session deliberately uses _materialize_stream_buffer_deferred). Add a tail-N accessor that uses the deferred variant, or gate on a store revision. The second show_decisions carries the rendered decision_id that answerable-decision accounting depends on, so do not drop it. Call set_decision_view only when (session_id, rendered decision_id) changes, and release it on suspend or unmount. Comparing before each Static.update and replacing repr(payloads) with a tuple of decision ids are safe.

title: Persona Buddy keeps a 10 Hz snapshot poll although the controller already pushes change notifications
trigger: Always on while the Buddy is enabled, open and mounted on the active primary screen. The feature is opt-in.
cost: Estimated at tens of microseconds per tick, 10 wakeups/s, well under 0.1% of a core. This is idle and battery hygiene, so P3 is correct.
fix: Have the controller expose the earliest lease expires_at (or schedule its own on_change at expiry). The widget then arms a one-shot set_timer to that deadline and relies on PersonaBuddyChanged for everything else. If a safety net is still wanted, keep a 1-2 s poll.
fix_notes: The poll is also the only thing that notices inputs the controller does not push: app focus changes (focused id is in the paint authority), screen.size compact transitions (21122 notes say on_resize does not recompute the compact classes) and lease expiry. Replacing it needs a one-shot timer at the earliest lease expires_at plus focus and resize hooks. A 1-2 s safety poll plus those hooks is the lower-risk step.

title: Every screen switch with the Buddy enabled re-runs the full visual resolve and PIL frame decode (per-view generation in the key, no frame cache)
trigger: Every primary-screen navigation, and every BaseAppScreen recompose that detaches the view, while the opt-in Buddy is enabled and open.
cost: Estimated. Most of the work is off-loop (to_thread), but Pixels.from_image and PIL work hold the GIL in bursts during the screen switch. There are also 2 SQLite reads including graph asset blobs and a remove plus mount of the view, and the pet paints blank until the resolve completes. It is bounded by MAX_PERSONA_BUDDY_PREPARED_FRAMES=128 and 1M cells. P2 is appropriate.
fix: Seed a new view's _accepted_render from controller.snapshot().visual when its cache_identity and render budget match, and drop view_generation from _resolution_authority (the is_current fence already guards stale views). In the controller, memoize _prepare_resolution / prepare_persona_buddy_frame with a small LRU keyed by (cache_identity, asset sha256, selected_frame, cols, lines).
fix_notes: Seeding _accepted_render from controller.snapshot().visual must keep the budget match (cols, lines) and the unavailable-confirm path intact. The resolution loop compares current_snapshot.visual identity for confirm_unavailable. Removing view_generation from the authority key alone changes nothing, because the new view's _resolved_authority is None. The simplest win is a small controller-side LRU on prepared frames keyed by (cache_identity, asset sha256, selected_frame, cols, lines). Also consider decoding all frames from one Image.open to avoid repeated seek-from-zero.

title: Retention runs reflog expire + gc --prune=now on every live shadow repo on every launch, even when nothing was pruned
trigger: Yes, but off-loop: once per launch at about 65 s after start, then every 24 h, via asyncio.to_thread (app.py:19010-19016, 19080).
cost: Measured: a no-op gc on an already-packed repo takes 70-170 ms of background CPU per live root. The expensive gc (about 2.6 s on 41-96 MB of loose objects) only happens when there is real packing to do, and that packing is needed.
fix: Skip reflog/gc for a root when this pass deleted no rows for it, or persist a last-gc timestamp and gc at most weekly, or use `gc --auto`.
fix_notes: The proposed fix is harmful. Skipping gc when no rows were pruned would let loose objects pile up without limit, because gc.auto=0, and every later git operation would slow down. `gc --auto` is a no-op under the pinned gc.auto=0 unless it runs as `git -c gc.auto=N gc --auto`. If anything is worth doing, it is that (gc only past a loose-object threshold), or a `count-objects` check first. Neither is worth doing for about 0.15 s of background work per launch.

The premise is wrong, though. change_tracking.py:19/376 pins gc.auto=0 on every shadow repo ('GC is scheduled by retention, never mid-turn'), so this pass is the ONLY thing that ever packs the loose objects that snapshots (git add/commit) and revert staging write. Row pruning cannot free objects in a live repo anyway, because ancestry keeps every snapshot reachable (module docstring lines 8-13). So gating gc on rows_pruned is unrelated to whether gc has work to do. I measured the cost in scratch repos. The first gc of a repo with loose objects took 2.6-2.7 s, and that is necessary work. A repeat gc on an already-packed repo took 0.07 s (10k files, 1.8 MB pack) and 0.15-0.17 s (5k incompressible files, 96 MB pack). reflog expire took 0.01 s. So a 'no-op' launch wastes about 0.1-0.2 s of background CPU per live root, once per launch, off-thread. Repo size is also capped by change_bounds (20k files / 2 GB per root).

cost: Measured on a 46.8k-entry synthetic tree: the full walk takes 602-661 ms, of which the per-directory root re-open is 297 ms. A query truncated at 500 matches takes about 67-72 ms. This is off-loop worker time and delays results rather than freezing the UI.
fix: When the new query extends the previous one, filter the previous matches instead of re-walking. Walk with a parent-fd stack (openat relative to the parent fd) instead of re-resolving from the root.
fix_notes: Do NOT keep an open fd for every entry on the `pending` list. On wide trees that list holds thousands of directories and would hit EMFILE. Use a depth-first stack of (fd, scandir iterator), so open fds are bounded by depth, and open each child with openat(name, O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY, dir_fd=parent_fd). The per-directory root re-open is a deliberate binding-swap re-check against root dev/ino, so keep one root revalidation per walk, or re-check periodically. Refining from the previous query's matches is only valid when the prior result was COMPLETE (not TRUNCATED at 500 or PARTIAL at 50k visits) and the new casefolded needle contains the old one. It also serves stale results if files change between keystrokes. Separately, time-throttle on_progress (for example every 100 ms or 1000 entries) so the walk does not keep the event loop repainting the status line.
evidence:
while pending:
    parent_parts = pending.pop()
    root_fd, error_code = _open_root_descriptor(current)
    directory_fd, ... = _open_target_descriptor(root_fd, parent_parts, "dir")  # openat per component
reason: The code matches. filter_paths (file_inspector.py:437-499) pops each pending directory, calls _open_root_descriptor (open+fstat of the root, :443), and then _open_target_descriptor, which dups the fd and runs openat for EVERY path component plus an fstat (:857-894). Every directory is re-resolved from the root. The caller is ConsoleWorkspaceFilesModal: Input.Changed at :1083 sets a 150 ms timer, then _request_filter submits to the latest-only _OperationLane, which runs the walk in asyncio.to_thread (:217). The finder missed that is_cancelled checks `generation != self._generation`, so a superseded walk stops at its next entry. Wasted work is therefore bounded by the gap between keystrokes, and only the settled query walks the whole tree. That part of the claim is overstated. I benchmarked the real filter_paths on a synthetic 46.8k-entry tree (4681 dirs, depth <= 5) with only _revalidate stubbed. A full no-match walk took 602-661 ms, and the per-directory root re-open alone took 297 ms, about 45-50% of the walk. That is avoidable latency on each settled query in a modal, it scales with tree size, and it holds the GIL for the Python-side work. So P2, not P3. A related cost: on_progress fires per entry, and the coalesced _FilterProgressReady is re-posted as soon as the UI drains the previous one. That keeps the event loop running Static.update continuously for the whole walk.

title: Server mode: the first TLDWAPIClient construction imports client.py plus 51 schema modules (about 420 ms) on the event loop, 0.1 s after first paint
trigger: Server-mode boot: after first paint, a 0.1 s set_timer runs a sync callback on the loop: `_deferred_wire_collections_capture_services`, then `_activate_collections_capture_authority`, then `provider.build_client()`, then a function-local import of tldw_api.client. This happens once per process. It happens again on a runtime switch to server (async `handle_runtime_backend_changed`, app.py:11548). If no auth token is present, the first server-service await from a screen handler pays it instead, also on the loop.
cost: Measured in the isolated env (scratch HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH, PYTHONPATH set to the audit tree, the tldw_chatbook module verified to resolve to the audit tree), with httpx, pydantic, loguru and kanban_schemas pre-imported, warm .pyc. `import tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.client` took 574 / 638 / 670 ms and loaded 86 new modules, 51 of them `*_schemas`. That is higher than the finder's 396 to 437 ms, probably because the machine was under concurrent load. At least 400 ms is confirmed.
fix:
Cheapest fix: warm the import off the loop.
- In `_schedule_deferred_startup_work`, when `runtime_policy.state.active_source == 'server'`, run `await asyncio.to_thread(importlib.import_module, 'tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.client')` before the capture wiring. For example, turn `_deferred_wire_collections_capture_services` into a deferred-startup task that awaits the to_thread import first.
- Do the same at the top of `handle_runtime_backend_changed` before `_activate_collections_capture_authority`.
- Alternatively, run `build_client()` inside the thread.

Add a guard test: in server mode, `tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.client` must be in `sys.modules` before `_activate_collections_capture_authority` runs on the loop, or the activation must not import it.

The structural reduction is F2.
fix_notes:
Reuse what already exists rather than adding new machinery. Make the server branch of `_activate_collections_capture_authority` wait on an off-loop warm-up: `await asyncio.to_thread(importlib.import_module, 'tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.client')`. Better, `await asyncio.to_thread(provider.build_client)`, which also moves the keyring and credential reads in `get_active_context()`/`_resolve_auth_token` off the loop.

That requires converting the sync timer callback into a deferred-startup task (`_create_deferred_startup_task` already exists).

Three caveats:
1. Do not race the warm-up. If the loop imports client.py while a thread is mid-import, the loop blocks on the per-module import lock for the rest of the import, which is no better. The loop must await the thread.
2. A thread import still holds the GIL during pydantic class construction. The loop only gets switch-interval slices, the same trade-off the codebase measured for the splash pre-import at app.py:844-860. The UI stays responsive but runs slower during the warm-up.
3. `handle_runtime_backend_changed` needs the same await. Combining this with F2(a) (defer_build) halves the remaining thread time.

A guard test asserting that client.py is in sys.modules before activation runs on the loop is reasonable.

app.py:16342  self.set_timer(DEFERRED_COLLECTIONS_CAPTURE_WIRING_DELAY_SECONDS,  # = 0.1
                  self._deferred_wire_collections_capture_services)
app.py:9915   client = provider.build_client()   # in _activate_collections_capture_authority, server branch

Checked on pin 840ed2ca58. bootstrap.py:195 has the function-local `from tldw_chatbook.tldw_api import TLDWAPIClient` inside build_runtime_api_client, and its own comment admits the ~450 ms cost.

The trigger chain is real and runs entirely on the loop:
- `_schedule_deferred_startup_work` (app.py:16325, called after `_ui_ready`) arms `set_timer(DEFERRED_COLLECTIONS_CAPTURE_WIRING_DELAY_SECONDS=0.1, _deferred_wire_collections_capture_services)` at app.py:16342.

The second trigger, async `handle_runtime_backend_changed` at app.py:11548, is also confirmed.

title: client.py god module needs 544 schema names at runtime from 51 modules, so every consumer of TLDWAPIClient pays for about 1,300 pydantic models; defer_build alone halves it
known_task: TASK-285 (Done; it identified client.py as the remaining cost centre but no follow-up task was filed)
trigger: The first TLDWAPIClient resolution in any process pays it: server-mode app (F1), MCP stdio server, tools and tests. It is paid in full even when a session uses one domain. The import cost itself is a one-off per process.
cost: I reproduced the finder's scratch experiment on pydantic 2.12.5 with no repo edits. Baseline import took 600 / 601 ms; with `pydantic.BaseModel.model_config['defer_build']=True` it took 263 / 299 ms, a reduction of about 50 to 56%. The deferred model reported `__pydantic_complete__=False` until first use. The 51-schema-module and 86-new-module counts were confirmed in the F1 probe.
fix:
Two-step plan:

(a) Low risk: add `model_config = ConfigDict(defer_build=True)` through a shared base, or on each schema module's root models. Keep the existing `extra=` settings by merging configs. This halves import cost and changes no API.

(b) Structural: stop importing response and request classes at `client.py` module scope.
- Move the 382 annotation-only names under `if TYPE_CHECKING:` (the file already has `from __future__ import annotations`).
- Resolve the 544 runtime names lazily through the existing PEP 562 facade, for example `from . import __init__ as _api` and then `_api.NoteResponse.model_validate(...)`, or per-method function-local imports. The facade's `__getattr__` then imports only the domains actually used.

Alternative for (b): split `TLDWAPIClient` into per-domain mixin modules that are imported lazily.

Keep `Tests/Packaging/test_tldw_api_import_closure.py` and add a probe asserting that `import tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.client` loads fewer than N `*_schemas` modules.
fix_notes:
(a) defer_build. Do it through a shared base or a per-module `model_config`. Never mutate `BaseModel.model_config` globally, because that would leak into every pydantic model in the process, including LLM and config models. Merge with each model's existing config (extra=, populate_by_name and so on). The trade-off: the first validation of each model builds its schema (about 0.5 ms or more, more for nested models), and on a hot path such as a streamed-chunk model that lands on the first chunk. That is acceptable, but be aware of it.

(b) Do not use the suggested `from . import __init__ as _api`. It imports a SECOND module object, `tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.__init__`, and re-executes the package body. Use `from tldw_chatbook import tldw_api as _api` or function-local imports instead.

The ~550 runtime sites make (b) a sprawling mechanical rewrite, which is exactly why TASK-285 stopped. Do (a) first, then (b) per domain. The proposed probe in `Tests/Packaging/test_tldw_api_import_closure.py` is a good regression net.

title: Each TLDWAPIClient owns a private httpx pool and SSLContext; about 30 from_config services mean about 30 fragmented pools, each paying about 9 ms of SSLContext build on the loop plus a fresh TLS handshake
trigger: Server mode: the first call through each distinct from_config service (Tools, MCP governance, Text2SQL, Evaluations, Watchlists, Kanban and so on) runs `_get_client()` on the loop inside an async service method. This is once per service per process, on less common screens.
cost: Measured with httpx 0.28.1: `AsyncClient(verify=True)` construction has a median of 9.8 ms (minimum 9.1 ms) over 15 runs, against 0.14 ms when passing a shared `create_ssl_context()`. The extra handshakes per pool are real but estimated and do not block the loop.
fix:
Option 1: in client.py, cache one process-wide SSLContext per verify setting. For example, add `_shared_ssl_context()` using `functools.lru_cache` over `httpx.create_ssl_context()` when `ssl_verify is True`, and pass it as `verify=`. An SSLContext is safe to share across clients.

Option 2, the larger win: build the `from_config` services from `self.server_context_provider`, or have `build_runtime_api_client_provider_from_config` return one app-wide memoized provider per resolved config. That gives one pool and one handshake, and shutdown closes everything.
fix_notes:
Option 1, done centrally: return a process-cached SSLContext from `tls_trust.httpx_verify()` (lru_cache over `httpx.create_ssl_context()`) instead of `True`. That reaches every httpx client in the app, not only TLDWAPIClient. There are two risks:
- Tests that assert `verify is True` will break.
- A cached context freezes SSL_CERT_FILE/SSL_CERT_DIR and trust-env at first use.

Option 2 is NOT a pure performance change. The legacy from_config providers resolve the endpoint and credentials from the legacy `[tldw_api]` app_config, whereas server_context_provider uses the active server target plus keyring credentials. Rerouting them changes which server and credential each service talks to, so it needs a behavioural review, possibly under the scope-service consolidation (TASK-32898/ADR-177).

At minimum, close the legacy providers' cached clients at shutdown.
reason:
client.py:1303 `_get_client` lazily builds `httpx.AsyncClient(..., verify=self.ssl_verify)` for each TLDWAPIClient.

ssl_verify comes from `Utils/tls_trust.httpx_verify()`, which returns the bool `True` under the default policy. httpx 0.28 therefore builds a fresh SSLContext and loads certifi on every client. It only returns a (possibly shared) SSLContext when a custom CA is configured.

app.py has exactly 29 `Server*Service.from_config(` sites (for example ServerToolsService at 10880). Each creates its own `LegacyConfigServerClientProvider` (bootstrap.py:263-266), which caches a private client (build_client near line 250). There are 13 `from_server_context_provider(` sites, which share `RuntimeServerContextProvider`'s single cached client.

Shutdown closes only `server_context_provider.close_cached_client()` (app.py:17801-17808), so the legacy providers' AsyncClients are never closed.

`_get_client` is awaited inside async service methods called from screen handlers, so the ~10 ms construction runs on the loop the first time each legacy service is used. No open task covers this.

title: All binary downloads are fully buffered in memory (_binary_request -> response.content); the chatbook export download then writes the whole blob synchronously from a button handler
trigger: A user action: pressing 'download-server-job' in Chatbook export management runs an awaited chain in the button handler on the loop. The network transfer is async, but the full body is held in RAM, and the sync write plus full fsync of the whole blob then blocks the loop. The path is infrequent.
cost: Estimated, not measured. The RSS spike equals the export size. The loop freeze is the write plus a full-barrier fsync of the whole blob, which on macOS F_FULLFSYNC can reach hundreds of ms for exports of 100 MB or more. Sizes of 50 to 500 MB are plausible for exports that contain media but were not verified.
fix:
Add one streaming primitive to `TLDWAPIClient`: `async def _download_to_path(method, endpoint, dest, params=None)`.
- Use `client.stream(...)`, with the same redirect and error handling as `_stream_request`.
- Write `aiter_bytes(1 << 20)` chunks to a temp file through `asyncio.to_thread(f.write, chunk)`, or open the file in a worker.
- `os.replace` at the end, keeping the 0o600 temp-file semantics of `atomic_write_bytes`.

Expose `download_chatbook_export_to_path` and use it in `ServerChatbookService.download_export_job`. Keep `_binary_request` for small payloads.

client.py:1491 `_binary_request` uses a non-streaming `client.request(...)` and returns `ReadingExportResponse(content=response.content, ...)` at 1517-1518, so the whole body is buffered.

`download_chatbook_export` at 13781 delegates to it. `ServerChatbookService.download_export_job` (server_chatbook_service.py:556-572) awaits the download, then calls `atomic_write_bytes(destination_path, content, mode=0o600)` at 571 synchronously inside the async def. The finder overstated the number of client methods sharing the primitive: `_binary_request(` appears 18 times in client.py including the def, so there are 17 call sites. No open task covers this.

title: The first TLDWAPIClient build imports the whole ~54-module schema surface synchronously on the event loop. For server-mode users this is a ~0.4 s freeze on every boot, just after first paint.
known_task: TASK-32804 (umbrella only; no specific open task)
trigger: Every boot with runtime active_source=='server' and a stored token: 0.1 s timer after _ui_ready, on the event loop. Also every on-loop switch to server via handle_runtime_backend_changed. Local-mode boots are unaffected because of the early return at app.py:9889. Even if this site were moved, about 50 other `.build_client()` call sites in Server*Service async methods would pay the same import on the loop at the first server call.
cost: Measured in an isolated subprocess (scratch HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH, PYTHONPATH=audit tree). Fresh import of tldw_api.client with pydantic, httpx and loguru preloaded: 549-695 ms over 3 runs. Incremental cost after `import tldw_chatbook.app`: 598-660 ms over 2 runs, loading 54 more tldw_api modules. That is at or above the finder's 402-445 ms (this machine may be loaded), so the claim of a ≥0.4 s GIL-holding freeze shortly after first paint holds. Keyring and TLS costs in get_active_context and the client ctor are extra and were not measured.
fix: Move the import off the loop. (1) Warm `tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.client` in the existing screen pre-import thread (_schedule_screen_preimport / _preimport_screens pattern), or in a dedicated to_thread, when the runtime source is server. Schedule it ahead of the 0.1 s capture-wiring timer, or make _activate_collections_capture_authority obtain the client via `await asyncio.to_thread(provider.build_client)`. (2) Combine with F2 (defer_build), which halves the block. (3) Longer term: client.py already has `from __future__ import annotations`, so annotation-only schema names can move under TYPE_CHECKING and runtime ones can use per-method or per-domain lazy imports. Add a guard test that boots with a server-mode fixture config and asserts tldw_api.client is not imported on the loop. Related umbrella: TASK-32804 (sync work on the event loop).
fix_notes: Do NOT call provider.build_client via asyncio.to_thread as proposed. RuntimeServerContextProvider.build_client mutates _cached_client/_cached_client_key with no lock (server_context.py:325-339), and other loop callers use it too, so running it off-loop races. The safer root-cause fix warms only the module import in a thread (`await asyncio.to_thread(importlib.import_module, 'tldw_chatbook.tldw_api.client')`) and runs capture activation after that completes, e.g. as a _create_deferred_startup_task that awaits the warm import and then calls _deferred_wire_collections_capture_services. Starting a warm thread in parallel is not enough: if the loop reaches the import while the thread holds the module import lock, the loop blocks until the thread finishes. The warm thread still contends for the GIL, but with a 5 ms switch interval the UI stays responsive instead of freezing for 0.5 s. Do the same for handle_runtime_backend_changed before line 11547. Combine with F2. Moving client.py's names under TYPE_CHECKING only helps for annotation-only names; most are constructed or validated at runtime inside methods, so that is a large diff. The proposed server-mode boot guard test is worthwhile.

title: Every depth-0 ChaChaNotes transaction pays a ~7 ms storage-admission handshake; Console message writes cost 8-11 ms and 2-3 run on the event loop per send
known_task: TASK-32804.1 (related: same admission handshake, fixed only for config reads; DB transactions not covered)
trigger: Every Console send: at least 2 depth-0 transactions run synchronously on the event loop in the async _run_direct_provider_reply (the trajectory flush in _attach_stream_usage, and the terminal update_message_content in mark_message_complete). Also every on-loop feedback, trace-event and usage-only write, and every agent tool marker (worker thread).
cost: Measured (isolated scratch profile): 6.7-10.6 ms per empty depth-0 transaction against 0.003 ms raw. The handshake costs 245 opens per transaction. Estimated 8-15 ms per send on the loop at a production path depth, 15-30 ms at the scratch depth.
fix: Amortize admission the way TASK-32804.1 did for config reads (_warm_config_cache_hit). Cache a validated admission lease per (pid, bootstrap root, db path) on the participant, revalidate only when the registry/pause generation changes (storage._changed notifications), and keep the full _scope walk for the first acquisition and after a pause. Nested and borrowed transactions already skip BEGIN, so make sure they also skip the handshake. In-slice follow-up: for update_message_content with writes disabled, avoid the extra citation owner-transition work (about 2.8 ms).
fix_notes: Risk is high, as the finder says. Admission exists so that a local pause (backup capture or restore) can close admission and drain every holder. A cached lease must still re-check `_pause is None`, `participant.closed` and core retirement under _lock on every operation (those checks are cheap), and the pause and drain path must invalidate or retire cached leases, or drain() will wait forever on a live lease. Before adding a new cache, consider reusing the process-lifetime startup hold (_startups[key] from admit_startup) and re-deriving _scope only when a registry or control-record generation changes. At minimum, move the _scope file I/O out from under the global _lock. Nested transactions already take the reuse branch, so they need no change. The citation-owner-transition sub-fix (~2.8 ms) is separate and low-value.
evidence:
# ChaChaNotes_DB.py:24221 TransactionContextManager.__enter__
    self._maintenance_context = _core_operation(self.db)   # -> acquire_storage per depth-0 txn
# chat_persistence_service.py:2873 (citation repo always wired by console_runtime)
    with self.db.transaction(immediate=True) as cursor:
        result = coordinated_update()
# controller:27275 (async, on loop)
    completed = self.store.mark_message_complete(assistant_message_id)
reason: Code is as quoted on 840ed2ca58. TransactionContextManager.__enter__ (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:24222) calls participants._core_operation -> _RepositoryParticipant.operation -> storage_admission._repository_operation. At depth 0 that path calls acquire_storage(path) (storage_admission.py:835/854). Every call redoes bootstrap.startup_permission, qualified_for, admission_authority and two _scope passes: _records, _registry with flock and a JSON read, _binding with pinned_directory walks. Nested transactions reuse the outer operation, so they are cheap. I re-measured in an isolated scratch profile: an empty depth-0 transaction() costs 6.7-10.6 ms and an IMMEDIATE one 7.9-10.1 ms. acquire_storage+close alone costs 4.3-5.9 ms. A raw sqlite BEGIN IMMEDIATE/COMMIT costs 0.003 ms. cProfile shows 245 posix.open, 69 lstat, 36 stat and 10 listdir per transaction. Trigger, verified: _run_direct_provider_reply (console_chat_controller.py:26857, an async def on the loop, not offloaded; only the _run_durable_db_call sites use to_thread) runs these synchronously on the success path. (1) _attach_stream_usage -> store.record_trajectory_timing(flush=True) -> write_trajectory_rows -> db.upsert_trajectory_rows, which is a transaction(immediate=True). (2) store.mark_message_complete (27275) -> _persist_existing_terminal/_persist_existing_message -> persistence.update_message_content (chat_persistence_service.py:2873, transaction(immediate=True)). That is at least 2 depth-0 transactions per send on the loop, plus feedback, trace and usage writes. Extra evidence: the second _scope pass (the one with file I/O) runs inside `with _lock:` on the process-wide RLock, so off-loop DB work (F5 discovery, pooled workers) contends with on-loop transactions. Not covered by an open task. TASK-31502 measures the quiescence locks at about 23 us per transaction. TASK-32804.1 fixed the same handshake only for config reads, by serving warm hits ahead of the guard, not by amortizing admission. The scratch path has about 11 components against about 6 in production, so production is probably about 4-5 ms per transaction, about 8-15 ms per send. That is still P1 per-send.

title: Scope service retires its worker SQLite connection after every call; each new connection spawns a Python helper subprocess (~65 ms), so every Library conversations page, Console resume and Home snapshot pays it again
trigger: Library conversations tab (every page, search submit and visit), Console resume of a saved conversation, the Home content snapshot and the STTS conversation list. Each lands on an asyncio.to_thread worker whose connection the previous call closed.
cost: Measured: +~60-77 ms per call (85.6 ms vs 8.2 ms median) and exactly 1 subprocess.Popen per call with close-after-call; 67.8 ms per fresh get_connection.
fix: Keep the TASK-31993.5 retirement guarantee without paying it per call. Route local conversation reads through one dedicated single-thread executor per CharactersRAGDB that owns a long-lived connection, and close it only from the recovery pause/retire hook (participant.retiring_threads / storage pause). Alternatively, cache the helper's prepare verdict per (st_dev, st_ino, mode) for the process lifetime and re-run it only on an identity change, so reopening a thread-local connection no longer spawns a subprocess.
fix_notes: The close-per-call is intentional (TASK-31993.5 AC#1). Recovery drain cannot close another thread's cached handle, because _core_closing refuses a foreign-thread close. TASK-31993.5 AC#3 also says 'no new general thread framework', so a dedicated per-DB executor contradicts a recorded constraint and needs an explicit decision. It must also let the pause hook submit the close onto that executor's own thread. Caching the helper's prepare verdict per (st_dev, st_ino, mode) weakens what the out-of-process helper exists to do: verify and prepare private file modes and identity at open time, a TOCTOU/symlink boundary. Treat it as a security review, not a perf tweak. Fixing it in the helper would also speed up every other connection-churn site (Subscriptions/db_offload.py has the same close-per-call pattern, and TASK-24457's 8 per-visit connections).
reason: chat_conversation_scope_service.py:189 (list_and_close) and :399 (read_local_tree) call db.close_connection() after every to_thread call. The next call on a pooled worker therefore opens a new thread-local connection through ChaChaNotes _get_thread_connection -> connect_private_sqlite (private_sqlite.py:1878). On non-Windows that path calls prepare_in_helper -> HelperLease.start, which runs subprocess.Popen([sys.executable,'-I','-S',helper]) at private_sqlite_process.py:366. Re-measured in isolation, counting Popen calls: list_conversations on a pooled thread costs 85.6 ms median (71.0 min) with 1.0 Popen per call when closing after each call, against 8.2 ms (6.4 min) and 0.08 Popen per call when the connection is kept. A fresh-thread get_connection alone costs 67.8 ms. Callers verified: library_conversations_controller._load_library_conversation_page (line 1204) uses app.chat_conversation_scope_service.list_conversations for each page and search. console_conversation_hydration (line 340) uses get_conversation_tree for Console resume. home_screen:501 and STTS_Window:735 call list_conversations. The work is off-loop but adds about 60-80 ms of user-visible latency, plus a Python child process, on every Library conversations page and every Console resume. TASK-24457 (Library opens 8 fresh connections per visit) is related, but it attributes the cost to PRAGMAs and screen re-instantiation. This finding adds a new site (the scope service's deliberate close-per-call) and new evidence: the helper subprocess spawn dominates connection cost, which applies to every connection-churn finding.

title: Every send re-base64-encodes all history images 2-3 times and json-digests the multi-MB data URLs for the cost fingerprint, all on the event loop
trigger: Per Console send (and regenerate/retry) in a session with image attachments in history: 3 payload builds and 2 full-payload digests on the event loop.
cost: Micro-benchmark (stdlib only, same operations): build 7.74 ms, fingerprint 22.06 ms for 5 x 1.5 MB images, so about 67 ms per send; linear in image bytes, about 135 ms at the 10-image cap.
fix: Cache the data-URL string per attachment: MessageAttachment is immutable, so memoize on the object or in a bounded dict keyed by attachment id. In fingerprint_payload, digest image parts by a precomputed sha256 of the raw bytes (computed once at attach time) instead of json-dumping the base64 URL. Reuse the dispatch build for the baseline fingerprint where the stages match, or compute it off-loop with asyncio.to_thread.
fix_notes: Digest image parts with a precomputed hash of the raw bytes. This is the biggest win (~2/3 of the cost). Baseline and current fingerprints must both use the same new scheme; stored baselines are in-memory only, so no migration is needed. A memoized data-URL cache keeps about 1.33x the image bytes per attachment alive, so bound it (for example a WeakKeyDictionary on the immutable attachment, or an LRU by total bytes). Reusing the dispatch build for the baseline is only valid when turn_context and the stages match (the baseline is the pre-skill-substitution stage), so keep the separate build or pass the pre-substitution list through.
reason: Code verified. _provider_message_payloads (console_chat_controller.py:29929) calls attachment_core.image_url_part, a fresh base64 encode per image per build. It runs in _submit_draft_body (line 10717, the dispatch payload) and again at line 26000 (baseline_messages, used only for fingerprint_payload). After the send, chat_screen._build_console_cost_state (line 11806) calls controller.compute_current_fingerprint, which does another _provider_messages_for_session plus fingerprint_payload. That call is gated on a payload_revision change while the session is not running, which happens once per completed send. fingerprint_payload -> _digest json.dumps(sort_keys) the whole row, data URL included, then sha1s it. All of these run on the loop, in async defs and a UI refresh. The image count is capped by the max_history_images budget (default 10); images are resized to 2048 px and capped at 10 MB. A standalone micro-benchmark reproduces the finder's numbers: for 5 x 1.5 MB images, one build costs 7.7 ms and one fingerprint 22.1 ms, about 67 ms per send; at the 10-image cap it would be about 135 ms. Downgraded from P1 to P2. The cost occurs only in sessions whose history holds image attachments, and it scales with image bytes: a single ~1 MB image is about 9 ms per send. The rubric puts cost that 'only scales with large data' at P2. The worst case can exceed 100 ms, so it sits at the top of P2. No open task covers it (grepped backlog for fingerprint_payload, image_url_part and compute_current_fingerprint).

title: write_trajectory_rows retries with time.sleep backoff (5 attempts, each able to wait the 15 s busy timeout); some callers are on the event loop
trigger: Only when upsert_trajectory_rows raises: lock held past the 15 s busy timeout, admission refused during a pause, or an integrity error. Reached on the loop from the per-send trajectory flush and from feedback and trace event writes.
cost: Estimated: about 0.3 s of loop-blocking sleep plus 5 x about 5-10 ms handshakes per failed batch; pathological lock case up to 5 x 15 s.
fix: Remove the sleep loop. SQLite's busy_timeout already waits for the winner, and upsert_trajectory_rows re-derives seq inside BEGIN IMMEDIATE. At most retry once without sleeping, and move the on-loop flush callers behind asyncio.to_thread (or the controller's _run_durable_db_call).
fix_notes: Do not retry deterministic errors (IntegrityError, RecoveryRequired or CharactersRAGDBError subclasses). At most retry once, with no sleep, on OperationalError 'database is locked'. Moving the on-loop flush behind _run_durable_db_call or to_thread must keep the ordering the store relies on (the trajectory flush comes before the terminal mark).
evidence:
for attempt in range(5):
    try:
        self.db.upsert_trajectory_rows(rows)
        return True
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        last_error = exc
        time.sleep(0.02 * (attempt + 1))
reason: Verified at chat_persistence_service.py:3198-3208: 5 attempts of db.upsert_trajectory_rows with time.sleep(0.02*(attempt+1)) between them, about 0.3 s total sleep. upsert_trajectory_rows opens transaction(immediate=True) (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:15667) on a connection with timeout=15 (line 3492). SQLITE_BUSY on BEGIN IMMEDIATE already waits on the busy handler, so the sleep adds nothing for lock contention. The realistic triggers are deterministic failures that retry needlessly: a storage-admission refusal during a recovery pause, or a constraint error. Each costs about 0.3 s of sleep plus 5 admission handshakes (F1) on the loop, and a sustained lock can cost up to 5 x 15 s. On-loop callers are verified: _attach_stream_usage -> record_trajectory_timing(flush=True), and record_feedback_event (console_chat_store.py:14848). Rare, so P3.

title: ConsoleActivityReceiptService holds its RLock across DB I/O that loop-side readers wait on; publish_ordinary re-reads all unseen receipts on the loop
known_task: TASK-32804 (umbrella: sync work on the loop); TASK-31506 covers only the poll frequency, not this I/O
trigger: publish_ordinary runs synchronously on the event loop for each inactive/hidden-session COMPLETED/FAILED/STOPPED transition, via _set_run_state called from async controller methods. The drain thread holds the RLock across DB writes while the switcher's 5 Hz poll and the workspace/buddy renders read it on the loop.
cost: The finder's figure is about 9 ms per background completion on the loop (not re-measured here), growing with the unseen count because of the full paged reload. Worst case is bounded by busy_timeout=5000 ms under AgentRuns write contention. Lock contention with hydration is a rare, roughly 16 ms, one-shot window.
fix: Do DB I/O outside the lock and publish the immutable snapshot tuple and generation by atomic attribute assignment, so readers need no lock. Replace the post-publish full reload with an append of the published row, and push publish_ordinary through to_thread.
fix_notes: Lock-free readers are safe only if generation, snapshot and state are published as ONE immutable tuple in a single attribute assignment. Separate atomic fields let a reader pair a new generation with an old snapshot. Writers must still serialize the marks reconcile. Replacing the post-publish reload with an append is risky. publish can supersede an earlier revision of the same logical_outcome_id (superseded_at/transition_revision), and the reload also picks up acknowledgements made by other connections. An append would have to remove superseded rows and keep the created_at DESC order, so keep the reload and just move it off-loop. publish_ordinary's return value is ignored by _publish_inactive_outcome, so fire-and-forget via to_thread works. Ordering against acknowledge and publish_fleet_drain is still kept by the RLock, but a background publish must not run after runtime dispose (check the authority token as ensure_activity_hydration does).
reason: All cited code exists on 840ed2ca58. console_activity_receipts.py:72 creates one RLock. hydrate_from_storage (270), publish_ordinary (283), publish_fleet_drain and acknowledge each hold it across AgentRuns SQLite I/O: a paged reload, then a ChaChaNotes marks list/set/clear in _reconcile_fleet_marks_locked. Traced who holds the lock and on which thread. hydrate runs off-loop via to_thread (console_runtime.py:3614-3645). acknowledge runs off-loop via to_thread (buddy_workspace.py:138). publish_fleet_drain runs on the child/drain thread (console_fleet_attention.py:312). publish_ordinary, however, is reached from ConsoleChatController._set_run_state -> _publish_inactive_outcome (controller 30098/30285 -> 30254). Its callers include async defs on the loop (_finalize_agent_reply, _run_direct_provider_reply, _submit_draft_inner, etc.), so a sync write transaction, a full paged reload and the marks reconcile run on the loop once per inactive or hidden-session terminal outcome. Loop-side lock readers are confirmed: the switcher poll at 200 ms (console_session_switcher_modal.py:466-470 -> chat_screen.py:5288-5297 reads projection_generation and hydration_state), plus unseen_snapshot readers in workspace.py:2929/3368 and buddy_speech.py:141/221. AgentRuns uses busy_timeout=5000 (AgentRuns_DB.py:324), so when that DB is write-contended, both publish_ordinary and any loop reader blocked behind the drain thread's lock can wait for as long as SQLite waits. In practice the hydration/poll overlap is narrow: hydration is one-shot per runtime and usually finishes before the first 200 ms poll. The cost is small (about 9 ms measured per background completion), so P3 is right. The category moves to loop-blocking because the most concrete confirmed cost is on-loop sync DB I/O in publish_ordinary, not the lock alone. TASK-31506 covers only the poll's duplicate activity_for work, not this. No open task covers receipt I/O.

title: Legacy citation migration idle unit re-parses the whole (<=32 MB) sidecar twice per unit and runs one ~24 ms guarded get_journal per conversation per unit (quadratic)
trigger: Deferred startup task (app.py:16372-16381) loops migrate_idle_unit via to_thread until the state is not running. It runs only when canonical citation writes are enabled and a legacy sidecar exists. It is a one-time drain plus one parse per later boot.
cost: Per unit: one full guarded admission (the finder measured about 24 ms), a reconnect, 2 whole-sidecar parses (the Python char loop dominates, roughly tens of ms per MB), and O(C) µs-level nested SELECTs. The total is about C units x (2 parses + admission), so it is quadratic only in the cheap SELECTs, not in 24 ms admissions. Estimated from code, not measured.
fix: Parse the sidecar once per migration pass, cached by (st_dev, st_ino, st_mtime_ns, st_size). Read all journals in one query (SELECT ... WHERE conversation_id IN (...)) inside a single guarded operation, and keep the worker connection across units.
fix_notes: The simplest safe fix is to pass the payload migrate_idle_unit already parsed into the batch step (one parse per unit), and to read the journal states once with a single SELECT conversation_id, state ... WHERE profile_id=? instead of per-id get_journal loops. A cross-unit parse cache keyed on stat must keep the TOCTOU guarantees _raw_sidecar enforces (st_ctime_ns, fd-vs-path dev/ino, re-stat inside the guarded op) and must still recompute the source fingerprint. Do NOT 'keep the worker connection across units'. The per-unit close_connection exists because to_thread uses pooled threads and ChaChaNotes connections are thread-local, so keeping them would leak connections onto arbitrary pool threads unless a dedicated worker thread is introduced. Keep _validate_json_lexical_depth, which is a recursion-safety guard; only avoid running it twice.
evidence:
_, payload = self._raw_sidecar()                 # whole-file read + json + _validate_json_bounds
for raw_conversation_id in sorted(conversations):
    journal = self.get_journal(conversation_id)   # @guarded: ~24 ms admission each
    ...
    result = self.migrate_next_batch(conversation_id)  # _source_snapshot -> _raw_sidecar again
reason: Code confirmed. migrate_idle_unit (citation_legacy_migration.py:1224) calls _raw_sidecar at 1230. It then calls get_journal per sorted conversation at 1246 until it finds a non-terminal one, and migrate_next_batch, which re-runs _raw_sidecar via _source_snapshot at 890. When that batch finishes a conversation, it scans every conversation's journal again (1255-1259). So both repeated sidecar parses per unit and O(C) journal reads per unit, about O(C^2) over the migration, are real. However, the finder's '~24 ms guarded admission per get_journal' is wrong. Every nested @guarded call inside a unit takes the reentrant fast path in chat_source_participants.operation (lines 267-281: when _LOCAL.active already contains the source, it only runs _validate plus raw._check and storage._check_operation, which are µs-level lock and attribute checks). The expensive full admission is paid once per unit, by the outer migrate_idle_unit. Each unit's real repeated cost is two whole-file reads, each followed by a char-by-char Python _validate_json_lexical_depth loop (line 127, about 50 ns/char over up to 32 MB), json.loads and a bounds walk, plus O(C) cheap PK SELECTs. The trigger is off-loop: app.py:16814 wraps each unit in asyncio.to_thread and closes the connection per unit (16811). It is also opt-in: ready requires canonical_writes_enabled, default false (config.py:5228, citation_trace_repository.py:604-611). The UI impact is only GIL contention from the pure-Python scan while it runs. Additional scope the finder missed: after migration completes, every boot with the sidecar still present runs one more unit (1 parse + C SELECTs) before returning COMPLETE. No backlog task covers this; TASK-553.9 is Done and is the feature task.

title: BLOB-hydrating reads where only version, ids or metadata are needed (per send finalize, per fork, and 10k-row leaf lookup)
trigger: Console fork: 2N BLOB-hydrating point reads on the event loop (issue plus validate fence). Agent fork_chat: 4 source reads, 3 of them BLOB-hydrating and unnecessary, on the agent worker thread. Edit or delete of an image message: one image copy. Stream finalize: effectively no BLOB cost, since assistant rows have no image.
cost: Proportional to image bytes: one multi-MB copy per image message per read. For text-only chats it is negligible apart from the 2N loop-side point SELECTs on Console fork, estimated at about 0.1 ms each. Estimated, not measured.
fix: Use get_message_by_id_without_blob in update_message_content, delete_message_subtree and get_console_fork_source_message. Pass include_image_data=False in effective_active_leaf, and let copy_conversation_active_path reuse its own rows to compute the leaf instead of calling effective_active_leaf.
fix_notes: Switching to get_message_by_id_without_blob is safe for get_console_fork_source_message, delete_message_subtree and update_message_content, since none of them reads image_data from current_message. Check that no test fake lacks the method; get_message_version already uses it (TASK-22226), which is the precedent. effective_active_leaf(include_image_data=False) is safe. For copy_conversation_active_path, compute the leaf from its own rows with the same pointer-else-max-timestamp logic, factored into a helper that takes rows, so the fork executor and the copy cannot drift. Replace get_conversation_tree(...)['conversation'] with db.get_conversation_by_id, but first confirm the tree's conversation dict has the same shape, especially normalized metadata and scope fields. Optionally batch the fork fence's per-message reads into one IN-query.
evidence:
current_message = self.db.get_message_by_id(message_id)   # update_message_content: needs version/role/metadata/content only
...
rows = self.db.get_messages_for_conversation(conversation_id, limit=FORK_READ_MAX_MESSAGES)  # effective_active_leaf: needs id/timestamp only, reads up to 10k image BLOBs
# copy_conversation_active_path then re-reads the same rows
reason: Confirmed on the pin. get_message_by_id (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:14207) selects image_data, and get_message_by_id_without_blob (14218) exists with a has_image flag. update_message_content (chat_persistence_service.py:2732) uses the BLOB read, but only needs role, metadata_json, version, content and conversation_id, all of which are in the without-blob projection. delete_message_subtree (3167) needs only version. get_console_fork_source_message (962) needs only version and content. effective_active_leaf (chat_conversation_service.py:1249) reads up to FORK_READ_MAX_MESSAGES=10_000 rows with include_image_data defaulting to True but uses only id and timestamp. copy_conversation_active_path (1284-1290) reads the rows with images, which it legitimately needs, then calls effective_active_leaf, which reads them all again. New scope: execute_agent_chat_create (console_chat_controller.py:18582) also calls get_conversation_tree(root_limit=10_000, depth_cap=10_000). That builds the full tree and batch-hydrates every image (_hydrate_tree_images, 1593) just to read tree['conversation'], so the agent fork path reads the source 4 times, not 3. That path runs on a worker thread (docstring at 18368), so the cost is memory and CPU, not loop. The Console fork path is on the loop. _fork_lineage_entry (console_chat_store.py:7323) calls get_console_fork_source_message once per prefix message, in both issue_fork_fence (called synchronously from request_console_chat_fork, session.py:2199) and validate_fork_fence (async _run_console_chat_fork, session.py:2451). That is 2N point reads on the loop, each copying the row's image BLOB. One correction: update_message_content on stream finalize targets assistant rows, which normally have NULL image_data, so the per-send cost is roughly zero. The BLOB cost applies to edits of image-bearing messages and to forks. P3 is right: these are rare, user-initiated actions whose cost scales with image bytes.

title: Chat/__init__.py eagerly imports six service modules (Library, Backup_Recovery, runtime_policy bootstrap to config)
trigger: Any non-TUI process importing any tldw_chatbook.Chat.* submodule, such as the MCP stdio server on its first chat tool, scripts or test workers. The TUI boot already imports the same modules, so the marginal cost there is zero.
cost: Measured: 541-734 ms warm for the Chat package __init__ closure (config 249-363 ms of that). The real marginal saving is smaller for importers of Chat_Functions, which need config anyway.
fix: Turn the package __init__ into a PEP 562 lazy __getattr__ facade, following the Local_Ingestion template.
fix_notes: A PEP 562 __getattr__ facade (the Local_Ingestion/TTS template) keeps `from tldw_chatbook.Chat import X` and mock.patch('tldw_chatbook.Chat.X') working, since patch uses getattr/setattr. Backup_Recovery/chat_source_participants._classes() looks up classes via sys.modules.get and still works, because any live instance implies its module is imported. Add a subprocess import-closure guard, as TASK-22503's AC does, so it cannot creep back. The payoff is modest because config is on almost every non-trivial path anyway.
evidence:
from .conversation_local_marks_service import (ConversationLocalMark, ConversationLocalMarksService)
from .chat_conversation_scope_service import ChatConversationScopeService   # -> Library -> Library_Collections_DB
from .chat_conversation_service import ChatConversationService              # -> Backup_Recovery.chat_source_participants
from .server_chat_conversation_service import ServerChatConversationService  # -> runtime_policy.bootstrap -> config
reason: Chat/__init__.py lines 1-9 eagerly import six service modules. I re-measured with full profile isolation (HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH in scratch, TLDW_TEST_MODE=1, PYTHONPATH=audit tree). `import tldw_chatbook.Chat.Chat_Deps`, a trivial leaf, costs 541-658 ms warm (900 ms cold) cumulative for the tldw_chatbook.Chat package, of which tldw_chatbook.config accounts for 249-270 ms. `import tldw_chatbook.Chat.Chat_Functions` costs 803 ms, of which the package __init__ is 734 ms. The TUI pays nothing extra: app.py:123-146 already imports these services at module scope. The non-app consumers are the MCP server, which imports Chat lazily inside its tool handlers (MCP/server.py:428, 606, so the stdio process pays on its first chat tool call), helper scripts and every test worker. The chain Chat/__init__ -> server_chat_conversation_service -> runtime_policy.bootstrap has also caused a circular import before (noted in TASK-22227). TASK-22503 (open) names Chat/__init__ in its chain but is scoped only to Library/__init__, so this is new scope. Side note: importing config wrote a config.toml into the isolated TLDW_CONFIG_PATH, a module-import side effect, which is why isolation was mandatory.

title: Attachment pipeline is async def around purely synchronous PIL and file work; callers spin a fresh event loop per attachment
trigger: Each Console file attach, drag-drop path and clipboard image paste (user action; up to 5 per message) creates one event loop, and for PDF/doc/ebook files one executor thread.
cost: About 0.3-2 ms of loop, and possibly executor, setup and teardown per attachment. Negligible next to the PIL or parse work itself. Estimated.
fix: Make load_processed_file, process_attachment_path and process_attachment_bytes (and prepare_image_payload) plain sync functions, and call them with asyncio.to_thread(fn, ...) directly.
fix_notes: Making the pipeline 'plain sync' is bigger than stated. It cascades into FileHandlerRegistry.process_file and all 10 or so FileHandler.process() implementations, _extract_local_ingest_text's internal to_thread, ChatImageHandler.process_image_file and prepare_image_payload, and the legacy _process_image_data adapter, whose async signature its docstring says is pinned by tests. Given the tiny payoff, the lazy option is to leave it, or add a one-line sync wrapper used by both chat_screen sites. Converting to sync only pays off if an on-loop caller ever appears.
evidence:
attachment = await asyncio.to_thread(
    lambda: asyncio.run(process_attachment_bytes(grab.png_bytes or b"", display_name=display_name))
)
# process_attachment_bytes: PILImage.open(...).verify() and ChatImageHandler.prepare_image_payload (sync PIL resize/save) behind 'async def'
reason: Confirmed at chat_screen.py:20476-20482 (clipboard) and 20511-20513 (file attach): asyncio.to_thread(lambda: asyncio.run(...)) runs once per attachment. process_attachment_bytes (attachment_core.py:340; the PIL verify and prepare_image_payload are at 379-388; line 367 is only the import) is async def around synchronous PIL work. I grepped every caller untruncated. The ONLY production callers of process_attachment_path, process_attachment_bytes, load_processed_file and file_handler_registry.process_file are those two chat_screen sites, both already off-loop. prepare_image_payload's other callers are inside chat_image_events and are reached only through the same path. So no loop-blocking exists today; the risk is latent. One more detail the finder missed: the PDF/document/ebook handlers await asyncio.to_thread internally (Utils/file_handlers.py:65). Inside asyncio.run on a worker thread, that creates, and on shutdown joins, a fresh default ThreadPoolExecutor per such attachment. This is hygiene with around 1 ms per user-initiated attach, so P3 is right.

title: Terminal re-projects every cell of every session on the UI thread per frame and at least twice per keystroke
trigger: Every keystroke runs this on the UI loop. chat_screen.py:2403-2409 on_console_terminal_input_requested -> ConsoleTerminalController.send_key -> _selected_session_id -> view_state, which snapshots all sessions. The echo comes back on the runtime thread: process_output (session_manager.py:598) -> _notify_subscribers -> _manager_changed (terminal.py:441) -> call_from_thread -> _queue_refresh -> screen.call_after_refresh(_refresh) -> view_state again. That is at least 2 all-session snapshots per keystroke. While output streams it is one per frame, coalesced by _frame_pending. This happens only while the Terminal workspace is open: the subscription is added in open_workspace and removed in detach_workspace (chat_screen.py:2327/2388/17114).
cost: Measured on the pin, isolated, with the real TerminalScreenModel and colored ls-style content. Full screen: 3.99 ms at 80x24, 22.3 ms at 200x50, 26.96 ms at 235x50. Blank screen: 3.13, 15.86 and 18.51 ms. This is worse than the finder's numbers. One full-width session costs about 40-55 ms per keystroke (2 snapshots), and every extra open session adds about 20-27 ms per snapshot pass.
fix: (a) Make _selected_session_id() read the existing cheap property runtime.selected_session_id (session_manager.py:634) and not build a view_state. (b) Have view_state snapshot only the selected session's screen; the other sessions need only projection metadata. (c) In _project_line, detect blank cells with `character == screen.default_char` and memoize _safe_style on the pyte style tuple (fg, bg, bold, ...), keeping a small dict. (d) Cache projected rows and invalidate them by an accumulated dirty-row set. Today dirty is cleared per feed; accumulate it until the next snapshot, so a keystroke echo re-projects about 1 row instead of rows x cols cells.
fix_notes: (a) is trivially safe. runtime.selected_session_id exists (session_manager.py:634), and runtime.send_key/send_paste/resize_session already validate the view token through _input_actor_for_view_locked/_valid_view_locked, so the view check is not lost. (b) is safe because only the selected session's screen is consumed (console_terminal_workspace.py:601) and focus_session notifies on a switch. (c) `character == screen.default_char` is only a sufficient fast path: keep the full _safe_style comparison as the fallback, because unsafe colors normalize to 'default'. A memo keyed on the (fg, bg, bold, italics, underscore, strikethrough, reverse, blink) tuple is pure and safe. (d) The dirty-row cache is medium risk. pyte and the custom _BoundedScreen mark rows dirty, and resize/alt-screen/reset mark all rows, but dirty is cleared per feed (_feed_parser:651), so it must accumulate until the next snapshot. The custom draw path must also keep adding rows (for example _clear_intersecting_wide_cells). Do (a)+(b)+(c) first; they remove most of the cost.
evidence:
# screen_model.py snapshot(): every row, every call
lines = tuple(self._project_line(active.buffer[row]) for row in range(self.rows))
# _project_line: _safe_style (dataclass + 2 regex) on EVERY blank cell
character.data != " " or _safe_style(character) != SafeTerminalStyle()
# session_manager.view_state: snapshots ALL sessions
snapshot = model.snapshot()   # for each candidate session
# terminal.py send_key -> _selected_session_id() -> runtime.view_state(view)
reason: The code matches on pin 840ed2ca58. TerminalScreenModel.snapshot (screen_model.py:610) projects every row, and _project_line (680-688) calls _safe_style on every column to find the last non-blank cell. TerminalSessionManager.view_state (session_manager.py:654-703) snapshots every session that has a model, up to MAX_SESSION_RECORDS=4. terminal.py:531 _selected_session_id builds a full view_state only to read selected_session_id, and send_key (348), send_paste (369), request_resize (386) and _resize_generation (508) all go through it. The only consumer of the snapshots, ConsoleTerminalWorkspace.project (console_terminal_workspace.py:601), uses only the selected session's screen, and _projection_fingerprint drops the hidden screens. So the extra snapshots are pure waste.

title: Terminal output parse re-projects every scrolled line cell by cell, capping throughput at 0.19 MB/s while holding the GIL and model_lock
trigger: The daemon thread terminal-runtime-<id> (session_manager._run_runtime, started in _start_runtime_locked) calls process_output whenever output_actor.pending_bytes > 0, that is, for every chunk the shell prints. It runs off the loop but holds the GIL and model_lock, so it contends with the Textual loop thread (switch interval 5 ms) and blocks the UI's view_state snapshot.
cost: Measured on the pin, isolated. 0.86 MB of 200-column colored ls output parsed at 0.35 MB/s unprofiled (0.14 MB/s under cProfile). The profile puts 3.57 s of 6.1 s in _retain_scrollback_line/_project_line and 655k _safe_style calls for 2951 lines. Plain 150-char lines give 2.85 of 4.08 s, and 40-char lines give 2.13 of 2.52 s. Scroll projection costs about 0.7-1 ms per line regardless of line length, which caps throughput near 1000-1400 lines/s at 200 columns. protocol_gate is minor (0.04-0.6 s). This confirms the finder's shape; the absolute MB/s depends on content density.
fix: Reuse F1's memoized projection: a default-char fast path plus a style memo makes the per-line cost scale with non-blank cells. Better still, retain scrollback lazily: keep a compact copy of the pyte row (or its (data, style-key) runs) and project only when the history view needs it. Optionally add a gate fast path that scans runs of printable bytes with bytes.translate or a regex, not per-byte method dispatch.
fix_notes: The shared blank-cell fast path and style memo from F1 give the largest win with the smallest diff: short lines stop paying for 200 columns. Lazy scrollback (keeping raw pyte rows or compact runs) interacts with the byte accounting in _retain_scrollback_line (accounted_bytes drives the MAX_SCROLLBACK_BYTES eviction), so the accounting must still be computed eagerly or approximated conservatively. Mutable pyte row dicts must not be retained by reference, because pyte reuses and moves buffer rows on scroll; copy them. The protocol-gate bulk-scan change is optional and low value (under 10% of the profile).
reason: The code matches. _BoundedScreen.index (screen_model.py:186-195) calls _on_scroll(self.buffer[top]) on every full-viewport scroll. _retain_scrollback_line (660) calls _project_line (680), which runs _safe_style (a dataclass plus 2 regex fullmatch calls) on every column, including trailing blanks, because the last-non-blank scan styles each cell. process_output (session_manager.py:570-598) runs the parser turn under model_lock, the same lock view_state takes for the UI snapshot. The 8 ms turn budget (io_actors.py process_parser_turn) is checked only between 1 KiB slices (MAX_PARSER_SLICE_BYTES=1024), so one slice with many newlines can run past it.

title: Terminal visible-refresh coalescing is dead: every parser turn (hidden sessions included) does a blocking call_from_thread into the UI loop
corrected: tldw_chatbook/UI/Console_Modules/terminal.py:441-444 (_manager_changed -> _marshal_to_ui) and terminal.py:456-462 (_refresh -> view_state); terminal.py:422 is jump_live and is not related.
trigger: The runtime thread of every RUNNING session notifies after every parser turn, hidden sessions included, while the Terminal workspace is open (the subscriber is ConsoleTerminalController._manager_changed). A hidden session's output triggers _refresh -> view_state, which snapshots all sessions (F1 cost), and the fingerprint then equals the last one, so the work is discarded.
cost: Estimated. The blocking round trip ties the runtime thread to loop latency, and each loop iteration can take a 20-27 ms snapshot at full width (F1, measured). A busy hidden session (for example a build) keeps triggering all-session snapshots on the loop at frame rate with no visible change.
fix: Honor ParserTurnResult.refresh_requested: notify only for visible-session turns that newly request a refresh. Call actor.acknowledge_visible_refresh() from terminal._refresh after projecting. Replace call_from_thread with a non-blocking handoff (loop.call_soon_threadsafe, or post_message); the callback's result is unused.
fix_notes: Fix risk is medium rather than low. If refresh_requested is honored, the acknowledge must run on every _refresh exit path, including the early returns on an unchanged fingerprint, a non-TerminalViewState value, and NoMatches. Otherwise _refresh_pending stays set and the visible terminal stops repainting. Acknowledging needs a new manager method, because the controller has no actor access. Replacing call_from_thread with non-blocking screen.call_later / post_message is safe: Textual's post_message detects a foreign thread and uses loop.call_soon_threadsafe. But without the refresh_requested gate that would enqueue one Callback per parser turn (about 125/s), so land both changes together. Lifecycle, rename and focus changes keep their own _notify_subscribers calls, so skipping notifications for hidden-session output does not lose metadata updates.

# ...but process_output ignores result.refresh_requested:
self._queue_model_replies(session_id, model, replies)
self._notify_subscribers()
# acknowledge_visible_refresh() has zero callers; wiring.py:
screen.app.call_from_thread(callback)   # blocks runtime thread
