No deadlock is possible: model_lock and the manager _lock are both released before _notify_subscribers.

title: Each terminal session runs a 200 Hz runtime-bridge poll and a 100 Hz input-flush poll while idle (on top of the known 50 Hz monitor)
known_task: TASK-31503 (adjacent: covers only the 50 Hz monitor thread, not these two loops)
trigger: Both threads are always on for every RUNNING session, even at an idle prompt and even when the Terminal workspace is closed. The runtime thread is started in _start_runtime_locked and the flusher in posix_backend._start_owner_workers (948-958), alongside the TASK-31503 monitor.
cost: Measured on a structural replica on this machine (PTY master, O_NONBLOCK, RLock x4, Event.wait(0), then stop.wait(0.005)): 0.64% of a core for the runtime bridge and 0.21% for the input flusher. That is about 0.85% per idle session, a lower bound because the real loop also runs record validation. Together with TASK-31503's about 1.5%, one idle session costs about 2.4% of a core. Kept at P2 because the feature is opt-in and each thread alone is under the 1% P0 bar.
fix: Runtime bridge: block in select()/poll() on the PTY master fd plus a self-pipe signalled by send_key/offer_* and stop, not a 5 ms sleep loop. Input flusher: use `self._input_pending.wait()` with no timeout, since close() already sets it (posix_backend.py:625). Land this in the same PR as TASK-31503 (monitor cadence).
fix_notes: The input flusher fix is a one-line change to self._input_pending.wait() with no timeout, safe as verified above. Keep the 10 ms EAGAIN backoff at lines 993-994. A select/poll-based runtime bridge is medium risk: _read_master also serves _output_buffer and the post-reap EOF scan (lines 1038-1054), which are not fd-readable events, and take_input/offer_reply need a wake source. A smaller interim fix: add a wake Event set by send_key/send_paste/offer_reply/stop, and back off idle waits from 5 ms up to about 50 ms after N idle passes. Output latency after an idle period then rises at most to the backoff cap, while input wakes immediately.

if not worked:

Each pass takes the manager RLock 4 times (take_input, _runtime_output_state, _read_runtime_output with os.read -> BlockingIOError, _poll_runtime_exit with wait_for_shell_exit(0)) and also evaluates self.permitted, a cheap app_config lookup. posix_backend._flush_pending_input (974-994) loops on _input_pending.wait(0.01). _close_requested is set only in request_priority_close (line 621), which also sets _input_pending (625), and finalize_shutdown goes through request_priority_close. title: Server mode: every build_client()/get_active_context() re-reads and parses mcp_server_targets.json through the hardened participant reader (7.6 ms), uncached
trigger: This runs in server mode only, on each server API call. There are 52 `build_client()` sites across about 50 service modules, reached through `await self._require_client().x()` inside async service methods that screen workers run on the loop (for example ServerNotificationsService.list_feed, server_notifications_service.py:103, and app.py:9909/9915, which call get_active_context and then build_client, reading the store twice). Local mode exits at _require_active_server_id.
cost: Measured on the pin in an isolated profile (config loaded, store bound=True): get_target costs 15.2 ms per call at the deep scratch path, against 0.033 ms for a raw json.load of the same file. The finder measured 7.6 ms. Estimated at about 4-7 ms at the default ~/.local/share/tldw_cli/default_user depth, because the cost scales with the number of path components walked. A server-mode screen visit that makes 2-4 calls pays about 10-30 ms on the loop.
fix: Memoize the resolved ConfiguredServerTarget (and ActiveServerContext) in RuntimeServerContextProvider. Key it on (runtime_context.snapshot() revision, credential-store read generation, target-store write generation or file (st_ino, st_mtime_ns, st_size)). Bump a generation in ConfiguredServerTargetStore.save_targets/update_target_status and in the provider's existing _invalidate_cached_client paths. Check that cheap key before calling get_active_context in build_client.
fix_notes: Much of this cost is the F6 admission/raw-scope machinery. If F6 makes admission O(1), the per-call cost falls sharply without a new cache. If a memo is added: (1) invalidate it on recovery activation, local pause and restore, not only on in-process saves, or a restored profile can serve a stale target; (2) cross-process writers (another chatbook instance, the MCP stdio server) need a file-identity validator, and a plain os.stat as a validator must not replace the guarded read on a miss; (3) keep resolve_target's fallback to resolve_active_target in the memoized path; (4) _capture_character_authority_context also calls ensure_authority_scope_id, which can write, so do not cache across it.
reason: The code matches. build_client (server_context.py:325) calls get_active_context before the client cache check. That calls resolve_target (637-639) -> ConfiguredServerTargetStore.get_target (server_target_store.py:84), which is @mcp_sources.guarded and goes through the nested list_targets/load -> _read_payload -> mcp_sources.reader under raw_participants._scope (acquisition plus pinned private-path walks). Nothing memoizes the target. TASK-32922 cached only the keyring secret (5 s TTL); TASK-31510 covers only the pre-paint legacy upsert. The finder's 'polled' trigger is refuted: ServerChatLoopService and ServerChatLoopScopeService have no production consumers (only the Chat/__init__.py re-exports), and the one 2 s poller found (Research_Window._auto_refresh_selected_run) is local-only. Downgraded to P2: server mode only, and the cost is per user action or per visit, not a timer.

title: Cross-slice: every core-repository connection()/transaction() pays storage admission (~245 open() syscalls, 4-7 ms), versus 0.02 ms raw, a regression since 2026-09-16
trigger: Every `with db.transaction()` on ChaChaNotes and every connection()/transaction() on the other participant repositories, on the loop or on workers. Loop examples verified in this slice: the MainNavigationBar.on_mount recompute (F7) and the EventObserver store calls (F8).
cost: Measured on the pin in an isolated profile after admit_startup(): an empty `with db.transaction(): SELECT 1` takes 5.16 ms, against 0.031 ms for execute_query('SELECT 1'), about 170x. cProfile per transaction: 245 posix.open, 75 lstat and 36 stat calls, and acquire_storage accounts for 0.145 of 0.158 s. The open() count matches the finder exactly. The scratch path is about 14 components deep; the default ~/.config/tldw_cli depth is about 5, so the cost there is estimated at about 2-3 ms per transaction, still about 100x the raw cost. It may be P0 once multiplied per send or visit, but that needs the census the finder proposes.
fix: Keep one long-lived admission hold per (pid, root, participant); the _holds/_Hold refcount machinery already exists. Make _repository_operation an O(1) check of a process-level admission generation. Bump that generation on pause, retire, maintenance, or selector change, and re-walk pinned directories only then. Add a micro-benchmark gate (transaction block ≤ 50 µs) next to TASK-31502's. Severity is likely P0 once multiplied across a visit or send; a per-path census of on-loop core operations is needed to confirm.
fix_notes: High risk, as the finder says. The admission checks guard cross-process recovery: another process can write recovery-bootstrap records (pending restore, re-enrollment), so an in-process generation counter alone is unsound. A cheap validator is needed, such as (st_dev, st_ino, st_mtime_ns) of the records and registry files taken through the already-pinned bootstrap directory fd, re-walking only on change. In-process pause/retire/maintenance/selector changes should bump a generation that _Operation.check already consults. Keep the per-operation _Operation bookkeeping (pause drain counts _operations). Add a micro-benchmark gate with a FILE-backed DB, because :memory: bypasses the path entirely. Coordinate with the owner of the in-progress TASK-32562 (backup/recovery cross-platform).
reason: The code matches. ChaChaNotes _TransactionContext.__enter__ (ChaChaNotes_DB.py:24221) enters _core_operation(self.db) (participants.py:420). For installed file-backed repositories (CharactersRAGDB, ClientNotificationsDB @_core_transaction at client_notifications_db.py:200/210, EventStateRepository, WorkspaceDB, AgentRunsDB and others, listed in _repository_types) that goes to _repository_operation (storage_admission.py:110), which calls acquire_storage (835) on every outermost operation. Only nested same-participant operations reuse the operation. _acquire_storage re-runs startup_permission (bootstrap _records/_registry reads), qualified_for, admission_authority, and _scope twice, each doing pinned private-path directory walks. The long-lived startup lease keeps the native _Hold alive, but the per-operation verification I/O is not cached. is_memory_db short-circuits, which is why in-memory DB tests never show this. git log confirms that storage_admission.py and _core_transaction landed in b5251e9a6e on 2026-09-16 (TASK-32628). No backlog task covers the admission cost: a grep for acquire_storage, storage_admission and _core_transaction finds only functional backup tasks. TASK-31502 is a different mechanism (the quiescence registry lock).

title: MainNavigationBar.on_mount forces a durable Console-attention recompute (sync ChaChaNotes transaction plus LIKE scan and sort) on every nav-bar mount
trigger: It runs synchronously on the loop. BaseAppScreen.compose (base_app_screen.py:385) yields a fresh MainNavigationBar, so it runs on every visit to a non-reusable screen, on every whole-screen recompose, and on every NavOverflowMenu open (main_navigation.py:1121).
cost: Estimated from the F6 measurement: one ChaChaNotes transaction costs 5.16 ms at scratch depth and about 2-3 ms at default depth, which dominates. The marks table is small, so the LIKE scan is a minor part; the finder measured 3.9 ms with 2000 rows against 4.5 ms with 0. That is about 3-5 ms per screen visit, which is P2.
fix: Remove the recompute from MainNavigationBar.on_mount and NavOverflowMenu.on_mount and rely on the cached projection plus the existing event-driven publishes. If a freshness check is still wanted, debounce it once per app via a worker (asyncio.to_thread). In the service, replace `LIKE 'console_unseen:%'` with a range predicate (`mark_type >= ? AND mark_type < ?`) plus a SQL LIMIT so the index is usable. Drop the duplicated apply/sync call.
fix_notes: The mount recompute is deliberate and pinned. Tests/UI/test_master_shell_navigation.py:173 test_fresh_navigation_mount_recomputes_durable_console_attention asserts calls == [{'force_projection': True}], and the docstring says 'Refresh durable attention when this transient projection opens'. It is the only path that picks up marks written by another process. Removing it requires changing that test and accepting the loss of cross-process freshness. The safer change keeps the refresh but runs it off the loop (asyncio.to_thread or a thread worker) with an app-level debounce. recompute already publishes via app.call_later, which posts thread-safely, and it holds its own _attention_operation_lock. The LIKE-to-range rewrite is marginal and needs a plan check without sqlite_stat1, per CLAUDE.md, if an index is involved. Dropping the duplicated sync_console_attention call is trivial and safe.

title: Schedules SSE EventObserver runs all event-state SQLite calls synchronously on the loop (4 admission-taxed operations per event); event_records is never pruned
trigger: Server mode, while the Schedules screen is mounted. schedules_workbench.py:909 uses run_worker(self._run_server_notification_observer, exclusive=True, group=...) with a coroutine, so it runs on the loop. The cost is paid per received SSE notification event and per (re)connect.
cost: Estimated: about 4 repository operations per event at about 2-5 ms each (the F6 measurement of 5.16 ms per transaction at scratch depth) gives about 10-20 ms of loop block per notification event. Notification traffic is low, hence P2. Row growth is on disk and slow at that traffic.
fix: Wrap store calls in the observer with asyncio.to_thread; the repository holds a connection per thread, so this is safe. Alternatively fold dedupe, ack and remember into one repository method or transaction. Call prune_stream_state on a daily cadence or at observer start.
fix_notes: Caveat on asyncio.to_thread: the repository holds one connection per thread (_held keyed per thread), so the default executor's thread churn accumulates held connections. Prefer one repository method that does the dedupe check, acknowledge and remember in a single transaction, run on one dedicated thread or through to_thread with a single-worker executor. _Operation.check pins thread and task identity, which is fine inside one to_thread call. Ordering matters: the handler must still run before the ack, so only the store calls move off the loop. Call prune_stream_state with max_count or older_than at observer start, under the IMMEDIATE transaction it already uses.

advance = self.store.acknowledge_event(event, expected_cursor=...)  # BEGIN IMMEDIATE txn
    self.store.remember_event(event)             # second txn
# schedules_workbench.py:909 run_worker(self._run_server_notification_observer)  -> coroutine on loop

EventObserver.run (event_observer.py:145-240) makes synchronous store calls inside an async def: get_cursor (168), is_duplicate_event (197), acknowledge_event (205), remember_event (209/212), and reset_cursor. The store is EventStateRepository, an installed participant ('runtime.event_state'), whose connection() carries @_core_transaction (event_state_repository.py:292) and whose transaction() nests connection() plus BEGIN IMMEDIATE. So every call pays F6's admission. acknowledge_event itself runs get_processed_cursor plus record_event_and_advance_processed_cursor, which makes about 4 or more admission-taxed operations per event. ServerNotificationEventsObserver.observe also calls record_observer_status twice per run (server_notification_events.py:131-155). prune_stream_state (1063) has zero production callers (untruncated grep). The retention-policy rows are stored (set_retention_policy) but never applied, and the only other delete path is clear_server_profile_state (1339), so event_records and dedupe rows grow without bound.

title: Buddy speech polls at 1 Hz, re-snapshotting the whole bound transcript (or a 5-hop workspace snapshot with N+1 metadata reads) every tick; the 2 Hz reconcile_scope interval is never stopped
corrected: tldw_chatbook/UI/Navigation/buddy_speech.py:76-87 (poll loop); tldw_chatbook/UI/Navigation/buddy_speech.py:164-172 (messages_for_session full snapshot); tldw_chatbook/UI/Navigation/buddy_speech.py:227 (issue_tts_message_speech_snapshot before queue dedupe); tldw_chatbook/Chat/console_chat_store.py:21618 (sync get_message_version SQLite read on loop); tldw_chatbook/UI/Navigation/buddy_management.py:933 (set_interval never cancelled); tldw_chatbook/UI/Navigation/buddy_workspace.py:29,42,54,85 (4 to_thread hops, 2 of them for in-memory reads)
trigger: The asyncio task is created by BuddySpeechCoordinator.configure (buddy_speech.py:71-72). reconcile_scope calls configure every 0.5 s via app.set_interval, which start_scope_tracking arms from persona_buddy_overlay.py:124 whenever the Buddy is desired and buddy_interaction config exists. It runs at 1 Hz for as long as Buddy speech is enabled with a conversation or workspace binding and the Buddy is enabled and open. The 2 Hz reconcile timer runs for the rest of the session once the Buddy has been visible.
cost: Estimated, with a measured proxy. dataclasses.replace on a synthetic 47-field dataclass (ConsoleChatMessage has about 47 fields) costs about 4.8 µs per message: 1.43 ms per 300 messages, so about 14 ms/s on a 3,000-message transcript. Each tick adds one synchronous SQLite PK read on the loop (about 0.1-0.5 ms, more under the TASK-31502 quiescence tax) plus presentation resolution. With a workspace binding: 4 executor round-trips/s plus N metadata SELECTs off-loop. The 2 Hz reconcile_scope tick is tens of µs, so it is only an idle-wakeup cost.
fix: Gate refresh on existing change counters (the store's display-projection revision via _bump_display_projection_revision, and activity_receipts.projection_generation), or subscribe to turn-settled events. Find the latest completed assistant message by iterating the store's internal list in reverse, not by snapshotting the transcript. Build the queue key first and skip _capture when key is in queue._seen. Stop _scope_timer when the Buddy is closed or disabled, or drive reconcile_scope from session-change events.
fix_notes: Cheapest win: build the key f"message:{session.id}:{message_id}" first and skip _capture when it is already in queue._seen. reset() clears _seen on rebind and after consent, so replays are unaffected. To find the latest message, do not simply switch to the existing iter_messages_newest_first (console_chat_store.py:11875): it calls the NON-deferred _materialize_stream_buffer, which task-33081 moved off the loop because it can write SQLite inline. Use a deferred variant, or only inspect rows whose status == 'complete'. Gate refresh on _bump_display_projection_revision / activity_receipts.projection_generation plus interrupt-host changes, but keep the decision/question path live. Drop the to_thread hops for hydration_state and unseen_snapshot. The 0.5 s scope timer is load-bearing: it is what turns the speech poller OFF when the Buddy closes. Stopping it must first run one final reconcile_scope. Re-arming already happens through the overlay's start_scope_tracking call.

title: vLLM setup form re-renders the entire projection (~70 query_one plus label updates) twice per keystroke
trigger: Every Input.Changed in the vLLM pane (model id, URL, bind address, numeric fields) and every TextArea.Changed on raw arguments, once profiles are loaded. Both paths go through _change_draft/_change_numeric_lexeme, then DraftChanged, then the screen's apply_state.
cost: Estimated: about 1-3 ms of Python per keystroke across the two renders (label re-visualization, 4 Select.set_options, the help-label query) plus refresh_lab_status, and layout refreshes that are coalesced to one reflow per frame. The finder's 2-5 ms is at the high end. The query_one share is negligible because of Textual's id cache.

title: DuckDuckGo search pages with up to 5 bare requests.post calls, a new TCP/TLS handshake per page, while the create_session() helper is dead
trigger: Every duckduckgo-backend perform_websearch call (agent web_search tool, deep-search fan-out per sub-query) that needs more than one results page. Typically 0 extra pages at result_count<=10, occasionally 1.
cost: Estimated one extra TCP+TLS handshake (~100-300 ms) per additional page on a worker thread. Typical is 0-300 ms per search, not ~1 s. Deep search multiplies this by the number of sub-queries. No event-loop impact.
fix: `with requests.Session() as s:` around the pagination loop (or reuse `create_session()`), keeping the same timeout and verify arguments.
fix_notes: Prefer a plain `with requests.Session() as s:` (or the TASK-19830 shared default-timeout session factory) around the loop, keeping timeout and verify. Do NOT simply reuse create_session(). It mounts Retry(total=5, status_forcelist=[429, ...]), which would add silent retries on 429 against an anti-bot-sensitive endpoint and raise worst-case latency. Delete create_session() as dead code instead.
evidence:
for _ in range(5):
    response = requests.post("https://html.duckduckgo.com/html", data=payload, timeout=SEARCH_BACKEND_TIMEOUT_S, verify=requests_verify())
...
def create_session() -> requests.Session:   # never called
reason: Code is as quoted. WebSearch_APIs.py:3201 calls bare `requests.post("https://html.duckduckgo.com/html", ...)` inside `for _ in range(5)`, which builds and discards a Session on every page, so no keep-alive. `create_session()` at :3151 is defined and never called: a full untruncated grep of Web_Scraping/ finds only the def. The tests patch `searx_create_session`, which is a different function. There is one real caller, perform_websearch at :2182, reached from Tools/web_tool_impls.py:1328 (agent web_search), Tools/web_search_tool.py:84, deep search at WebSearch_APIs.py:607, and search_backend_settings.py:276. These run on tool or worker threads, not the event loop (web_tool_impls guards its cache with a threading lock for 'concurrent tool threads'), so this is wall-clock latency, not UI blocking. The finder overstates frequency. Pagination continues only when page 1 returns fewer than max_results after ad and dedupe filtering. result_count is capped at 10 (SEARCH_MAX_RESULT_COUNT=10, and web_search_tool clamps to at most 10), and deep search defaults to 10. So a typical search makes 1 request, sometimes 2; 5 is only the worst case. search_backend_settings passes 1. No open task covers it: TASK-3060 (timeouts) and TASK-19830 (default-timeout session, LLM_Calls scope) are both Done and neither covers keep-alive here.

Separately, `_default_url_article_scraper` (local_media_reading_service.py:4484-4490) calls future.result() on a fresh ThreadPoolExecutor when a loop is running. That would block the loop if ever called from it, which is worth a check by whoever touches this path.

The sitemap helpers call scrape_article, which fails fast as above. The thread-local loop (:229-231) is created once per thread and reused while the thread lives. title: Academic provider lanes build a fresh httpx.Client per call (no pooling across queries/iterations)
trigger: Research run (Research window or Console deep research) -> per round, up to 5 sequential search_papers calls -> up to 10 concurrent provider lanes on to_thread workers, each constructing and closing its own httpx.Client. It is never on the event loop.
cost: Measured: httpx 0.28.1 Client() construction takes a median of 8.1 ms (min 7.9, max 9.7; n=20, isolated, no network), mostly SSL context and CA bundle load, on worker threads. Estimated: one TCP+TLS handshake per provider per query (about 100-300 ms wall, overlapped across concurrent lanes). Only queries 2-5 of a round within the 5 s keepalive could reuse connections, so the saving is at most about 1 s wall per round in a minutes-long LLM-bound run.
fix: Create one shared httpx.Client (with limits and timeouts) per search_papers call, or module-lazily, and pass it via the existing `client=` parameter to every lane. Close it at engine shutdown.
fix_notes: A client created per search_papers call gives no benefit (a distinct host per lane, each called once). To get any reuse, use one lazily created module- or engine-scoped client, closed at engine shutdown. Security risk: do NOT give the shared client follow_redirects=True just because OSF needs it. Semantic Scholar sends an x-api-key header, and a redirect-following shared client would reopen the cross-origin header leak that task-19557 closed. Pass follow_redirects=True per request for OSF only. A client shared across concurrent to_thread lanes relies on httpx/httpcore pool thread-safety, which works in practice. Keep per-request timeouts as they are (_request_with_retries passes timeout=). Low value overall; bundle it with other research-lane work instead of fixing it alone.

title: Assistant-anchor write (BEGIN IMMEDIATE) runs synchronously on the event loop at every agent-turn finalize
trigger: Once per agent send at finalize, on the loop, plus one metadata read per Stop.
cost: Measured the no-op-row UPDATE through set_run_assistant_message_id at 10.1 ms median; nearly all of it is the F7 admission floor. Lock waits behind a child's append_steps are normally a few ms, since writers hold the lock briefly; 5000 ms is only the busy_timeout ceiling. P2 holds because the write itself is sub-ms once F7 is fixed.
fix: In the controller, await asyncio.to_thread(self._agent_bridge.record_run_assistant_message, run_id, persisted). The publication_signal.anchor_published() bump is thread-safe and stays inside. Do the same for _latest_unanchored_primary_run_id on the stop path.
fix_notes: await asyncio.to_thread(self._agent_bridge.record_run_assistant_message, run_id, persisted) is safe: publication_signal is lock-protected and the wrapper's try/except must stay around the await. to_thread keeps running if the awaiting task is cancelled, which is acceptable for this bookkeeping write. Keep the await sequential so any later resume or stop read sees the anchor.
evidence:
# console_chat_controller.py:29065 (inside async _finalize_agent_success, on the loop)
self._record_run_assistant_message(run_id, completed)
# :29117 -> self._agent_bridge.record_run_assistant_message(run_id, persisted)
# console_agent_bridge.py:9753
self._db.set_run_assistant_message_id(run_id, persisted_message_id)   # with self.transaction(): BEGIN IMMEDIATE
# AgentRunsDB busy_timeout = 5000 ms
reason: _finalize_agent_success (controller :29001) is an async method awaited on the loop after run_reply returns from the maintenance/to_thread call (:28386-28392, :28792). _record_run_assistant_message (:29098-29123) calls bridge.record_run_assistant_message synchronously at :29117. That calls AgentRunsDB.set_run_assistant_message_id (AgentRuns_DB.py:2563-2579): transaction(), BEGIN IMMEDIATE, then a WAL commit. The failure, cancel and stop variants (:28595, :28766, :28892, :28933, :28963, :29056, :29065, :29080, :29091) run the same path. The stop path's latest_primary_run_metadata read (:29143, :19246) is also on the loop. Every Console send takes the agent path (agent_runtime_enabled defaults to True). The coverage is generic only: the TASK-32804 umbrella and TASK-2834.

title: _previous_primary_run_id full-hydrates every primary run to read the newest id; the metadata helper already exists
trigger: Every regenerate, retry or variant send: controller :28404 supersede_previous=bool(prepare_retry or variant_mode) -> bridge run_reply :7316-7319, on a to_thread worker.
cost: Isolated synthetic DB with 8 steps of ~600 B per run, median of 5 runs. list_runs(primary) took 7.4, 9.1 and 127 ms (noisy) at 30, 100 and 300 turns. latest_primary_run_metadata took 7.2, 7.2 and 12.3 ms. The delta grows with history, which is consistent with the finder's 18 vs 9.7 ms and 45 ms figures. The ~7 ms per-query floor is the shared per-statement overhead, not this finding's.
fix: record = self._db.latest_primary_run_metadata(conversation_id); return record["id"] if record else None. This is the same semantics that latest_primary_run_id already uses.
fix_notes: The fix is safe: the semantics are identical, including the kind filter in SQL and the tie-break ordering. It matches latest_primary_run_id at :9518. Coordinate with TASK-15662 (To Do), which plans to change the selection to the retried message's own run. That change should also stay metadata-only, e.g. a LIMIT 1 query on assistant_message_id, rather than re-introduce list_runs.
evidence:

    return records[0]["id"] if records else None

Trigger traced: the only supersede_previous=True caller is console_chat_controller.py:28404 (prepare_retry or variant_mode). run_reply is dispatched via _run_maintenance_agent_call, which uses asyncio.to_thread (controller ~:6607). So the cost is OFF the loop, but it runs before run_turn and adds straight to time-to-first-token on regenerate, retry and variant sends. No open task covers it. TASK-15662 (To Do) touches the same function for correctness only, not perf.

title: Console first paint constructs AgentRunsDB (schema init plus orphan reconcile) synchronously on the loop via the bridge-ensure path in compose_content (adjacent to slice)
trigger: First Console compose per process. Console is the default landing tab (default_tab="chat"), so this runs on every boot. compose_content -> _console_agent_section_lines -> _ensure_console_agent_bridge -> ensure_agent_bridge -> AgentRunsDB(), with reconcile_on_init=True, synchronously on the event loop.
cost: My isolated scratch benchmark (explicit scratch path, HOME/XDG/TLDW_CONFIG_PATH isolated) measured AgentRunsDB() on a fresh DB at 93-154 ms. Reopen plus reconcile on an empty DB took ~100 ms, and reopen with the path already swept took ~75 ms. cProfile shows ~43 ms in private_sqlite_process HelperLease.start (subprocess spawn) and ~74 ms in _initialize_schema. The finder's 303 ms on a 22.8 MB DB is consistent with TASK-32804.10's own 295 ms at 250k step rows for the reconcile scan. The historical-snapshot derive (F4/F12) is added on top before paint.
fix: This extends TASK-32804.10, whose AC#3 moved only the Settings compose site. Pre-warm ensure_activity_receipt_service via asyncio.to_thread at Console mount (or app deferred startup) with reconcile_on_init=False plus reconcile in a worker. Let compose render the rail's placeholder state when the bridge is not ready, then request the coalesced agent-fleet sync once it is.
fix_notes: 1) Pre-warming via asyncio.to_thread is compatible with the existing code: ensure_activity_receipt_service already closes the init connection when get_ident() != _receipt_owner_thread_id. However, ~28 synchronous _ensure_console_agent_bridge() call sites exist, including chat_screen.py:10154 controller construction and fleet.py:154 on mount. If any of them runs before the warm-up finishes, it either constructs on the loop anyway or blocks on _activity_receipts_lock. They all need a non-constructing accessor or must await the warm task. 2) A bridge of None currently renders 'Agent: unavailable', so a distinct loading state is needed. 3) With reconcile_on_init=False, the reconcile docstring (AgentRuns_DB.py:2389-2399) says no surface may observe a stale 'running' orphan before the sweep. The rail, fleet and wake paths must gate on sweep completion, as launch wake already does with wait_for_recovery. 4) The root cost is the unbounded terminal-history re-scan on every boot. Bound it, e.g. only rows lacking lifecycle capture via a flag or index, or a watermark, so an off-loop worker does not also grow forever.

agent_status_line, agent_steps_text, _ = self._agent._console_agent_section_lines()
# agent.py:982 -> self._console_runtime().ensure_agent_bridge(...)
# console_runtime.py:3548  if self.ensure_activity_receipt_service() is None ...
# :3492  runs_db = AgentRunsDB(Path(db_path).parent / "agent_runs.db")   # reconcile_on_init=True default
# docstring :3473: "Call via ``asyncio.to_thread`` from async presentation code."
reason: All cited lines check out. chat_screen.py:16357 is inside compose_content (def at :16204) and calls self._agent._console_agent_section_lines(). That reaches agent.py:1144 _ensure_console_agent_bridge, then :982 runtime.ensure_agent_bridge, then console_runtime.py:3548 ensure_activity_receipt_service, then :3492 AgentRunsDB(...) with the default reconcile_on_init=True. That runs base_db schema init, a private-sqlite helper subprocess spawn and reconcile_orphaned_runs (AgentRuns_DB.py:2359). The reconcile runs once per process (_swept_paths) and, inside BEGIN IMMEDIATE, selects EVERY terminal primary and subagent run in the whole DB (:2525-2528). It then batch-hydrates and json-parses every step payload (:2531), so the boot cost grows without bound with lifetime agent history. I grepped every caller of ensure_activity_receipt_service: only buddy_workspace.py:27 uses asyncio.to_thread. ensure_agent_bridge is called synchronously from agent.py:982, fleet.py:154 (mount-time _claim_console_fleet_wake_marks) and console_launch_wake.py:200 (an async task on the loop). The controller construction at chat_screen.py:10154 also ensures it synchronously. There is no pre-warm anywhere. The change-retention AgentRunsDB construction runs off-loop but only 65 s after startup (app.py:19010), so the Console compose is the first constructor. config.py:3713 default_tab = "chat", so this is the default boot landing path. TASK-32804.10 (In Progress) has AC#3 'Neither runs on the event loop from a compose path' ticked, but only the settings panel site (settings_agents_panel.py:143-144, reconcile_on_init=False) was changed. The Console compose site is untouched, so this is new scope and evidence against a claimed-done AC. The prior core review flagged the same seam as P3 [D3] (qa/core-code-review-2026-09-17/slices/CHAT-bridge.md:89), without the reconcile or any measurement, and it was never tasked. Upgraded to P0: measured at ≥~100 ms on boot, the default tab, before the Console's first paint, and it grows with history.

title: Raw-shell progress sink re-encodes the whole preview and reformats the marker on every output event, with no coalescing
trigger: Model shell_exec calls: controller :16879 wires agent_bridge.raw_shell_progress_sink, and it fires once per coalesced output chunk (≤20 Hz per stream) until the 32 KiB preview fills. Off the loop.
cost: Measured format_raw_cli_content at 0.22, 1.10 and 2.71 ms for 4, 16 and 32 KiB previews, and len(s.encode()) at 0.57 µs at 32 KiB. Worst case is a line-per-50 ms command filling 32 KiB over ~27 s: ~550 events averaging ~1.1 ms, so ~0.6 s of CPU off-loop (~2% of a core), plus the per-event O(transcript) store rebuild. Fast bursts produce few 8 KiB events and negligible cost.
fix: Track preview byte counts incrementally on _RawShellMarkerState. Throttle _update_raw_shell_marker to at most one update per ~100 ms (always flush on result or settle).
fix_notes: Tracking byte counts incrementally saves nothing measurable, so drop that half. The better fix is making _literal_terminal_text C-speed (str.translate with a precomputed control-char table, or a re.sub over [\x00-\x08\x0b-\x1f\x7f-\x9f]). A ~100 ms bridge-side throttle is fine if the result and settle paths always flush, but it only halves an already 20 Hz-capped rate. Keep the flush in _settle_raw_shell_marker so the terminal state is never dropped.
evidence:
# :10286 _append_raw_shell_preview
used = len(stdout.encode("utf-8")) + len(stderr.encode("utf-8"))
# :10457-10493 raw_shell_progress_sink, per RawCliStreamEvent, under _raw_shell_marker_lock:
#   state.stdout, state.stderr, clipped = self._append_raw_shell_preview(...)
#   self._update_raw_shell_marker(state)  -> format_raw_cli_content(whole preview) + store.update_tool_marker(...)
reason: The code matches: bridge :10286 re-encodes stdout and stderr, and raw_shell_progress_sink :10457-10493 calls _update_raw_shell_marker for every RawCliStreamEvent under _raw_shell_marker_lock. Two of the finding's premises are wrong, though. (a) 'No coalescing' is false: the producer (raw_cli_executor.py:90-92, 772-818 _CoalescingOutput) batches pipe reads into ≤8 KiB chunks flushed at most every 50 ms per stream. The executor's own _accept (:713-754) also caps the shared preview at 32 KiB and stops emitting text events after that. So the event rate is ≤~20/s per stream and the total is bounded. (b) The re-encode is negligible (measured 0.57 µs at 32 KiB). The real per-event cost is format_raw_cli_content -> _literal_terminal_text (console_raw_cli.py:73-80), a per-character Python generator join over the whole preview. Each event also runs store.update_tool_marker -> _recompute_active_path (console_chat_store.py:12044, :22020), an O(transcript) rebuild that bumps the display revision. It all runs on the executor or sink thread, off the loop; the loop only picks up changes on the 0.2 s poll, so loop-side cost is bounded at 5 Hz. The real residual is GIL-competing CPU during slow-trickling shell output.

title: Three independent full-hydration derivations of the same agent history run on the loop for one conversation open
trigger: Opening or resuming a saved conversation that has agent history: the resume path (workspace.py:6420), the next transcript sync (chat_screen.py:18284, on a revision-key miss) and the next rail sync (agent.py:~1250, on a historical-cache miss). All run on the event loop.
cost: Isolated synthetic DB with 8 steps of ~600 B per primary run and a subagent every 5th turn; DB-only median sum of the three derivations' queries. That came to ~84 ms at 30 turns, ~64 ms at 100 turns and ~384 ms at 300 turns, with a ~5-10 ms floor per statement. This is the same order as the finder's 73, 186 and 410 ms; my 100-turn figure is lower. Crossing 100 ms therefore needs a larger conversation than the finder states, but it scales with history on a common path.
fix: Introduce one per-conversation AgentHistoryView built off the loop (asyncio.to_thread) from metadata-first queries: primary anchors, last-N steps and count, direct children, change snapshots, and delivered notes, each read once. Cache it on the bridge keyed by (conversation_id, publication revision, run generation), and serve resume markers, change-review markers and the historical rail from it. This subsumes F1, F2, F4 and F9 in one PR.
fix_notes: resume_marker_messages genuinely needs every primary run's steps to rebuild markers, so a 'metadata-first' view cannot remove that hydration. It can only move it off the loop (the caller is already async, so wrap the DB read in asyncio.to_thread) and share it. Cheap independent wins: switch change_review_marker_messages to a metadata-only primary query (it never reads steps and currently hydrates subagents too), and make _derive_historical_snapshot use latest_primary_run plus a children-of-primary query. A single cached AgentHistoryView is medium risk: the three consumers invalidate differently (change-review publication revision, historical cache invalidated on in-process run start/finish, resume at open only), so a shared key can serve stale rail or markers. Folding F9 into the same PR is scope creep: F9 is a worker-thread send-path fix, not a conversation-open path.
evidence:
# one conversation open, all on the UI loop within the first ticks:
resume_marker_messages        -> list_runs(primary, hydrated) + change_snapshots + delivered_notes + local_command_resume_records
change_review_marker_messages -> list_runs(ALL kinds, hydrated) + change_snapshots_for_conversation (again)
_derive_historical_snapshot   -> list_runs(primary, hydrated) + list_runs(subagent, hydrated)
reason: I verified all three derivations and that each runs on the loop. (1) resume_marker_messages (:9900) is called from agent.py:2290 _inject_resume_agent_markers, which is called synchronously at workspace.py:6420-6425 inside async _resume_console_workspace_conversation. It queries list_runs(primary, hydrated) (:9957), change_snapshots_for_conversation, delivered_notes_for_conversation and local_command_resume_records. (2) change_review_marker_messages (:9874) is called from ConsoleChangeReviewProjection.project (UI/Console_Modules/transcript.py:117-137) inside async _sync_native_console_transcript (chat_screen.py:18284). It is cached on (conversation_id, publication revision), so it misses on open. It calls list_runs with NO kind filter, which hydrates steps for every primary AND subagent run, and then uses only agent_kind, id and assistant_message_id. It also re-runs change_snapshots_for_conversation. Caveat: it only runs when runtime.change_review_coordinator is not None, i.e. git is available. (3) _derive_historical_snapshot (:10596) is reached via historical_snapshot (:9410, cached per conversation, misses on first open) from _console_agent_section_lines (agent.py:~1250, the rail and poll path, when the live snapshot is idle). It hydrates ALL primary runs to use only [0] plus all subagent runs. None of the three is offloaded. No open task covers this: I grepped backlog/tasks for list_runs, AgentRunsDB, historical_snapshot and resume_marker_messages, and every hit is Done or unrelated. TASK-32804.12 and .6 do not mention it.

title: Every send re-audits every local skill's trust (dir scans + manifest HMAC + storage admission) on the event loop
trigger: Every manual send (async prompt_queue.dispatch -> sync _admit_console_turn_to_runtime on the loop), every queue add/edit, retry/regenerate/continue/edit/summarize via resolve_turn_configuration_snapshot, and fleet wakes. No thread offload anywhere on the chain.
cost: My isolated bench (real LocalSkillsService + SkillTrustService unlocked, CPU time via process_time because the machine was at load 38-55): 1 skill 78 ms, 5 skills 322 ms, 5 locked 230 ms at HOME depth 15. 2,661 posix.open per skill; 779k Python calls per 5-skill capture. At HOME depth 24: 21,135 opens and 1.05M calls, so the cost scales with the depth of the profile path, not the skill path. Fitting that gives about 48% of the opens and about 69% of the calls at a real ~/.local/share/tldw_cli/default_user (7 parts), i.e. about 40-55 ms per skill and about 100-200 ms for 5 skills per send. Consistent with the finder's quieter 196-261 ms wall time at scratch depth. Severity is P0 for users with 4 or more local skills and grows to 0.5 s or more at 20. Users with zero user skills pay about 0.
fix: (a) Cache the catalog snapshot per app, keyed on the index file mtime/generation, the trust-manifest generation and the builtin-disabled set; invalidate on skill mutations and trust changes. (b) Stop computing definition_digest for every skill at capture time. Compute it lazily in ensure_frozen_definition for the mentioned skill only, or reuse the fingerprints status_for_skill already scanned so each skill is scanned once, not twice. (c) Run the capture inside asyncio.to_thread from the async send and queue paths so a cache miss cannot freeze the UI. (d) Load the manifest once per capture instead of once per skill, which is O(S^2) today.
fix_notes: (a) A cache keyed only on index mtime + manifest generation misses out-of-band edits to skill files. The re-scan exists to detect tampering, so the key must include per-skill-dir stat (mtime_ns/ino/size of each file, or at least the dir tree), or the catalog must accept a stale verdict and rely on the execute-time ensure_skill_trusted/pin checks. State which. (b) Reusing the status scan's fingerprints for definition_digest is the cheapest, lowest-risk win: it halves the scans. (d) Loading the manifest once per capture is safe. (c) Offloading is riskier than stated. _admit_console_turn_to_runtime is deliberately synchronous (custody ordering), and the rest of the snapshot reads non-thread-safe store/session objects. Offload only the skill-trust file work, e.g. pre-capture via asyncio.to_thread in the async dispatch before calling the sync admission. The biggest lever is F8: the per-skill admission handshake itself.
reason: Code matches the pin: capture_skill_context_maximum (console_chat_controller.py:1300-1332) walks local._visible_records(), which re-reads the index JSON and the builtin SKILL.md. For each user skill it calls _summary_for_record -> _trust_fields_for_record -> trust_service.status_for_skill (skill_trust_service.py:477). That runs _execution_scope (acquire_storage per source path, execution_scope, local_content_lifetime.operation), then _load_valid_manifest (a full HMAC manifest load per skill, so O(S^2)), then _scan_skill. It then calls current_fingerprint_digest (@content_call admission plus a second _scan_skill). Nothing caches any of this. The app comment at app.py:8783 even says the loader 'runs on every skills read, including the Console's per-send capture'. Trigger traced: prompt_queue.dispatch (async, awaited from chat_screen._dispatch_console_draft_send) -> _stage_normal_chain -> _launch_chain (prompt_queue:996) -> wiring._admit_console_turn_to_runtime (sync, wiring:256-271) -> session._build_console_turn_execution_context (session:3603). It is also reached via _capture_configuration on queue/edit (prompt_queue:732/932/984) and via controller.resolve_runtime_turn_configuration_snapshot (22581) on retry/regenerate/continue/edit and fleet wake (console_runtime:2372). None of it is offloaded. Built-ins skip trust, so with zero user skills the cost is negligible. It scales linearly with user skills, with an O(S^2) manifest term. Not covered by any open task (grepped backlog for capture_skill_context/skill_context_maximum/_execution_scope: none). Extra detail: when trust is locked and a key cache exists, _try_cached_unlock also attempts a keyring read per status call. That read is mitigated by _cached_keyring_read's TTL cache.

title: Rest of the per-send turn snapshot does sync MCP-store, DB and manifest work on the loop, and two builders implement it
trigger: Same snapshot path as F1 (every send/queue/retry/regenerate/edit/wake), plus _compose_mcp_provider once per agent run (agent_runtime defaults to true; default Console sends compose MCP). All sync on the event loop.
cost: Measured with a real UnifiedMCPControlPlaneService(local_service=LocalMCPControlService(LocalMCPStore(user_data_dir/'local_mcp_store.json'))), profile isolated to scratch. capture_mcp_definition_maximum: 1.09M Python calls, 18,320 posix.open, 506 ms CPU (process_time) at HOME depth 15. At depth 24: 1.58M calls, 29,093 opens, 866 ms CPU. get_kill_switch alone: 383k calls, 6,306 opens, 138 ms CPU. describe_local_mcp_capabilities is only about 8 ms. Extrapolating to a real 7-part profile path gives roughly 190-330 ms per snapshot, then about the same again in _compose_mcp_provider per agent run. That is well past the P0 threshold for a default-config send. The machine was heavily loaded, so treat the absolute ms as ±2x; the call and open counts are load-independent.
fix: Read the permission store once per snapshot and pass the payload to both the kill-switch check and effective_tool_states. Memoise describe_local_mcp_capabilities, since it is a static manifest. Cache the MCP definition maximum keyed on the permission-store generation plus the external-catalog revision. Move the whole snapshot capture into asyncio.to_thread from the async send paths, keeping the thread-confined store reads on the loop. Collapse session._build_console_turn_execution_context and controller.resolve_runtime_turn_configuration_snapshot into one builder so each fix lands once. Reuse the snapshot's kill-switch and definition hashes in _compose_mcp_provider instead of re-reading.
fix_notes: The kill switch is security-sensitive. Do not reuse the snapshot's kill-switch value in _compose_mcp_provider: the fresh re-read there exists so a switch flipped between capture and dispatch takes effect. Make the read cheap instead (a stat-validated cache). The permission file is also written by other processes (mcp-unified stdio server, MCP hub), so a cache key must be the file's (st_mtime_ns, st_ino, st_size) plus the recovery selection, not an in-process generation counter. Loading the store once and passing the payload to both the kill-switch check and effective_tool_states is safe and immediate, as is memoising describe_local_mcp_capabilities (static). Moving the whole snapshot to to_thread conflicts with the synchronous custody-admission design and with non-thread-safe store/session reads, so offload only the MCP/skill file work. Collapsing the two builders is worthwhile but they differ (rag_defaults source_types, direct_library_tools source), so reconcile carefully. The dominant cost is the F8 admission handshake.

title: Capture-On trace-provenance admission runs a BEGIN IMMEDIATE write txn with N point reads on the event loop every send
trigger: Every MANUAL/QUEUED send with capture on (the default), and prepared continuations; sync inside an async method with no to_thread.
cost: I did not re-run the DB bench (it needs the full coordinator/repository wiring). The structure checks out: O(history) point SELECTs, a BEGIN IMMEDIATE, and one INSERT plus commit per send. The finder's 9.6-15.9 ms for 50-400 rows on a file DB is plausible and at the per-send P1 threshold. Under write-lock contention the wait is bounded only by busy_timeout, the same risk TASK-22205 documented.
fix: Run the transaction body through self._run_durable_db_call, which already handles the :memory: case and runs on a worker thread with operation_owned_connection. Compute the store.get_message(...) owner lookups and the sidecars on the loop first. Batch _current_revision into one SELECT ... WHERE live_message_id IN (...) chunked read. Reuse an existing FrozenTracePolicy row when the policy fields are unchanged instead of inserting one per send. TASK-31505 covers only the custom-PII subprocess inside this same transaction; this finding is the default no-PII path.
fix_notes: _run_durable_db_call runs the callable on a worker via _run_owned_chat_db_operation. The current transaction body calls self.store.get_message (not thread-safe) only in the pre-loop section, which is already outside the txn, so keep all store/provider_messages work on the loop and pass only ids and frozen values into the worker body. Batching _current_revision needs chunking under SQLite's variable limit. Reusing a policy row across sends changes provenance semantics (descriptors reference a per-request policy object and policy_id); confirm that trace readers and exports do not assume a unique policy per request before deduping. The PII branch (TASK-31505) must still compute redactions before the txn.

title: 0.2 s transcript tick calls context_control_inputs, re-running durable snapshots, branch-memory SQL and a recovery config scope on every tick
trigger: 5 Hz tick during any active run (and every event-driven native sync); unconditional call on the loop.
cost: Ran the finder's probe3 in my own isolated scratch (200 persisted messages, file DB): context_control_inputs = 60.5k Python calls and 842 posix.open per call; wall 49 ms under load 38-55 (_global_context_policy_overrides 33 ms, _select_session_effective_memory 13.7 ms, _durable_context_snapshots 2.4 ms). operation(config) alone is 11-12 ms CPU at scratch depth, 597 opens (939 at depth 24), about 49% of that at real depth. Cache _global_context_policy_overrides by config generation and drop the per-call operation(config) scope, since get_cli_setting is already cache-backed. Dropping the operation(config) wrapper changes the 'consistent 9-key snapshot' guarantee; caching the parsed overrides by config generation keeps that guarantee and is cheaper. Moving attachment digests to persist time also helps the send path (F6).

trigger: Per send (several full-transcript passes) and once per completed turn for the cost chip; cost is O(messages) and O(image bytes).

The finder's per-pass figure (2.28 ms per 400-message snapshot) matches my messages_for_session measurement of 1.46 ms at 200 messages under load, and the pass count of about 8-10 is consistent with the call sites I read. That gives about 18-23 ms per send at 400 messages, about 3 ms at 50, plus base64 and json-dump costs proportional to history images. Fingerprinting images by persisted digest changes the fingerprint format, so baselines computed before the change will report a spurious cache break once.

title: Root cause: recovery storage admission re-reads control records and re-opens every path component on each guarded call
trigger: Reached on every send (F1 skill trust scopes, F2 MCP kill-switch and store loads, F5 data-dir) and every 0.2 s Console tick during runs (F4 operation(config)).
cost: Measured (CPU time, isolated scratch, HOME depth 15 vs 24). get_user_data_dir 39 vs 74 ms. operation(config) 11 vs 27 ms. get_kill_switch 138 vs 350 ms. capture_mcp_definition_maximum 506 vs 866 ms. Open counts scale linearly with path depth: about 103 extra opens per component for get_user_data_dir and 870 for a 5-skill capture. Real 7-part profile estimate: about 48% of the opens and 55-69% of the Python calls at scratch depth. Aggregate admission overhead is at least about 200-400 ms per default send, so the root cause is P0 by the rubric. The pieces are already reported as F1, F2, F4 and F5; merge them rather than double-counting.
fix: Cache the parsed control-record registry and admission authority in memory, keyed on the admission directory's (st_mtime_ns, st_ino) and the registry.lock generation. Pin verified directory fds once per process or session instead of re-opening every component per call. At minimum, let read-only fast paths (config reads, store loads, trust status) skip the full admission once the profile is verified. This belongs to the Backup_Recovery owner, but it multiplies F1, F2, F4 and F5.
fix_notes: This is high risk: the admission layer is a TOCTOU and recovery-safety boundary, and cached fds or records can mask a concurrent restore or rollback. Safer first steps: (1) collapse nested re-acquisition, so a guarded call inside an active admission for the same source reuses the lease (the retained= plumbing already exists in observed()/_execution_scope); (2) cache the parsed control-record registry keyed on the control dir's (st_mtime_ns, st_ino) and the registry.lock generation, re-validated per call with one fstat; (3) only then consider long-lived pinned dir fds. Coordinate with TASK-32562's owner, who deliberately avoided caches, and extend TASK-32804.1's benchmark pin to the non-config seams.

#   bootstrap._control_records 945x (listdir + read every record, no cache)
#   private_paths._open_verified_parent 1800x (open each path component)
# operation(config): ~600 open() per call; get_user_data_dir(): ~1,590 open() per call
reason: Profiled the hot seams myself. One 5-skill capture: acquire_storage (storage_admission.py:835) 45 calls, control_records.admission_authority 45, bootstrap._control_records (161) 315 calls (listdir plus read of every record each time), bootstrap.pinned_directory 1,200, private_paths._open_verified_parent (434) 600, and 8,685 native opens. One unified-service get_kill_switch: 3 nested mcp_source_participants.guarded wrappers, 16 recovery_activation.selected_path, 34 observed(), 20 acquire_storage and 6,306 opens. operation(config) (config_participants.py:295) is about 600 opens; get_user_data_dir is 1,590. There is no memo of the parsed control records or admission authority, and every nested guarded layer re-acquires. This one mechanism is what makes F1, F2, F4 and F5 expensive, so fixing it once collapses all four. TASK-32562 (the Backup_Recovery owner's in-progress program) records 'no cache or production deadline changes', so this needs owner coordination.

title: Per-session controller maps are never pruned on session close; run-state history grows unbounded with no production reader
trigger: Every provider turn calls _watch_post_turn_usage (28575 stop path, 28750 normal finalizer). Closing a session goes through finalize_session_close, which leaves the watch entry and the other per-session maps in place. Growth follows the number of sessions closed over the app's lifetime, driven by user actions. It is not a timer or a per-tick cost.
cost: Estimated, not measured. Per closed session the leak is roughly the size of that session's last request payload: the full history as sent (hundreds of KB for a long context) plus any attached image bytes (can be MB). Opening and closing tens of long or image-bearing sessions in one app run gives tens of MB. The history lists and small maps are negligible (bytes per turn). This is P2: it scales with data size and session count and is not a constant tax.
fix: In finalize_session_close, pop session_id from every per-session map (one helper listing them). Cap _run_state_histories to the last N statuses, or delete it if only tests read it. Clear _post_turn_usage_watch on close.
fix_notes: The biggest win with the smallest diff: drop the back-reference once dispatch recovery no longer needs it, by setting signals._trace_preparation = None after the provider call settles (or storing a weakref). That frees the continuation for live sessions too. Then, in finalize_session_close, pop session_id from _post_turn_usage_watch, _run_states, _run_state_histories, _context_accounting_by_session, _payload_fingerprint_baselines, _cache_warm_until, _cache_last_activity, _micro_compaction_counters and _ordinary_outcome_ids. Do NOT pop the fence counters _session_lifecycle_revisions or _session_close_generations. They are monotonic generation fences (6529-6548, and release_session_close_fences deliberately leaves the generation latched on timeout), and resetting them to 0 risks an ABA match for a restored session with the same id. finalize runs only after the drain, so dropping the watch there does not lose fleet re-attach money: _fleet_usage_reattach_sources is keyed separately and popped on drain. Delete _run_state_histories outright (no production reader) and rewrite the 4 tests that read it, rather than capping it. Tests/Chat/test_console_run_state_per_session.py pins orphan retention in run_states(), but it closes sessions through store.close_session directly, so a pop in finalize_session_close does not break it.
evidence:
self.run_state_history_for(target).append(run_state.status)   # every transition, never trimmed
# grep pop/del/clear counts: _run_states 0, _run_state_histories 0, _payload_fingerprint_baselines 0,
#   _cache_warm_until 0, _cache_last_activity 0, _context_accounting_by_session 0,
#   _micro_compaction_counters 0, _session_lifecycle_revisions 0, _ordinary_outcome_ids 0

Line 4848 declares _run_state_histories. finalize_session_close (14228-14270) pops only _session_close_states, _chat_create_session_grants and _active_citation_repair_sessions, then calls prompt_queue_coordinator.remove_session and _clear_project_instruction_delivery. Untruncated greps over the controller find no pop, del or clear for _run_states, _run_state_histories, _payload_fingerprint_baselines, _cache_warm_until, _cache_last_activity, _context_accounting_by_session, _micro_compaction_counters or _ordinary_outcome_ids. _post_turn_usage_watch is popped only at 26425, and only when stream_signals is None. run_state_history and run_state_history_for have zero production callers outside their own definitions (a repo-wide grep of tldw_chatbook finds none; 4 test files read them), so the history list is write-only in production. The finder under-rated the retained size. _post_turn_usage_watch[sid] holds the turn's ConsoleProviderStreamSignals. Its _trace_preparation field is set by provider_gateway._bind_trace_preparation (console_provider_gateway.py:3027, controller 12635-12641) to _TraceAcceptedPreparation(owner=continuation), and nothing ever resets it. title: Session-tab markers are O(S^2): run_marker_for re-derives the busy set over all sessions per tab, per 0.2 s tick
trigger: 5 Hz on the event loop while any Console run is active (set_interval(0.2) timer, self-stopping when idle). Also runs on every event-driven _sync_native_console_chat_ui (session switch, send, resume).
cost: The finder measured 0.03, 0.23 and 1.03 ms for 5, 15 and 30 sessions; I did not re-measure. The quadratic shape is plausible from the code. At a realistic 3-10 tabs it is well under 0.2 ms per tick, and at 30 tabs about 0.5% of a core during runs. P3 is correct.

fix_notes: Compute the busy set once per sync: add run_markers_for(session_ids) that calls _live_busy_session_ids() once and applies the same NEEDS_APPROVAL > RUNNING > unvisited precedence. Build one {sid: activity_for(sid)} map per tick and reuse it for queue_counts. Keep the approvals snapshot under _approval_state_lock as fleet_summary_counts does. Caching on _lifecycle_revision is riskier: run-state writes in _set_run_state do not obviously advance that revision, so a stale busy set could show a wrong glyph.
reason: The code matches. run_marker_for (7242) calls self._live_busy_session_ids() at 7277 for every session that has no pending approval. _live_busy_session_ids (6950) rebuilds {s.id for s in store.sessions()} (a list copy, console_chat_store.py:5171) and calls activity_for(sid) for every session. Each activity_for takes a store lock (dispatch_recovery_needs_queue_hydration), builds a registry.snapshot and constructs a ConsoleControllerActivity dataclass. fleet.py:274 calls _console_run_marker_with_unseen, then run_marker_for (wired at wiring.py:1408-1411), once per session, so the total is S*(S+1) activity_for calls. chat_screen.py:18846 adds another S activity_for calls for queue_counts, and fleet_summary_counts plus the poll gate in_flight_run_count add further passes. The trigger is real: _start_console_transcript_sync_timer uses set_interval(0.2) (chat_screen.py:18947) and runs _sync_native_console_chat_ui, which calls _sync_console_native_session_tabs (18764). The timer runs only while _console_transcript_poll_needed() is true, i.e. during active runs, wake delivery or pending review. No matching open task: TASK-31506 covers the session-switcher modal, not the tab strip, and grep of backlog/tasks for run_marker_for, _live_busy_session_ids and prepare_session_run_markers finds only Done tasks unrelated to performance.

title: Maintenance/trace-dispatch waits sleep-poll the loop at 20-50 Hz instead of awaiting an event
trigger: The dispatch wait spins only when a send reaches provider dispatch while a physical trace compaction holds the pause, which is rare. The drain spins only inside a backup or maintenance window.
cost: 20-50 loop wakeups per second, only during those rare windows. Negligible steady-state cost. Estimated, not measured.
fix: Replace the threading.Event flag with a paired asyncio.Event (set and clear via loop.call_soon_threadsafe) and await it. For the drain, await asyncio.wait on the retained task set with a timeout.
fix_notes: pause() and resume() are called from a worker thread (inside run_owned_db_call), so a paired asyncio.Event must be set and cleared through loop.call_soon_threadsafe, with the owning loop captured up front. The resume in finally must still reach waiters even when the loop is shutting down. For the drain, the finder's asyncio.wait on 'the retained task set' is wrong for _maintenance_calls. That map is dict[asyncio.Task, int], a per-caller-task depth counter (4311-4338), and the caller task can outlive its maintenance call (for example a whole turn). Waiting for that task to complete would over-wait, or deadlock if that task is the one awaiting. It needs an event signalled when the depth drops to 0. Given the negligible benefit and that about 10 participants share the pattern, either fix it once in a shared helper or leave it.
reason: The code matches. _wait_for_trace_maintenance_dispatch (5589-5593) loops `while self._trace_maintenance_dispatch_paused.is_set(): await asyncio.sleep(0.05)`, and its callers are 27038 and 28287 on the dispatch path. maintenance_drain (6555-6568) sleep-polls at min(remaining, 0.02). pause and resume are driven only by PhysicalTraceCompactor.run_after_gc (console_trace_maintenance.py:236-250), which the legacy trace-maintenance loop reaches through run_owned_db_call (console_runtime.py:3324-3380). That is a worker-thread call, which is why this is a threading.Event. The pause window is short (idle, lease and physical compaction only), and the compaction defers when a provider is active. maintenance_drain is a duck-typed maintenance-participant hook, called only during backup or maintenance windows. The same sleep-poll drain pattern is repeated in about 10 other participants (TTS, STT, dictation, audio_cpp and others). Real, but cold: this is hygiene. No matching open task (TASK-31501 is the 1 Hz write-lock poll, not this wait).
